context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: # II. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich,  98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z vs Z) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

context.text: Fig. 1. (Color online) TG-DSC profile of the Li7La3Zr2O12 precursor solution.

Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

context.text: Fig. 2. (Color online) X-ray diffraction pattern of Li7La3Zr2O12.

The XRD patterns of the samples are shown in Fig. 2. Analyses of the patterns confirmed the cubic structure. The LLZO sample was synthesized successfully, and the XRD patterns matched well with the reference pattern obtained from the database (PDF 01-080-9103). The lattice parameter of the sample was found to be a = 12.9827 ˚A. However, peaks associated with an impurity of La0.5Zr0.5O1.75 were also observed in the XRD patterns. This impurity was formed by volatilization of Li.

The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = L(A R) , where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 × 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 × 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

context.text: Fig. 4. (Color online) (a) Nyquist plots of Li7La3Zr2O12 measured at 25 ◦C, (b) the equivalent circuit model used to fit the impedance data and (c) Arrhenius plot for the total conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12.

Figure 4(c) shows the temperature dependence of the total ionic conductivity (Arrhenius plot) of the LLZO pellets at temperatures of 25 - 70 ◦C, where the Arrhenius equation is given by σ = AT exp - −EakBT  , where σ is the ionic conductivity, T is the absolute temperature, A is the pre-exponential constant, kB is the Boltzmann constant and Ea is the activation energy for the ionic conductivity. The activation energy determined from the slope of the log (σT ) versus 1/T plot for the total conductivity of the sample is 0.53 eV. The activation energy for the LLZO material is lower (0.53 eV) than that for the reference LLZO material (0.67 eV) [26]. The lower activation energy is due to a transition from the tetragonal to the cubic phase, and the lower activation energy can improve the conductivity by facilitating the movement of lithium ions [27].

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

matches.text: Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

After drying at 80°C for 24 hours, the powders were cold pressed into pellets (10 mm in diameter and 1–3 mm in thickness) at a pressure of 200 MPa. The pellets were covered with cover powders, placed in a modified alumina crucible (shown in Figure 1b), with an alumina lid and sintered in air with a heating rate of 1°C/min to 1100°C for 1–32 hours. The detailed procedure for the preparation of LLZTO is shown in Figure 1a.

During sintering the pellets were covered with powders to reduce the loss of lithium. Four columns, with four pellets in each column, of samples were sintered at one time. Only the middle two pellets were used as the bottom pellet was in contact with the crucible and the top pellet exhibited different sintering behavior, presumably because the atmosphere was different as it was closer to the air above the cover powder. Two kinds of cover powders were used. One is referred to 15Li, which is the powder after the heat-treatment of 700°C and before the ball milling and with 15 wt% excess LiOH. The other one is referred to 15Li LiOH, which is a mixture of 15Li and 6 wt% LiOH. This mixture was jar milled for 12 hours before the use in sintering. The notches in the crucible were found to be necessary (Figure S1 in Supporting Information) to allow an optimal amount of gas exchange between inside of the crucible and surrounding atmosphere to establish the local gas atmosphere to promote the sintering behavior.

context.text: Samples with excess Li added in two different steps were fabricated in this work. One group of samples has the excess LiOH added only at the 1st step of the co-precipitation process. The other group has the excess LiOH added in two steps, the first is during the coprecipitation process and the second is the ball milling process. No significant differences in the phase content, morphology and conductivity were observed between adding the Li in one or two steps (Figure S2-S5 and Table S2 in Supporting Information), so results for only one case will be presented. In this work, 25Li and 75Li samples have the excess Li added in one step, while 30Li and 65Li samples all have the excess Li added in two different steps (details of the amount of excess LiOH added during different steps are shown in Table S1 in Supporting Information).

Material characterizations.—The phase content was determined using X-ray diffraction (XRD) with a Bruker D8 diffractometer with a Cu X-ray source at 40 mA and 40 kV. Morphology and elementary mapping were obtained by using a JEOL JSM-7000F scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and a backscattered electron (BSE) detector. The density of the sintered pellet was measured by the Archimedes method in ethanol. The relative density value was determined by dividing the bulk density by the theoretical density of tetragonal LLZO ( 5.108 g/cm3).17 The chemical analyses of the Li, Al, La and Zr content were carried out by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) (Perkin Elmer Model Optima 4300DV). Conductivity was measured by AC impedance spectroscopy using a frequency response analyzer (Solartron 1260) in the frequency range 0.5 Hz-30 MHz and an amplitude of 50 mV. The silver electrodes were fabricated by coating silver paste (Silver Paste Plus from SPI Supplies, 72% silver solids) on both sides of the pellet and curing at room temperature for 2 hours. The impedance spectra were fit to equivalent circuit models using ZView software.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.

A small amount of LiOH in the cover powder (3 wt% LiOH) led to nonuniform shrinkage, while with a cover powders containing 100 wt% LiOH all pellets melted and stuck to the crucible. The LiOH 15Li mixture (6:94 by weight) cover promoted uniform sintering of pellets and resulted in desirable lithium ion conductivity from LLZTO.

SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

The possible mechanism for the densification of LLZTO.—To study the possible mechanism for the effect of LiOH in the cover powder on the densification of LLZTO, 65Li pellets were sintered at the same sintering temperature of 1100°C for different sintering times. SEM and back scattered electron (BSE) images of fracture cross sections of 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 hours with the cover powder of 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 7.

After sintering for 1 hour (Figure 7a), there are connected pores and many small grains with sizes of 2–3 μm connected by an interparticle phase. After sintering for 4 hours (Figure 7c), the grains grew and became better connected. After 8 hours (Figure 7d), the grains have continued to grow, and the pores were reduced and did not appear to be connected. As also shown in BSE images in Figures 7g–7h, in which the interparticle phase is darker than the grains, it is found that the grain size increased, the amount of the interparticle phase decreased and the samples are still porous after the sintering of 1 hour to 8 hours (Figures 7a–7d). There is little change between 8, 16 and 32 hours sintering, as shown in Figures 7d–7f.

Tantalum appears to be relatively uniformly distributed in the sample. Compositions from ICP analysis of 65Li sintered with different cover powders and different sintering times are listed in Table IV, atomic ratio of Li:Al:La:Zr is normalized by La content as shown in the formula of Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12. The ICP analysis, which presents the overall sample composition, indicates that Al exists in all LLZTO samples, but that the amount of aluminum is higher and increases with increasing time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover. In addition, the Li content is lower in the sample sintered with 15Li cover powder than that with 15Li + LiOH cover. These results suggest that the 15Li + LiOH cover powder reduces the loss of Li and promotes the transfer of aluminum from the crucible to the sample.

The RT total Li+ conductivities of 65Li pellets sintered for 4 to 32 hours are shown in Figure 9. The conductivity increases significantly after 4 hours sintering, and it does not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. The relative densities of these pellets shown in Table V follows a similar trend to that of the total Li+ conductivities. The relative density is only 61% for pellets sintered for 4 hours, and it is larger than 80% for 8 to 32 hours. Samples sintered for 16 and 32 hours have similar relative density of 90%. As shown in Table IV, the amount of aluminum increases with increasing sintering time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover, and aluminum only exists at the phases between grains (Figure 8), it is concluded that the amount of Al-containing phase in the dense pellets also increases with the sintering time. The increased amount of Al-containing phase may be one reason that the conductivity does not increase as much as might be expected from the relative density change from 83 to 90%.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: Fig. 1. (Color online) TG-DSC profile of the Li7La3Zr2O12 precursor solution.

Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. context.text: The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = L(A R) , where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 × 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 × 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

matches.text: LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: Fig. 1. (Color online) TG-DSC profile of the Li7La3Zr2O12 precursor solution.

Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

context.text: The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = (ALR), where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

Figure 4(c) shows the temperature dependence of the total ionic conductivity (Arrhenius plot) of the LLZO pellets at temperatures of 25 - 70 ◦C, where the Arrhenius equation is given by σ = TA exp  k−BETa , where σ is the ionic conductivity, T is the absolute temperature, A is the pre-exponential constant, kB is the Boltzmann constant and Ea is the activation energy for the ionic conductivity. The activation energy determined from the slope of the log (σT ) versus 1/T plot for the total conductivity of the sample is 0.53 eV. The activation energy for the LLZO material is lower (0.53 eV) than that for the reference LLZO material (0.67 eV) [26]. The lower activation energy is due to a transition from the tetragonal to the cubic phase, and the lower activation energy can improve the conductivity by facilitating the movement of lithium ions [27].

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2, 5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 × 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g  1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g  0.94) and Li(2) site (g  0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

context.text: Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2, 5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 × 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g  1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g  0.94) and Li(2) site (g  0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 × 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I. 51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li SiO to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta O powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li  LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li  LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: # II. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich,  98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z vs Z) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z vs Z) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

context.text: Fig. 2. (Color online) X-ray diffraction pattern of Li7La3Zr2O12.

The XRD patterns of the samples are shown in Fig. 2. Analyses of the patterns confirmed the cubic structure. The LLZO sample was synthesized successfully, and the XRD patterns matched well with the reference pattern obtained from the database (PDF 01-080-9103). The lattice parameter of the sample was found to be a = 12.9827 ˚A. However, peaks associated with an impurity of La0.5Zr0.5O1.75 were also observed in the XRD patterns. This impurity was formed by volatilization of Li.

The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = L(A R) , where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 × 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 × 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.
