Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: Samples with excess Li added in two different steps were fabricated in this work. One group of samples has the excess LiOH added only at the 1st step of the co-precipitation process. The other group has the excess LiOH added in two steps, the first is during the coprecipitation process and the second is the ball milling process. No significant differences in the phase content, morphology and conductivity were observed between adding the Li in one or two steps (Figure S2-S5 and Table S2 in Supporting Information), so results for only one case will be presented. In this work, 25Li and 75Li samples have the excess Li added in one step, while 30Li and 65Li samples all have the excess Li added in two different steps (details of the amount of excess LiOH added during different steps are shown in Table S1 in Supporting Information).

Material characterizations.—The phase content was determined using X-ray diffraction (XRD) with a Bruker D8 diffractometer with a Cu X-ray source at 40 mA and 40 kV. Morphology and elementary mapping were obtained by using a JEOL JSM-7000F scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and a backscattered electron (BSE) detector. The density of the sintered pellet was measured by the Archimedes method in ethanol. The relative density value was determined by dividing the bulk density by the theoretical density of tetragonal LLZO ( 5.108 g/cm3).17 The chemical analyses of the Li, Al, La and Zr content were carried out by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) (Perkin Elmer Model Optima 4300DV). Conductivity was measured by AC impedance spectroscopy using a frequency response analyzer (Solartron 1260) in the frequency range 0.5 Hz-30 MHz and an amplitude of 50 mV. The silver electrodes were fabricated by coating silver paste (Silver Paste Plus from SPI Supplies, 72% silver solids) on both sides of the pellet and curing at room temperature for 2 hours. The impedance spectra were fit to equivalent circuit models using ZView software.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: # II. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich, 98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z′ vs Z′′) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

The XRD patterns of the samples are shown in Fig. 2. Analyses of the patterns confirmed the cubic structure. The LLZO sample was synthesized successfully, and the XRD patterns matched well with the reference pattern obtained from the database (PDF 01-080-9103). The lattice parameter of the sample was found to be a = 12.9827 ˚A. However, peaks associated with an impurity of La0.5Zr0.5O1.75 were also observed in the XRD patterns. This impurity was formed by volatilization of Li.

The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = (ALR), where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

Figure 4(c) shows the temperature dependence of the total ionic conductivity (Arrhenius plot) of the LLZO pellets at temperatures of 25 - 70 ◦C, where the Arrhenius equation is given by σ = TA exp  k−BETa , where σ is the ionic conductivity, T is the absolute temperature, A is the pre-exponential constant, kB is the Boltzmann constant and Ea is the activation energy for the ionic conductivity. The activation energy determined from the slope of the log (σT ) versus 1/T plot for the total conductivity of the sample is 0.53 eV. The activation energy for the LLZO material is lower (0.53 eV) than that for the reference LLZO material (0.67 eV) [26]. The lower activation energy is due to a transition from the tetragonal to the cubic phase, and the lower activation energy can improve the conductivity by facilitating the movement of lithium ions [27].

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

(1) is replaced with (n + n0 − αnx − xc)µ , where n and n0 are the respective numbers of Li atoms and vacancies in the crystal lattice unit.[151] Besides, the 2D conduction mechanism is found at relatively lower temperature directly by neutron powder diffraction study,[152] while higher temperatures increase the oxygen vibration and open up the originally blocked bottleneck to enable the third dimension for Li-ion diffusion[153] and delocalizes Li ions from the 2D La-poor layer to realize a higher degree of disorder.[154] Considering the quasi-2D conduction mechanism and the preferential La distribution, equation (1) can be further revised as: σ ∝ neff(n0 − nc)µ = 12x(1 − 12x)(0.5 − g(La2))1.3.[152] The deviation from Arrhenius can be explained by the long-range correlation of mobile carriers, which can be inferred both from the abnormal activation energy measured by IS.[153,155] as well as from activation energy discrepancies between IS and measurements of 7Li NMR spin-lattice relaxation.[156] The total conductivity of Li3xLn2/3−x[U + FFFF]1/3−2xTiO3 is limited by grain boundary resistance, which can be reduced by high temperature sintering; however, the high-temperature, longduration thermal process leads to Li evaporation, making accurate control of Li content difficult. Therefore, this system can hardly be applied in all-solid-state batteries.

The Li-ion compounds Li5La3M2O12 (M = Ta, Nb), with garnet structure, were reported in 1988, and the structure was examined by x-ray diffraction, without knowing the Li distribution, due to limited experimental resolution of Li atoms.[157] However, this system did not attract much attention as a solid electrolyte until 2003, when Thangadurai and Weppner found that it is a good Li-ion conductor with high conductivity and a wide electrochemical window.[158] In contrast to the common perovskite or NASICON solid state electrolyte, the garnet family excludes Li-reducible Ti4+, so it can directly contact Li metal without damage, which has been viewed as its distinguishing advantage.[159] In 2004, Thangadurai and Weppner, together with Adams, used the bond valence sum method to verify the structure, and they minimized the mismatch of the Li-bond valence state as the isosurface to map the conduction pathways visually. It was concluded that Li ions occupy the octahedral sites other than tetrahedral vacancies.[160] The Li-ion occupation pattern is of great importance for understanding the diffusion mechanism but was not located precisely until 2006, by Cussen. It was revealed from neutron powder diffraction data that Li ions occupy both tetrahedral (80%) and octahedral sites (43%), and the latter are responsible for the mobile carriers via a clustering mechanism.[161] NMR results indicate that the Liion distribution depends on the annealing temperature; that is, the high annealing temperature implies that more Li ions can be quenched at the octahedral sites as mobile carriers, which leads to higher ionic conductivity.[162] In 2012, Han and Yusheng Zhao utilized variable-temperature neutron diffraction (HTND), combined with the maximum-entropy method (MEM) for data refining, to estimate the Li nuclear-density distribution and visualize the conduction pathway experimentally for the first time. These results confirm that displacement is directly driven by temperature.[163] More efforts in calculation have gradually elucidated the Li-ion diffusion mechanism; for example, conductivity and distinct mechanisms for different M elements and various Li concentrations,[164] structural phase transition,[165] concerted[166,167] or asynchronous phenomena,[168] point defects,[169] local structure and dynamics performance,[170] often in combination with experimental data. Other efforts focused on enhancing conductivity. Substituting and doping with lower-valence elements, e.g., replacing La by Sr[171] or Ba,[172] replacing M (= Nb, Ta) partly[173] or totally[174] by Zr, can increase Li content and thus improve conductivity. The highest conductivity found was 4 × 10−4 S/cm in Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO),[174] the most attractive composition so far. LLZO has cubic and tetragonal phases. Cubic phase LLZO has higher conductivity and can be synthesized by doping Al or Ga, or by pulsed laser annealing.[175–179] Cubic phase thin film can be obtained from epitaxial growth[180] or aerosol deposition (AD).[181] The latter method prevents the electrolyte from reacting with the active electrode by avoiding the annealing process, although the obtained electrolyte exhibits extremely low conductivity (1.0 × 10−8 S/cm@140 ◦C) and worse cyclic performance if applied in all-solid-state batteries. Nebulized spray pyrolysis results in a thin-film hybrid of both phases.[182] The disadvantages of LLZO used in sandwich-structure all-solidstate batteries include high interface resistance and poor cyclic stability,[183] both of which can be ameliorated by introducing a thin Nb interlayer between the electrolyte and cathode (LiCoO2).[184]

In 2012, a novel class of solid electrolyte, called lithiumrich anti-perovskites (LiRAP) was reported by Zhao et al.[185] LiRAP is named for the following reasons: It has a structure similar to perovskites with electronically-inverted ions located in the corresponding lattice sites. In other words, as compared with the traditional perovskite ABX3, X is occupied by Li+ with positive charge, leading to a high concentration of Li ions (i.e., “Li rich”), A and B by halogen− (F−, Cl−, Br−, I−) and chalcogen2− (O2−, S2−) separately with negative charges.[185] Almost at the same time, Li3OCl happened to be discovered as a byproduct during synthesizing Li5OCl3.[186] In the following year, phase diagram calculation results indicated that Li3OCl was in a less stable state (metastable phase) than Li2O and LiA (A = Cl, Br) at 0 K[187] and could be stabilized by exerting a certain temperature.[187,188] By accommodating dopants and substitutions (e.g., halogen mixing, Li sites doped by higher-valence-state elements, and depletion of lithium halides) as well as local disorder from thermal treating process without phase transition, (anti-) perovskite has greater tolerance for structure modulation[189] to ensure structural stability and enhance conductivity. In this case, Li3OCl0.5Br0.5 has room temperature conductivity of 6.05 × 10−3 S/cm.[185]

context.text: Another promising system is about sulfide solid state electrolytes with the high conductivity and negligible grain boundary, even when prepared by cold pressing. The main limitation of the system is its stability to electrodes, including the (electro)chemical reaction and space charge layer problems. One effective solution is to apply different solid state electrolytes to satisfy various demands of cathodes and anodes,[100,132,345] and another is to introduce the buffer layer into the interface between the electrode and electrolyte.[349–351]

Considering the environmental safety of the fabricating process and practical applications, oxides often attract the more extensive attention. However, oxides usually have high grain boundary resistance, and the higher density with less grain boundary can only be obtained by sintering at high temperature for a long time, resulting in higher cost. Replacing the ceramic by glass or glass-ceramic is an effective and economical way to eliminate the grain boundaries.[75–78] In addition, oxides usually have higher mechanical strength, leading to the point contact with electrodes and high interface resistance. One solution is to mix the oxides and sulfides together and take advantage of both of them: low resistance of bulk and grain boundary, together with high chemical stability, and can be fabricated by cold pressing with the lower cost. In addition, the good ductility of the mixture contributes to the better physical contact with electrodes.[335] As for the NASICON and perovskite families, the compositions with highest conductivity usually contain Ti4+, which is not stable to anodes with low potential.[343,344] LLZO in the garnet family has relatively high conductivity, free from Ti, resulting in good chemical stability. However, when LLZO is applied in an allsolid-state battery, the interface resistance is usually very high due to the bad physical contact and space charge layer effect. Also, another reason was proposed by a recent study, which indicates that low conductivity can arise from the formation of Li2CO3 in the condition of humidity.[356] If this is so, smaller bulk and more boundaries can increase the conductivity, and fine control of structure can be realized during the preparation process.[357]

For inorganic materials, the interface contact resistance is always a difficult problem. In addition, despite the higher hardness of inorganic materials, they are short of flexibility, which causes many challenges in the practical applications of full cells: How to match the volume change with electrodes during the Li ions’ intercalating/deintercalating? How to match the thermal expansion arising from the increase of temperature under work? For (hybrid) electrical vehicles and other mobile devices, how to solve the ceramic fragmentation and short circuit problems ascribed to sudden shock? Considering all the problems above, organic polymers have unrivalled superiority in the aspects of flexibility and elasticity. Combining the advantages of polymers and ceramics may be the silver bullet.[266,358–361] Common polymers used today have a narrow electrochemical window and low conductivity, and the large volume fraction restricts the energy density. In contrast, liquid electrolytes (including organic electrolytic solution and ionic liquid) promise to reach higher conductivity. In addition, they may have better wettability of electrodes, and can improve the contact performance greatly by adding a relatively small amount in response to the safety problem (for organic electrolytic solution). Therefore, the composition of liquid and solid may be a further direction for research.[362]

Garnet-type metal oxide such as Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is considered as one of the most promising solid electrolytes among the inorganic solid electrolytes4, for it shows high Li+ ionic conductivity, high stability with lithium metal and wide electrochemical window5. The sintering process6, doping strategy7-9, microstructure10 and composite design11 have been widely investigated to enhance its performance. The LLZO solid electrolyte can be synthesized by solid state reaction12, sol-gel method13, spark plasma sintering14 and hot-press sintering method15. Solid state reaction at high temperature is preferred because the cost is relatively low and the procedure is simple, which is suitable for large-scale industrial producing. The LLZO electrolyte sample prepared by solid state reaction has a moderate ionic conductivity in the order of 10-4 S/cm. Doping various elements into LLZO can increase the Li-ion conductivity and the Ta doped sample, Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12(x=0.6), has an ionic conductivity of about 1×10-3 S/cm 16, 17. However, because of the high volatility nature of Li element, Li is easy to lose during the high temperature sintering which leads to form the undesirable La2Zr2O7 as an impure phase. In order to prepare the stoichiometric LLZO, the lost Li should be compensated and the most common means is to cover the tablet samples up with the mother powder 18. The mother powder with the same chemistry composition as the samples acts as the sacrificial component to ensure the sample to form the right garnet phase. The amount of the sacrificed mother powder usually reaches the ratio 1:1 in weight to the samples and after sintering, the mother powder cannot be reused. That is the problem, as we know that the mother powder contains the rare earth element La and the element Ta that are expensive. Therefore, the conventional solid state reaction with mother powder protecting method is not economical. We noticed that the effect of the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

mother powder is merely providing another Li source to compensate the lost Li. We proposed an alternative method to compensate the lost Li where the mother powder is replaced by Li2CO3. In this method, Li2CO3 is separated from the sample and it will melt and decompound above 730ºC. The decomposed Li2CO3 provides a Li2O atmosphere and ensures the sample to form the pure garnet phase. The method is also suitable for other oxide solid electrolytes. Li2CO3 is much cheaper than the mother powder and this method will lower the synthesis cost of LLZO as well as other oxide solid electrolytes, which is important for the large-scale application of the solid state batteries in the future.

LLZO is usually prepared by solid-state reaction at high temperature above 1100 °C. In the experiment, Al2O3 was added to the preheated powders as a sintering aid that will form a liquid of LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4 eutectic 19. As Li2CO3 is much more excessive, the sintering temperature might be lowered. We prepared the LLZTO samples with 1g Li2CO3 providing the protective atmosphere (L1 sample) at different temperatures. Fig.3 (a) shows the XRD patterns of L1 samples prepared at 1060°C, 1100°C and 1140°C respectively. All these samples have LLZTO as the main phase and there exists LiAlO2 phase. As it can be seen in the patterns, the intensity of LiAlO2 increases as temperature increasing and the samples prepared at 1140°C contain considerable amount of LiAlO2. The evidence can also be seen in the SEM images of these samples as shown in Fig.4. In the SEM images of LLZTO, the dark areas represent the LiAlO2 phase. Fig.4(a) shows the micro-morphology of LLZTO sample prepared at 1060°C, there are some pores that maybe due to the temperature is not high enough to form the necessary eutectic liquid of LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4. As the XRD pattern of 1060°C shows, there is little LiAlO2. The LLZTO samples prepared at 1100°C and 1140°C are nearly free of pores. It is obvious that samples of 1140°C contain much more LiAlO2 phase than that of 1100°C, which is in accord with the result of XRD. Because LiAlO2 can block the lithium ions transfer and thus decreases the ionic conductivity, the samples with excessive LiAlO2 may not be suitable for solid electrolyte. For these reasons, we select 1100°C as the sintering temperature to synthesize LLZTO.

context.text: Electrochemical systems are prevalent in many areas including electronics, photovoltaics, batteries, and biological and diagnostic systems.[1–4] With respect to power storage, batteries composed of electrochemical cells store charge in the form of labile ions that traverse between two electrodes through an electrolytic medium (electrolyte). Ionic mobility through this medium dictates the rate of charge or discharge possible for the cell.[5–7] The electrodes must undergo ionic insertion and extraction while maintaining functional morphology as well as crystalline and electronic properties for the battery-s operation. In the case of secondary cells, this process must be relatively reversible to allow repeated charge/discharge cycles.[8] Lithium alkali ions have been extensively used in the production of secondary batteries (Li-ion) for mobile, portable, and commercial applications.[9–12]

Presently, the electrolyte of the vast majority of commercial Li-ion batteries utilizes a carbonate-based organic liquid electrolyte. Safety concerns have inspired researchers to investigate alternative solid electrolytes, which may consist of ceramics, polymers, or lithiated oxides, with higher safety margins with respect to shock sensitivity, puncture resistance, or temperature compared to traditional liquid organic electrolytes.[13–16] These electrolytes must transport lithium ions through the medium with high ionic conductivity; however, further development is needed to improve the mobility to reach levels comparable with liquid electrolytes.[17, 18] Currently, garnet LiLaZrO2 (LLZO) and sulfide electrolyte materials are popular candidates.[19, 20] Properties including morphology, crystallinity, grain size, grain boundaries, and porosity play a significant role in dictating the performance of ionic systems.[21] To this end, we selected a series of first-row transition metal oxides (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) synthesized through an evaporative-induced self-assembly method, which gives rise to nanostructured particles with regular porosity and crystallinity,[22] and chemically lithiated them using a simple method. These materials were then pelletized and incorporated into two-electrode cells for electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements.

context.text: In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich,  98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z vs Z) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

context.text: Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Abstract—Solid electrolytes Li7–xLa3Zr2−xNbxO12 (x = 0.0–2.0) were synthesized by the sol-gel method, with Nb2O5 used as one of the starting compounds. The suggested synthesis procedure made it possible to lower the annealing temperature and shorten the annealing duration as compared with the solid-phase synthesis method, from 1200°C during 36 h to 1150°C during 1 h. The infl uence exerted by the doping of the Li7La3Zr2O12 compound in the Zr sublattice with niobium (Nb5+) on its crystal structure, morphology, and electrical conductivity. It was found that the compounds obtained with x > 0.1 are single-phase and have the Ia–3d cubic structure. The scanning electron microscopy was used to examine the morphology and the grain size of the resulting solid electrolytes. The average grain size of the ceramic samples was found to be 1–4 μm. The resistivity of the solid electrolytes Li7–xLa3Zr2−xNbxO12 (x = 0.0–2.0) was measured by the method of electrochemical impedance. It was found that Li6.75La3Zr1.75Nb0.25O12 has the highest total lithium-ion conductivity at 25°C: 4.0 × 10–5 S cm–1. It was shown that the sol-gel method is promising and can be used to obtain solid electrolytes based on Li7La3Zr2O12 doped with Nb5+ ions.
Keywords: solid electrolyte, Li7La3Zr2O12, garnet-like structure, sol-gel synthesis, lithium-ion conductivity, electrochemical impedance

matches.text: # Synthesis and Study of Conductivity of Al-Substituted Li7La3Zr2O121

context.text: The recently discovered solid electrolyte with a garnet structure and the overall formula of Li7La3Zr2O12 attracted much attention since the first publication [3]. High lithium-ion conductivity combined with the stability in contact with metallic lithium, high decomposition voltage (6 V vs. Li+/Li), easy availability and low const of the initial materials make lithium–lanthanum zirconate Li7La3Zr2O12 promising as a solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries [3‒7]. In this connection, synthesis and study of ion conductivity Li7La3Zr2O12 are of current concern.

At present, different methods of Li7La3Zr2O12 synthesis are published: solid-phase, sol–gel, solid-phase with mechanical preactivation, combined solidphase-liquid, codeposition, sintering, synthesis from molten salts in the LiCl–KCl eutectics) [8–13]. The most widespread methods are high-temperature solidphase sintering of a multicomponent mix of the initial reagents in the form of lanthanum and zirconium oxides and lithium salts and also the sol–gel technique. A fault of the conventional method of solid-phase synthesis of lithium–lanthanum zirconate Li7La3Zr2O12 on the basis of refractory oxides of La2O3 (tmelt \~ 2320°C) and ZrO2 (tmelt \~ 2700°C) and lithium carbonate Li2CO3 is the high sintering temperature (1230°C) for a prolonged period of time and necessity of repeated burden changes to obtain a homogeneous final product. Thus, in [3] the initial powders of La2O3, ZrO2, and LiOH were ground using a ball mill for 12 h to obtain Li7La3Zr2O12; this process was repeated twice after thermal treatment at 900°C and after thermal treatment at 1125°C. The reaction product was compacted into tablets and sintered at 1230°C for 36 h under the mother powder. Ion conductivity (3 × 10–4 S/cm at 25°C) was measured at the example of tablets with the density of 92%. This value of specific ion conductivity of the new lithium–ion conductor of Li7La3Zr2O12 with a garnet structure is higher than the ion conductivity of all the earlier described lithium garnets [3]. However, synthesis of such a structure is related to prolonged conditioning of the lithium–containing material at the high temperature (36 h at 1230°C). The overall synthesis time was more than 90 h. One should point out that the authors obtained the cubic modification by sintering at the high temperature with a considerable conditioning time. Formation of the cubic modification of Li La Zr O was also favored by synthesis of the solid electrolyte in an alumina crucible, as the crucible material interacted with the reaction mixture, which resulted in the uncontrolled doping of Li7La3Zr2O12 by A13+ ions. In the further works, the doping of the solid electrolyte based on lithium and lanthanum zirconate by aluminum oxide was used for stabilization of the high-conductivity cubic modification.

The initial materials of Li2CO3, La2O3 and aqueous solution of ZrO(NO ) were used for synthesis of Li7La3Zr2O12 using the citrate–nitrate technique [9]. These components were dissolved in a mixture of dilute nitric and citric acids. The overall solution was evaporated at 80°C up to transparent gel. At the next stage, the gel was dried and subjected to pyrolysis at \~200°C. Then the powder was sintered at 900°C for 3 h, but the nonconducting impurity phase of La2Zr2O7 was present in the final product. The citrate–nitrate technique allows obtaining a product with a uniform grain size distribution. The faults of this method include a prolonged stage of gel formation and low ion conductivity value. Conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12 synthesized using the citrate–nitrate technique was 5.2 × 10−6 S/cm at 20°C. Conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12 was measured for tablets with the density of \~70% of the theoretical value after their sintering at 1100°C for 1 h.

context.text: The initial materials of Li2CO3, La2O3 and aqueous solution of ZrO(NO ) were used for synthesis of Li7La3Zr2O12 using the citrate–nitrate technique [9]. These components were dissolved in a mixture of dilute nitric and citric acids. The overall solution was evaporated at 80°C up to transparent gel. At the next stage, the gel was dried and subjected to pyrolysis at \~200°C. Then the powder was sintered at 900°C for 3 h, but the nonconducting impurity phase of La2Zr2O7 was present in the final product. The citrate–nitrate technique allows obtaining a product with a uniform grain size distribution. The faults of this method include a prolonged stage of gel formation and low ion conductivity value. Conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12 was measured for tablets with the density of \~70% of the theoretical value after their sintering at 1100°C for 1 h.

A method of synthesizing powdered Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12 is known that includes two sintering stages [10]. Addition of Al in the form of γ-Al2O3 powder at the final stage requires hours–long grinding in a ball mill. The maximum ion conductivity value of Alsubstituted Li7La3Zr2O12 measured for tablets with the density of 90% was 1.6 × 10−4 S/cm.

As already pointed out, Li La Zr O is characterized by the garnet structure and has two crystalline modifications: cubic and tetragonal. It is found that conductivity of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 at the room temperature is several orders of magnitude higher than that of the tetragonal one [14, 15]. Aluminum is the best studied element for stabilization of the cubic garnet structure at the room temperature. The authors of [12] suggest a new “self-compaction” method with no molding for preparation of high-density cubic Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12. The method of cold or hot isostatic molding is economically unfeasible due to the ultrahigh pressure and low efficiency. The relative density of an Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12 sample (0.10 mol of Al) was \~93–96% and the overall specific ion conductivity was 1.41 × 10−4 S/cm at 30°C.

As already pointed out, Li La Zr O is characterized by the garnet structure and has two crystalline modifications: cubic and tetragonal. It is found that conductivity of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 at the room temperature is several orders of magnitude higher than that of the tetragonal one [14, 15]. Aluminum is the best studied element for stabilization of the cubic garnet structure at the room temperature. The authors of [12] suggest a new “self-compaction” method with no molding for preparation of high-density cubic Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12. The method of cold or hot isostatic molding is economically unfeasible due to the ultrahigh pressure and low efficiency. The relative density of an Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12 sample (0.10 mol of Al) was \~93–96% and the overall specific ion conductivity was 1.41 × 10−4 S/cm at 30°C.

The causes for the significant scatter of conductivity values of Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12 are discussed in [16]. Numerous samples of Li7La3Zr2O12 (44 pieces) with a similar Al content were prepared using the same solid phase method at the temperature of 1150 and 1230°C. In the best case, the sample conductivity was σ \~ 8 × 10–4 S/cm, which is the maximum value among Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12; the conductivity values of σ < 10−4 S/cm were determined in other cases. It appears impossible to use the XRD technique to establish the causes for such a scatter of ion conductivity values. Spatial nonuniformity of ion conductivity was observed by the authors of [16] by means of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy technique. Probably, the gradient in the element distribution is responsible for ion conductivity nonuniformity. This assumption is confirmed by the distribution of elements obtained using the method of inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry with laser ablation (LA-ICP-MS). Incidental changes in the composition can also be the cause of large ion conductivity scatter in nominally identical Li7La3Zr2O12 samples [16].

Numerous samples of Li7La3Zr2O12 (44 pieces) with a similar Al content were prepared using the same solid phase method at the temperature of 1150 and 1230°C. In the best case, the sample conductivity was σ \~ 8 × 10–4 S/cm, which is the maximum value among Al-substituted Li7La3Zr2O12; the conductivity values of σ < 10−4 S/cm were determined in other cases. It appears impossible to use the XRD technique to establish the causes for such a scatter of ion conductivity values. Spatial nonuniformity of ion conductivity was observed by the authors of [16] by means of the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy technique. Probably, the gradient in the element distribution is responsible for ion conductivity nonuniformity. This assumption is confirmed by the distribution of elements obtained using the method of inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry with laser ablation (LA-ICP-MS). Incidental changes in the composition can also be the cause of large ion conductivity scatter in nominally identical Li7La3Zr2O12 samples [16].

Thus, despite the considerable number of publications on synthesis and properties of lithium–lanthanum zirconate with a garnet structure, a lot of questions remain that require the further studies. In particular, a synthesis method with reproducible results is required for Li7La3Zr2O12 that can be used for batch– product of the solid electrolyte.

It was found that the fitting results can conform well to the experimentally determined dependence of Li content on ionic conductivity.[150] One abnormal phenomenon was found, however: for some doping cases, an increase of lattice parameters results in a reduction of ionic conductivity. In view of this, it has been speculated that the difference between the atomic radii of the dopant and the primary lattice atoms leads to local lattice distortion. A further correction is that the second term in the right hand side of Eq. (1) is replaced with (n + n0 − αnx − xc)µ , where n and n0 are the respective numbers of Li atoms and vacancies in the crystal lattice unit.[151] Besides, the 2D conduction mechanism is found at relatively lower temperature directly by neutron powder diffraction study,[152] while higher temperatures increase the oxygen vibration and open up the originally blocked bottleneck to enable the third dimension for Li-ion diffusion[153] and delocalizes Li ions from the 2D La-poor layer to realize a higher degree of disorder.[154] Considering the quasi-2D conduction mechanism and the preferential La distribution, equation (1) can be further revised as: σ ∝ neff(n0 − nc)µ = 12x(1 − 12x)(0.5 − g(La2))1.3.[152] The deviation from Arrhenius can be explained by the long-range correlation of mobile carriers, which can be inferred both from the abnormal activation energy measured by IS.[153,155] as well as from activation energy discrepancies between IS and measurements of 7Li NMR spin-lattice relaxation.[156] The total conductivity of Li3xLn2/3−x[U + FFFF]1/3−2xTiO3 is limited by grain boundary resistance, which can be reduced by high temperature sintering; however, the high-temperature, longduration thermal process leads to Li evaporation, making accurate control of Li content difficult. Therefore, this system can hardly be applied in all-solid-state batteries.

The Li-ion compounds Li5La3M2O12 (M = Ta, Nb), with garnet structure, were reported in 1988, and the structure was examined by x-ray diffraction, without knowing the Li distribution, due to limited experimental resolution of Li atoms.[157] However, this system did not attract much attention as a solid electrolyte until 2003, when Thangadurai and Weppner found that it is a good Li-ion conductor with high conductivity and a wide electrochemical window.[158] In contrast to the common perovskite or NASICON solid state electrolyte, the garnet family excludes Li-reducible Ti4+, so it can directly contact Li metal without damage, which has been viewed as its distinguishing advantage.[159] In 2004, Thangadurai and Weppner, together with Adams, used the bond valence sum method to verify the structure, and they minimized the mismatch of the Li-bond valence state as the isosurface to map the conduction pathways visually. It was concluded that Li ions occupy the octahedral sites other than tetrahedral vacancies.[160] The Li-ion occupation pattern is of great importance for understanding the diffusion mechanism but was not located precisely until 2006, by Cussen. It was revealed from neutron powder diffraction data that Li ions occupy both tetrahedral (80%) and octahedral sites (43%), and the latter are responsible for the mobile carriers via a clustering mechanism.[161] NMR results indicate that the Liion distribution depends on the annealing temperature; that is, the high annealing temperature implies that more Li ions can be quenched at the octahedral sites as mobile carriers, which leads to higher ionic conductivity.[162] In 2012, Han and Yusheng Zhao utilized variable-temperature neutron diffraction (HTND), combined with the maximum-entropy method (MEM) for data refining, to estimate the Li nuclear-density distribution and visualize the conduction pathway experimentally for the first time. These results confirm that displacement is directly driven by temperature.[163] More efforts in calculation have gradually elucidated the Li-ion diffusion mechanism; for example, conductivity and distinct mechanisms for different M elements and various Li concentrations,[164] structural phase transition,[165] concerted[166,167] or asynchronous phenomena,[168] point defects,[169] local structure and dynamics performance,[170] often in combination with experimental data. Other efforts focused on enhancing conductivity. Substituting and doping with lower-valence elements, e.g., replacing La by Sr[171] or Ba,[172] replacing M (= Nb, Ta) partly[173] or totally[174] by Zr, can increase Li content and thus improve conductivity. The highest conductivity found was 4 × 10−4 S/cm in Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO),[174] the most attractive composition so far. LLZO has cubic and tetragonal phases. Cubic phase LLZO has higher conductivity and can be synthesized by doping Al or Ga, or by pulsed laser annealing.[175–179] Cubic phase thin film can be obtained from epitaxial growth[180] or aerosol deposition (AD).[181] The latter method prevents the electrolyte from reacting with the active electrode by avoiding the annealing process, although the obtained electrolyte exhibits extremely low conductivity (1.0 × 10−8 S/cm@140 ◦C) and worse cyclic performance if applied in all-solid-state batteries. Nebulized spray pyrolysis results in a thin-film hybrid of both phases.[182] The disadvantages of LLZO used in sandwich-structure all-solidstate batteries include high interface resistance and poor cyclic stability,[183] both of which can be ameliorated by introducing a thin Nb interlayer between the electrolyte and cathode (LiCoO2).[184]

In 2012, a novel class of solid electrolyte, called lithiumrich anti-perovskites (LiRAP) was reported by Zhao et al.[185] LiRAP is named for the following reasons: It has a structure similar to perovskites with electronically-inverted ions located in the corresponding lattice sites. In other words, as compared with the traditional perovskite ABX3, X is occupied by Li+ with positive charge, leading to a high concentration of Li ions (i.e., “Li rich”), A and B by halogen− (F−, Cl−, Br−, I−) and chalcogen2− (O2−, S2−) separately with negative charges.[185] Almost at the same time, Li3OCl happened to be discovered as a byproduct during synthesizing Li5OCl3.[186] In the following year, phase diagram calculation results indicated that Li3OCl was in a less stable state (metastable phase) than Li2O and LiA (A = Cl, Br) at 0 K[187] and could be stabilized by exerting a certain temperature.[187,188] By accommodating dopants and substitutions (e.g., halogen mixing, Li sites doped by higher-valence-state elements, and depletion of lithium halides) as well as local disorder from thermal treating process without phase transition, (anti-) perovskite has greater tolerance for structure modulation[189] to ensure structural stability and enhance conductivity. In this case, Li3OCl0.5Br0.5 has room temperature conductivity of 6.05 × 10−3 S/cm.[185]

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 × 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

context.text: A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 × 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I. 51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li SiO to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta O powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # 1. Introduction

Solid-state Li-ion batteries (LIBs) have attracted much attention as the next generation battery system due to high energy density and high safety. Especially, the safety issue in the present LIBs using flammable organic liquid electrolytes would be solved using inorganic solid electrolytes. Garnet-type Li La Zr O and its chemical variants have been intensively investigated as solid electrolyte materials after the first report of Li La Zr O by Murugan et al.1) The cubic form of Li7La3Zr2O12 shows an excellent Liion conductivity among oxide materials and a wide electrical potential window. As previously reported, the partial substitution of Zr site in Li7La3Zr2O12 with Ta or Nb is an effective way to improve the Li-ion conductivity (³10¹4 S/cm at room temperature).2)­7) Recently, we successfully synthesized the garnet-type Li La Zr Ta O (LLZT) samples via conventional solid-state reaction and revealed a relation between crystal structure and electrochemical property.8),9) However, high temperature above 1100°C was needed to prepare a single-phase LLZT sample by the solidstate reaction. From the viewpoint of industrial manufacturing, Li vapor during high-temperature reaction gives significant damage to electric furnaces. Moreover, excess Li source should be added to compensate for its volatilization during high-temperature heating.

In the case of Li La Zr O , various low-temperature synthetic methods using sol­gel processes10)­13) or some precursor materials such as pyrochlore-type La2Zr2O714),15) have been developed to avoid Li loss during hightemperature treatment. However, LLZT samples have not been synthesized yet using such low-temperature methods.

context.text: 2Department of Chemical Engineering, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama 36849, USA

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

context.text: # ABSTRACT

Lithium-ion (Li+) batteries suffer from problems caused by the chemical instability of their organic electrolyte. Solid-state electrolytes that exhibit high ionic conductivities and stable to lithium metal are potential replacements for flammable organic electrolytes. Garnet-type Li,LazZrO12 is a promising solid-state electrolyte for next-generation solidstate Li batteries. In this study, we prepared mono-, dual-, and ternary-doped lithium (Li) garnets by doping tantalum (Ta), tantalum-barium (Ta-Ba), and tantalum-bariumgallium (Ta-Ba-Ga) ions, along with undoped-Li,LazZrO (LLZO) cubic garnet electrolyte, using a conventional solid-state reaction method. The effect of multi-ion doping on the Li+ dynamics in the garnet-type LLZO was studied by combining analyses of joint Rietveld refinement against X-ray diffraction and high-resolution neutron powder diffraction with the results of Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and multinuclear magic angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance. Our results revealed that Li+ occupancy in the tetrahedrally coordinated site (24d) increased with increased multi-ion doping in LLZO, whereas Li+ occupancy in the octahedrally coordinated site (96h) remained constant. Among the investigated compounds, the ternary-doped garnet structure Li6.65Gao.05La2.95Ba0.05Zr1.75Tao.25O12 (LGLBZTO) exhibited the highest total ionic conductivity of 0.72 and 1.24 mS cm-1 at room temperature and 60 C, respectively. Overall, our findings revealed that the dense microstructure and increased Li+ occupancy in the tetrahedral-24du site played a key role in achieving the maximum roomtemperature Li-ion conductivity in ternary-doped LGLBZTO garnet, and that the prepared ternary-doped LGLBZTO was a potential solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries without polymer adhesion.

context.text: # Introduction

Inorganic solid-state electrolytes (SEs) for all-solid-state Li-ion batteries (ASsLIB) are promising replacements for the flammable, toxic, flowing, and volatile organic liquidbased electrolytes due to their great safety, high performance, and reliability.1, 2 Moreover, SEs are sufficiently stable in contact with Li metal, which can address the well-known problems in conventional batteries, such as explosion hazards by an internal short circuit (dendrites) and thermal runway.3,4 However, the challenge is in the design of appropriate solid electrolyte with high ionic conductivity (> 10-4 S cm-), negligible electronic conductivity, and good electrochemical stability.5-8 The garnet-like material of the stoichiometry LiLazZrO12 (LLZO) was first discovered as a fast Li+ conductor by Murugan et al. in 2007.9 The LLZO SE material has been a research hotspot due to its relatively high Li-ion conductivity (210-4 Scm-1) at room temperature, wide electrochemical window (> 5 V vs. Li+/Li), and good compatibility with Li anodes.10, 11 However, LLzO is crystallized in two polymorphs: a thermodynamically stable tetragonal polymorph with ordered Li+ distribution (space group: I41/acd, No. 142)12 and a high-temperature stable cubic polymorph with highly disordered Li+ distribution (space group: Ia3d, No. 230).12, 13 The Li\* ions in the cubic phase partially occupied the tetrahedral-24dui1 and distorted octahedral-96hti2 sites, whereas the Li+ ions in the tetragonal polymorph fully occupied three crystallographic sites: tetrahedral-8a (Li1), distorted octahedral-16f (Li2), and 32g (Li3).12, 13 As a result of the disordered Li+ distribution and partial occupation in cubic phase, the Li-ion conductivity of the cubic phase is about two orders of magnitude higher than that of the tetragonal counterpart at room temperature.14, 15 Hence, many studies focused on the optimization of the garnet cubic phase by promoting Li+ disorder framework and on the improvement of the Li-ion conductivity (ranging from \~10-4 S cm-1 to 10-3 S cm-1) at room temperature.6 Geiger et al. noticed the highly conductive cubic polymorph along with the tetragonal polymorph when LLZO was synthesized in an Al-containing crucible; An LLZO sintered in a Ptcrucible yielded a solely tetragonal phase.16 They argued that the unintentional doping of Al from the crucible into the LLZO framework at the Li site during the high-temperature sintering stabilized the cubic polymorph. Many studies investigated the role of Al in achieving a fast-ionic cubic conductor by intentionally adding Al into the LLZO garnet during the synthesis.4, 17-19 However, the preferential site (tetrahedral-24d. or octahedral-96hti2 sites) for Al ions remains unclear. The formation of highly conducting cubic polymorph from alumina crucible often requires high sintering temperatures (>1200 C) and long sintering time, which may cause substantial Li loss from the sample.20, 21 A trivalent doping cation (Ga3+), as a substitute for Lit, was found to stabilize the similar cubic phase and improve the Li-ion conductivities compared with Al3+22, 23 Moreover, Ga doping can stabilize the cubic phase at a low synthesis temperature of about 1000 C (sintering temperature is about 1100 C).24

Recent studies demonstrated that doping of supervalent-cation (Ta5+, Nb5+, Sb5+, and Bi5+ at the Zr4+ site) into the garnet-type LLZO remarkably improved the Li-ion conductivities at room temperature.25-29 The doping alters the structure by creating Li+ vacancies for charge neutrality and by increasing the disorderliness in the framework, thereby promoting the stabilization of the highly conductive cubic phase. In contrast, partial substitution of low-valent alkaline earth metal cations (Ca2+, Sr2+, and Ba2+) at the La3+ site in the LLzO garnet framework has a substantial effect on the Li-ion conductivities.30, 31 Divalent doping at the La site increases the Li+ concentration in the framework, which leads to improved Li-ion conductivities. Additionally, replacement of La3+ by large size dopant ions expands the lattice, enlarging the bottleneck size for Li+ migration, thereby increasing the Li-ion conductivities.32 In strategic doping in the LLZO garnet, each doping ion has an important role in modifying the garnet framework. Thus, choosing the doping ion can effectively enhance the Li-ion conductivity in LLZO. Recently, simultaneous multi-doping strategy on LLZO resulted in enhanced ionic conductivity (ranging from \~10-4 cm-1 to 10-3 S cm-1) at room temperature.33 However, further endeavors are still needed to investigate the site preference and role of each dopant ion with respect to the Li+ dynamics in doped LLZO systems. We aim to identify the preferred site of the dopant ion, preferred Li occupancy in the 24d.i1/96hL2 sites, and the role of the dopant in the Li-ion conduction by using neutron diffraction techniques.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.
