context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

Figure 4. EDS results of the interparticle phase on the sample of (a) 30Li, EDS point of spectrum 1, (b) 65Li, EDS point of spectrum 2, sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powder of 15Li LiOH. Concentrations are in atomic%.

The possible mechanism for the densification of LLZTO.—To study the possible mechanism for the effect of LiOH in the cover powder on the densification of LLZTO, 65Li pellets were sintered at the same sintering temperature of 1100°C for different sintering times. SEM and back scattered electron (BSE) images of fracture cross sections of 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 hours with the cover powder of 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 7.

After sintering for 1 hour (Figure 7a), there are connected pores and many small grains with sizes of 2–3 μm connected by an interparticle phase. After sintering for 4 hours (Figure 7c), the grains grew and became better connected. After 8 hours (Figure 7d), the grains have continued to grow, and the pores were reduced and did not appear to be connected. As also shown in BSE images in Figures 7g–7h, in which the interparticle phase is darker than the grains, it is found that the grain size increased, the amount of the interparticle phase decreased and the samples are still porous after the sintering of 1 hour to 8 hours (Figures 7a–7d). There is little change between 8, 16 and 32 hours sintering, as shown in Figures 7d–7f.

Tantalum appears to be relatively uniformly distributed in the sample. Compositions from ICP analysis of 65Li sintered with different cover powders and different sintering times are listed in Table IV, atomic ratio of Li:Al:La:Zr is normalized by La content as shown in the formula of Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12. The ICP analysis, which presents the overall sample composition, indicates that Al exists in all LLZTO samples, but that the amount of aluminum is higher and increases with increasing time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover. In addition, the Li content is lower in the sample sintered with 15Li cover powder than that with 15Li + LiOH cover. These results suggest that the 15Li + LiOH cover powder reduces the loss of Li and promotes the transfer of aluminum from the crucible to the sample.

The RT total Li+ conductivities of 65Li pellets sintered for 4 to 32 hours are shown in Figure 9. The conductivity increases significantly after 4 hours sintering, and it does not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. The relative densities of these pellets shown in Table V follows a similar trend to that of the total Li+ conductivities. The relative density is only 61% for pellets sintered for 4 hours, and it is larger than 80% for 8 to 32 hours. Samples sintered for 16 and 32 hours have similar relative density of 90%. As shown in Table IV, the amount of aluminum increases with increasing sintering time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover, and aluminum only exists at the phases between grains (Figure 8), it is concluded that the amount of Al-containing phase in the dense pellets also increases with the sintering time. context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

Garnet-type metal oxide such as Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is considered as one of the most promising solid electrolytes among the inorganic solid electrolytes4, for it shows high Li+ ionic conductivity, high stability with lithium metal and wide electrochemical window5. The sintering process6, doping strategy7-9, microstructure10 and composite design11 have been widely investigated to enhance its performance. The LLZO solid electrolyte can be synthesized by solid state reaction12, sol-gel method13, spark plasma sintering14 and hot-press sintering method15. Solid state reaction at high temperature is preferred because the cost is relatively low and the procedure is simple, which is suitable for large-scale industrial producing. The LLZO electrolyte sample prepared by solid state reaction has a moderate ionic conductivity in the order of 10-4 S/cm. Doping various elements into LLZO can increase the Li-ion conductivity and the Ta doped sample, Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12(x=0.6), has an ionic conductivity of about 1×10-3 S/cm 16, 17. However, because of the high volatility nature of Li element, Li is easy to lose during the high temperature sintering which leads to form the undesirable La2Zr2O7 as an impure phase. In order to prepare the stoichiometric LLZO, the lost Li should be compensated and the most common means is to cover the tablet samples up with the mother powder 18. The mother powder with the same chemistry composition as the samples acts as the sacrificial component to ensure the sample to form the right garnet phase. The amount of the sacrificed mother powder usually reaches the ratio 1:1 in weight to the samples and after sintering, the mother powder cannot be reused. That is the problem, as we know that the mother powder contains the rare earth element La and the element Ta that are expensive. Therefore, the conventional solid state reaction with mother powder protecting method is not economical. We noticed that the effect of the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

mother powder is merely providing another Li source to compensate the lost Li. We proposed an alternative method to compensate the lost Li where the mother powder is replaced by Li2CO3. In this method, Li2CO3 is separated from the sample and it will melt and decompound above 730ºC. The decomposed Li2CO3 provides a Li2O atmosphere and ensures the sample to form the pure garnet phase. The method is also suitable for other oxide solid electrolytes. Li2CO3 is much cheaper than the mother powder and this method will lower the synthesis cost of LLZO as well as other oxide solid electrolytes, which is important for the large-scale application of the solid state batteries in the future.

Both LLi2CO3 and LMOTHER were sintered for 16h at 1100°C. The LLi2CO3 sample was compensated by 1g outside Li2CO3 and the LMOTHER sample was wrapped by 1g mother powder. The densities of LLi2CO3 and LMOTHER samples are 4.42 and 4.51 g·cm-3, respectively. Fig.8 (a) shows the primitive EISs of the two samples as well as the fitted curves of the samples. The R(RC)C model was used to fit the EISs and the goodness of the fits are rather well. The results show that the normalized resistance of LLi2CO3 sample is 4027 Ω∙cm and that of LMOTHER sample is 3901 Ω∙cm. The reciprocal of the normalized resistance is the conductivity of the samples. Then the obtained conductivities of LLi2CO3 and LMOTHER are 2.48×10-4 S/cm and 2.56×10-4 S/cm, respectively. The LMOTHER and LLi2CO3 samples have similar conductivities and the value This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

of LLi2CO3 is a bit lower than that of LMOTHER. The LMOTHER and LLi2CO3 samples were sintered under different environment. For the LLi2CO3 sample, it is surrounded by an atmosphere of high Li2O concentration and the gaseous Li2O can easily permeate into the sample. The permeated Li2O will facilitate the formation of eutectic phase such as LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4, and more Li2O will exist at the boundary of the grains. The Li2O at the grain boundary can also aid the sintering but its Li-ion conductivity is higher than that of LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4 18. For the LMOTHER sample, it is surrounded by the mother powder that has the same ingredient of the sample. The samples were protected by a local atmosphere created by the mother powder. On the other hand, the lost elements can also be compensated by ions diffusion between the solid phases. The activation energy of Li-ions diffusion in the garnet phase was evaluated by measuring the EISs at evaluated temperatures. Utilizing the Arrhenius equation =  o-Exp(-Ea/kT), the In o \~1/Tplot was made and then linear fitted. The plots are shown in Fig.8 (b), and the data points lie near a straight line. The slopes of the fitting lines are calculated to evaluate the activation energy Ea. The Ea value of LMOTHER is 0.356 eV and of LLi2CO3 is 0.371 eV. Li-ions diffusion activation energy of LLi2CO3 sample is higher than that of LMOTHER sample, which may be due to the complex compounds at the grain boundary of the LLZTO samples synthesized by outside Li2CO3 compensation. From the discussion above, both the Li-ions conductivity and activation energy of the samples with outside Li2CO3 compensation are close to those of samples covered with protective mother powder.

context.text: # (1) Powder Preparation

Cubic LLZO, with the nominal composition Li6.19Al0.27- La3Zr2O12, was prepared using a solid-state synthesis method.15,24 Li2CO3 (99.9% Alfa Aesar, Ward Hill, MA), La (OH) (99.95% Alfa Aesar), ZrO (99.9% Inframat Advanced Materials LLC, Manchester, CT), and Al2O3 (50 nm Gamma “B” from Mager Scientific Inc., Dexter, MI) precursors were mixed for 8 h at 400 rpm using a planetary mill (PM 100; Retsch, Haan, Germany) with an 500 mL agate vial and 45 agate balls of 10 mm diameter. Al O was added to stabilize the cubic polymorph at room temperature and 10 wt% excess Li2CO3 was added to compensate for Li loss during calcination. After mixing the precursors, the powder was cold-pressed into pellets at 385 MPa in a 1.27 cm diameter stainless steel die. The cold-pressed pellets were placed on LLZO mother powder to prevent a reaction with the Al2O3 crucible and then calcined at 1000°C for 4 h in air. The heating rate was 100°C per h. After calcination, the pellets were manually crushed with an agate mortar and pestle followed by planetary ball-milling for 15 min at 350 rpm using the same agate milling media described above.

context.text: For the solid state reaction synthesis of Al containing Li7La3Zr2O12, various precursors have been used. Since there is a lack of general agreement for choosing precursors, a quantitative approach to build a consensus is required. In this study, a thermodynamic point of view for selecting the precursors in the field of Li7La3Zr2O12 synthesis was covered according to the Gibbs free energy and enthalpy change of precursors' decomposition reactions. In terms of Gibbs free energy change calculations, LiOH, La(OH)3, and Al(OH)3 were favorable whereas, LiOH, La2O3, and Al(OH)3 were the preferred precursors for the enthalpy change calculations. Pellets prepared by using the favored precursors calculated from enthalpy change showed improved densification, higher ionic conductivity (2.11 × 10−4 S/cm), and lower activation energy (0.23 eV) compared with Gibbs free energy change. As a thermodynamically favored aluminum precursor, Al(OH)3 was discussed in the present study and hinders the ionic conductivity in comparison to Al2O3.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = (ALR), where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

1Hv mnunnvt v1 uopmg munu-ivno (Ua, Du, anu 1aJ ou uv mvipnvivgy o1 uopcu LLZO samples was examined using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM). Fig. S5 shows the FE-SEM images of the undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dual-doped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO obtained at room temperature along with the optical image of LGLBZTO with 0.5mm thickness. Substantial changes in the morphology of the microstructure were observed between the undoped LLZO and multidoped LLZO samples. The SEM image of the undoped LLZO revealed that the grains were not contacted well with each other. Furthermore, there were irregular pores among the grains, which is consistent with the low density of the undoped LLZO. By contrast, the SEM images of the mono-doped LLZTO and dual-doped LLBZTO exhibited dense and homogeneous morphology without any noticeable pores among the grains, which are reduced owing to their grain growth and mergence. A close inspection of the ternarydoped LGLBZTO revealed that mixtures of small and large grains were present in the microstructure. The microstructure appeared to be highly dense and compact by filling the gaps between large grains with small grains. This result corroborated the high density of the ternary-doped LGLBZTO, which was close to the theoretical density. The fabrication of differently sized grains by mixing large particles with small particles resulted in the dense microstructure.3 Almost no porosity was detected for the dualdoped LLBZTO and ternary-doped LGLBZTO. Hence, multi-doped LLZOs are expected to exhibit high Li-ion conductivities. The letters \*LGLBZTO' behind the pellet can be seen clearly that indicates the translucent nature of the pellet with reduced grain boundaries. The particle size distributions for the undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dual-doped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO were measured at room temperature. The d(0.1), d(0.5), and d(0.9) of the undoped and multi-doped LLZOs particles substantiated the SEM microstructure (Table S2).

To study the effect of doping on Li+ transportation, the ionic conductivities of the undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dual-doped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO were measured using the AC impedance technique with Au as the blocking electrode. A typical Nyquist impedance plot for the ternary-doped LGLBZTO (Li6.65Gao.05La2.95Bao.0sZr1.75Tao.25O12)withAu|LGLBZTO|Au configuration was recorded at room temperature (Fig. 4a). The undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dualdoped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO all showed one partially depressed semicircle at the high-frequency region with a low-frequency diffusion spike. This semicircle can be assigned as the total impedance, including the contribution from bulk and grain boundary impedances, and the low-frequency spike can be attributed to Li+ blocking at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The impedance data were fitted using an equivalent circuit model consisting of (R;)(Rg,CPEg)(CPE). The right intercept of the semicircle on the real axis at the high-frequency region represents the bulk resistance of the sample, which was denoted as R, in the equivalent circuit. Rg was referred as grain boundary resistance; CPEg, and CPE were referred as the constant phase element contributions attributed to the grain boundary capacitance, and the diffusion capacitance at the electrode/electrolyte interface, respectively. The diameter of the semicircle at the middle frequency corresponded to the total resistance, which is the sum of the resistance of the grain and grain boundary response (R, + Rgt). The contributions of grain and grain boundary responses were difficult to distinguish from the impedance spectra. The total Li-ion conductivity of the specimen, ot (S cm-1), was achieved by the total resistance normalized with respect to the thickness and cross-sectional area of the specimen. context.text: # Introduction

Interest in Li-ion batteries (LIBs) is constantly growing from portable electronics; to electric vehicles; to flexible batteries in wearable electronics.1–3 Along with this increasing demand for LIBs, substitution of conventional flammable and volatile liquid electrolytes with inorganic solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) is essential to improve the safety and capabilities of the batteries.4 Thin film based all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) facilitate miniaturization of microelectronic devices and flexible batteries with higher safety and energy densities.2 In addition to the chemical and electrochemical stability, mechanical stability in particular at the interface of SSE/electrode of ASSBs is also essential for the batteries performances. On one hand, microcracks can form due to elevated internal and/or external stresses, leading to the crack propagation, delamination, and fragmentation of electrodes and SSEs/electrode interfaces. For example, electrode volume changes during charging/discharging increases internal stresses and introduces bending/ stretching to the SSE which eventually aggregate the formation of microcracks.5–9 On the other hand, Li dendrite formation and growth introduces stress at the SSE/Li electrode interface that results in mechanical deformation which is the very complex phenomena because all chemical, electrochemical, and mechanical factors are involved.6,10 Two main types of SSEs are polymer and inorganic electrolytes. Polymer SSEs are believed to facilitate the interfacial contact issues due to their soft and flexible nature, however the volume changes of electrodes especially Li anode, introduce partial delamination at the interface.11 Inorganic ceramic SSEs are also fabricated because of their higher strength and stability in air, while their poor interface stability remains as an issue.12 Among thin film fabrication techniques, atomic layer deposition (ALD) enables uniform, pinhole-free ultra-thin films which provides good interfacial contact between inorganic SSEs/ electrodes.13–15 Despite such contact establishment, the contact needs to be mechanically stable. Previous research has suggested that elastic deformation of SSEs materials accompanied by some degree of ductility is desirable to maintain good interfacial contact with an electrode during cycling in order to preserve the battery cycling performance.13,14,16 Low stiffness sulfide SSEs with a low range of Young’s modulus (E) (14–25 GPa for Li2S-P2S5) 8,17,18 were considered as favorable SSEs for the bulk battery design to accommodate volume changes of the electrodes.8 However, Bucci et al.19 developed a cohesive zone model to simulate damage evaluation and presented quantitative conditions that facture would occur. They indicated that electrolytes with E ∼ 15 GPa were more prone to micro-cracking in compare to SSEs with higher E. Based on this model for SSEs with E = 15 GPa, fracture was prevented when the electrode expansion was below 7.5%, and the fracture energy of SSEs was greater than Gc = 4 J m−2 . In addition, oxide electrolytes exhibiting high E (77, 150, and 192 GPa in amorphous LLZO, LIPON, and Li La TiO , respectively)16,20,21 have been reported; however, the impact of inorganic SSEs mechanical behavior on battery performance is unknown. Moreover, there are a few models that incorporated electro-chemo-mechanical behavior of solid electrolytes to address interface stability in contact with Li metal. Li nucleation in the grain boundary of ceramic electrolyte was modeled by Raj and Wolfenstine22 with coupling mechanical stresses and the electrical potential. They showed that critical current above Li nucleation depends on ionic conductivity and fracture strength of the SSE. Monroe and Newman23,24 modeled the lithium deposition in a polymer electrolyte and considered the contribution of bulk and surface stresses to Li deposition electrochemical reactions. They concluded that deposition stability increased by increasing electrolyte shear modulus because of more contribution of bulk pressure and surface stresses. Based on Monroe and Newman model,24 researchers constructed hybrid SSEs with high modulus (elastic of shear modulus) to suppress dendrite formation and growth, however it has been found that Li dendrite can grow and penetrate both polymer and rigid ceramics.25–27 It is still unclear which model can explain the mechanisms of Li dendrite growth. The SSE modulus is not the only mechanical factor that limits the Li dendrite growth and other mechanical properties such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, and flexure strength of brittle inorganic SSEs require more attention. Recently organic, inorganic and hybrid coating layers have shown potentials for suppressing Li dendrite at the interface of SSE/ Li metal.15 Fu et al.,28 designed and developed a hybrid system of polymer embedded with nano-sized ceramic domains called as “soft ceramic” structure as dendrite-suppressing SSE by applying a universal chemomechanical model that can assess fundamentally pressure- or density-driven dendrite suppressing. In addition to all the efforts on modelling and designing compatible interfaces, a study by LePage et al. 29 showed that “creep” is a dominant deformation mechanism for Li metal in batteries which further complicates the interfacial mechanical stability issues. These studies show that better understanding of mechanical behavior of nanoscale organic and inorganic SSEs are essential prior to investigate their theoretical and experimental electro-chemomechanical implications.

Previously studied amorphous LPO and LTO thin films with moderate ionic conductivity (∼10−8 S cm−1 at 25 °C) have been used as SSEs for ASSBs,30,31 and as coating layers on the electrodes of LIBs to significantly improve the battery performance.31–35 A summary of electrochemical studies of the impact of LTO and LPO coatings on electrode materials in LIBs cyclic performance is presented in Table 1. Both LPO and LTO exhibited electrochemical and chemical stability, and ionic conductivity for coating cathode materials as well as facilitating better contact between electrode materials and electrolytes as shown in Table 1.31–34 The mechanism behind preserving the structural degradation of electrode material is not well understood and a more detailed understanding of the mechanical stability of SSEs in ASSBs against internal and/or external stresses during charging/discharging is needed.14,15 In this study, the elastic and fracture behavior of ALD prepared LTO, and LPO SSEs thin films were studied and compared for the first time. The mechanical behavior of a range of ultra-thin ALD prepared suspended SSEs thin films (5 nm–30 nm thickness) were studied using an atomic force microscope (AFM) film deflection technique. The film under AFM deflection emulates stress levels present in the SSE at the nanoscale, and the results will help to identify the potential influence of SSEs mechanical performances for on their operation in flexible ASSBs.

They showed that critical current above Li nucleation depends on ionic conductivity and fracture strength of the SSE. Monroe and Newman23,24 modeled the lithium deposition in a polymer electrolyte and considered the contribution of bulk and surface stresses to Li deposition electrochemical reactions. They concluded that deposition stability increased by increasing electrolyte shear modulus because of more contribution of bulk pressure and surface stresses. Based on Monroe and Newman model,24 researchers constructed hybrid SSEs with high modulus (elastic of shear modulus) to suppress dendrite formation and growth, however it has been found that Li dendrite can grow and penetrate both polymer and rigid ceramics.25–27 It is still unclear which model can explain the mechanisms of Li dendrite growth. The SSE modulus is not the only mechanical factor that limits the Li dendrite growth and other mechanical properties such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, and flexure strength of brittle inorganic SSEs require more attention. Recently organic, inorganic and hybrid coating layers have shown potentials for suppressing Li dendrite at the interface of SSE/ Li metal.15 Fu et al.,28 designed and developed a hybrid system of polymer embedded with nano-sized ceramic domains called as “soft ceramic” structure as dendrite-suppressing SSE by applying a universal chemomechanical model that can assess fundamentally pressure- or density-driven dendrite suppressing. In addition to all the efforts on modelling and designing compatible interfaces, a study by LePage et al. 29 showed that “creep” is a dominant deformation mechanism for Li metal in batteries which further complicates the interfacial mechanical stability issues. These studies show that better understanding of mechanical behavior of nanoscale organic and inorganic SSEs are essential prior to investigate their theoretical and experimental electro-chemomechanical implications.

context.text: Electrochemical systems are prevalent in many areas including electronics, photovoltaics, batteries, and biological and diagnostic systems.[1–4] With respect to power storage, batteries composed of electrochemical cells store charge in the form of labile ions that traverse between two electrodes through an electrolytic medium (electrolyte). Ionic mobility through this medium dictates the rate of charge or discharge possible for the cell.[5–7] The electrodes must undergo ionic insertion and extraction while maintaining functional morphology as well as crystalline and electronic properties for the battery-s operation. In the case of secondary cells, this process must be relatively reversible to allow repeated charge/discharge cycles.[8] Lithium alkali ions have been extensively used in the production of secondary batteries (Li-ion) for mobile, portable, and commercial applications.[9–12]

Presently, the electrolyte of the vast majority of commercial Li-ion batteries utilizes a carbonate-based organic liquid electrolyte. Safety concerns have inspired researchers to investigate alternative solid electrolytes, which may consist of ceramics, polymers, or lithiated oxides, with higher safety margins with respect to shock sensitivity, puncture resistance, or temperature compared to traditional liquid organic electrolytes.[13–16] These electrolytes must transport lithium ions through the medium with high ionic conductivity; however, further development is needed to improve the mobility to reach levels comparable with liquid electrolytes.[17, 18] Currently, garnet LiLaZrO2 (LLZO) and sulfide electrolyte materials are popular candidates.[19, 20] Properties including morphology, crystallinity, grain size, grain boundaries, and porosity play a significant role in dictating the performance of ionic systems.[21] To this end, we selected a series of first-row transition metal oxides (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) synthesized through an evaporative-induced self-assembly method, which gives rise to nanostructured particles with regular porosity and crystallinity,[22] and chemically lithiated them using a simple method. These materials were then pelletized and incorporated into two-electrode cells for electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements.

context.text: # Abstract

Freeze casting is used for the first time to prepare solid electrolyte scaffolds with oriented porosity and dense ceramic walls made of Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO), one of the most promising candidates for solid state battery electrolytes. Processing parameters - such as solvent solidification rate, solvent type, and ceramic particle size - are investigated, focusing on their influence on porosity and ceramic wall density. Dendrite-like porosity is obtained when using cyclohexane and dioxane as solvents. Lamellar porosity is observed in aqueous slurries resulting in a structure with the highest apparent porosity and densest ceramic scaffold but weakest mechanical properties due to the lack of interlamellar support. The use of smaller LLZO particle size in the slurries resulted in lower porosity and denser ceramic walls. The intrinsic ionic conductivity of the oriented LLZ ceramic scaffold is unaffected by the freeze casting technique, providing a promising ceramic scaffold for polymer infill in view of designing new types of ceramic-polymer composites.

For the cyclohexanebased slurry, the diameter of the pores decreases to ≈ 10 µm (Figure 4 a, b), half of the size observed with the larger particle size (Figure 3 a, b). In the case of the dioxane-based slurry, the alignment of the dendrite-like pores becomes even more obvious (Figure 4 c, d), with an average pore diameter of ≈ 40 µm, twice as large as the pores observed with the larger particle size (Figure 3 c, d). Density and porosity measurements of the sintered solids were performed following Archimedes’ method (Table 1). For a larger particle size, the quenched cyclohexane-based slurry provides a similar apparent porosity (65%) to the cyclohexane- and dioxane-based slurries cooled at 3°C·min-1 (61 and 57%, respectively). context.text: # 4. Conclusions

Freeze casting enabled the preparation of dense Li7La3Zr2O12 garnet scaffolds with directional open porosity. Scaffolds prepared with cyclohexane- and dioxane-based LLZO slurries showed a dendrite-like porous network, with some degree of pore alignment in the case of dioxane, while the scaffold prepared from a water-based slurry presented lamellar porosity. The solid prepared with a water-based slurry is characterized by the highest amount of apparent porosity (75%) and the highest LLZO percent theoretical density (93%); however, the solid was found difficult to handle due to the lack of interlamellar support. The rate of slurry solidification is shown to be an important parameter in controlling the directionality and ordering of the porous network. Solidification by quenching of a cyclohexane-based slurry results in the homogenous distribution of porosity and the absence of directionality. Decreasing the particle size of the LLZO powder for cyclohexane- and dioxane-based slurries leads to a denser ceramic scaffold but lower apparent porosity. The solids prepared with cyclohexane-based slurries have an ionic conductivity in the range of 10-7 S·cm-1 which is comparable to the ionic conductivity of uniaxially pressed and sintered tetragonal LLZO, if taking into consideration the amount of apparent porosity. This similar conductivity indicates that solids prepared by freeze casting under controlled atmosphere  could provide a competitive ionic conductivity if prepared with LLZO garnet powder unexposed to air.

context.text: # 2.Experimental details

Li6.4Gao.2La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) samples were prepared in this study via solid state reaction. The starting materials used were LiCO3 (>99.9%, Aldrich), Ga2O3 (>99.9%, Aldrich), La2O3 (>99.9%, Aldrich) and ZrO2 (>99.9%, Aldrich). The appropriate amount of starting materials were mixed thoroughly in a pestle mortar and then pre-dried at 150 C for 30 mins in an electric vacuum drying oven. The dried mixture was annealed in a tube furnace (GSL-1700X) at 850C for 4h under the flow of dry air to remove any volatile components. The resultant powders were ground thoroughly again in the pestle mortar. Then the annealed powders were loaded into an attrition mill (JM-1L) to achieve a thorough mix and reduce the particle size. The duration for the attrition milling was varied in the range of 8 h - 96 h. Ethanol was used as the solvent and the ratio of materials and balls was 1:3 in this study. And the rotation speed was maintained 600 rpm throughout the milling process. The attrition-milled powders were dried in an electric vacuum drying oven and then thermally treated again in the tube furnace at 850C for 4h under the flow of dry air. At this stage, the obtained powders were ready for the preparation of LLZO pellets. These obtained powders were pressed into a small coin in a 15mm diameter by applying a pressure of 10MPa for 10mins. Finally, the green pellets were sintered in the tube furnace at 1230C for 6h under the flow of dry air. All the sintered pellets were polished and painted with silver paste on both sides for electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) analysis.

The particle size distribution of all the powders was characterized by the laser diffraction method (BT-9300H). The density of the samples was determined by the mass and the volume. The crystallographic structure of all the powders was identified by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) method (TD-3500x). Diffraction patterns were acquired with a Cu K radiation at room temperature between scattering angles of 10 and 80 with a step size of 0.02. EIS measurements were carried out at a Princeton Versasta3 station by applying a stimulus amplitude of 10mV over the frequency range of 0.1-1x10 Hz at both room temperature and elevated temperatures. The microstructures were examined by using a field emission scanning electron microscope (JSM-7800F).

The attrition-milled powders were dried in an electric vacuum drying oven and then thermally treated again in the tube furnace at 850C for 4h under the flow of dry air. At this stage, the obtained powders were ready for the preparation of LLZO pellets. These obtained powders were pressed into a small coin in a 15mm diameter by applying a pressure of 10MPa for 10mins. Finally, the green pellets were sintered in the tube furnace at 1230C for 6h under the flow of dry air. All the sintered pellets were polished and painted with silver paste on both sides for electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) analysis.

context.text: 2Department of Chemical Engineering, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama 36849, USA

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

The possible mechanism for the densification of LLZTO.—To study the possible mechanism for the effect of LiOH in the cover powder on the densification of LLZTO, 65Li pellets were sintered at the same sintering temperature of 1100°C for different sintering times. SEM and back scattered electron (BSE) images of fracture cross sections of 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 hours with the cover powder of 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 7.

After sintering for 1 hour (Figure 7a), there are connected pores and many small grains with sizes of 2–3 μm connected by an interparticle phase. After sintering for 4 hours (Figure 7c), the grains grew and became better connected. After 8 hours (Figure 7d), the grains have continued to grow, and the pores were reduced and did not appear to be connected. As also shown in BSE images in Figures 7g–7h, in which the interparticle phase is darker than the grains, it is found that the grain size increased, the amount of the interparticle phase decreased and the samples are still porous after the sintering of 1 hour to 8 hours (Figures 7a–7d). There is little change between 8, 16 and 32 hours sintering, as shown in Figures 7d–7f.

Tantalum appears to be relatively uniformly distributed in the sample. Compositions from ICP analysis of 65Li sintered with different cover powders and different sintering times are listed in Table IV, atomic ratio of Li:Al:La:Zr is normalized by La content as shown in the formula of Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12. The ICP analysis, which presents the overall sample composition, indicates that Al exists in all LLZTO samples, but that the amount of aluminum is higher and increases with increasing time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover. In addition, the Li content is lower in the sample sintered with 15Li cover powder than that with 15Li + LiOH cover. These results suggest that the 15Li + LiOH cover powder reduces the loss of Li and promotes the transfer of aluminum from the crucible to the sample.

The RT total Li+ conductivities of 65Li pellets sintered for 4 to 32 hours are shown in Figure 9. The conductivity increases significantly after 4 hours sintering, and it does not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. The relative densities of these pellets shown in Table V follows a similar trend to that of the total Li+ conductivities. The relative density is only 61% for pellets sintered for 4 hours, and it is larger than 80% for 8 to 32 hours. Samples sintered for 16 and 32 hours have similar relative density of 90%. As shown in Table IV, the amount of aluminum increases with increasing sintering time when sintering with a 15Li LiOH cover, and aluminum only exists at the phases between grains (Figure 8), it is concluded that the amount of Al-containing phase in the dense pellets also increases with the sintering time. The increased amount of Al-containing phase may be one reason that the conductivity does not increase as much as might be expected from the relative density change from 83 to 90%.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

In this study, a Li3BO3 (LBO) compound is synthesized via the heat-treatment of polymeric precursors containing Li and B in air at 700 C for 5 h to use as a sintering additive for the densification of Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZ) solid electrolyte. The synthesized LBO powder is suitable for promoting the densification, cubic phase stability, and ionic conductivity of LLZ. X-ray diffraction analysis indicated that monophasic cubic LLZ could be obtained by the addition of LBO in sintering, changing to cubic LLZ phase from LZ impurities detected in raw LLZ. The sintered LLZ-12 wt% LBO showed that the densification of the LLZ with LBO occurred by a coupling effect including the particle rearrangement of LLZ in the melted LBO phase and grain growth of LLZ particles. The density of the LLZ-12 wt% LBO composite sintered at 1100 C for 8 h was 3.72 g/cm3 (86% of theoretical density); the composite showed the high Li-ion conductivity of 1.18 × 10−4 S · cm−1 at 28 C.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: # II. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich, 98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z′ vs Z′′) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 × 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I. 51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li SiO to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

context.text: # Experimental

LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta O powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(R CPE )(R CPE ), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A × Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 × 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li + LiOH, which is 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

The possible mechanism for the densification of LLZTO.—To study the possible mechanism for the effect of LiOH in the cover powder on the densification of LLZTO, 65Li pellets were sintered at the same sintering temperature of 1100°C for different sintering times. SEM and back scattered electron (BSE) images of fracture cross sections of 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 hours with the cover powder of 15Li  LiOH are shown in Figure 7.

After sintering for 1 hour (Figure 7a), there are connected pores and many small grains with sizes of 2–3 μm connected by an interparticle phase. After sintering for 4 hours (Figure 7c), the grains grew and became better connected. After 8 hours (Figure 7d), the grains have continued to grow, and the pores were reduced and did not appear to be connected. As also shown in BSE images in Figures 7g–7h, in which the interparticle phase is darker than the grains, it is found that the grain size increased, the amount of the interparticle phase decreased and the samples are still porous after the sintering of 1 hour to 8 hours (Figures 7a–7d). There is little change between 8, 16 and 32 hours sintering, as shown in Figures 7d–7f.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

matches.text: In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

context.text: Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.
