context.text: All thermodynamic data were calculated between 0°C and 1000°C (the maximum calcination temperature found without excessive Li losses so that all decomposition reactions were expected to be completed) with a step size of 100°C by using a thermodynamic software (HSC Chemistry Software (Outokumpu)) and presented on 1 mole Li O, La O , and Al O formation basis under 1 atm air pressure. By using optimized data from HSC, LLZO was synthesized by solid state reaction method; 30 mole % Al was added to stabilize cubic phase. In order to evaluate the performance, stoichiometric amounts of thermodynamically favored powders along with ZrO2 were mixed in agate mortar grinder (Retsch RM200) for 1 hour. The excess Li to compensate Li losses during calcination and sintering was selected as 15 mol %. Powders were calcined at 1000°C which was established to be the highest calcination temperature to prevent excessive Li losses for 6 hours and then sintered at 1000°C, 1100°C, and 1200°C which was lower than the minimum temperature required for cubic phase stabilization without Al stabilizer addition for 12 hours within its powder bed. After calcination, powders were ground again for 1 hour, and 1.5 g of calcined powders was isostatically pressed to obtained pellets (15 mm diameter) at 240 MPa for 45 minutes; 10°C/min heating rate was set for calcination and sintering studies.

context.text: In this study, we fabricated and characterized two kinds of Al-doped Li La Zr O (LLZO) powders with the modified sol–gel synthesis and solid-state processing, respectively. Moreover, the two kinds of LLZO powders were compared in detail examining the powder size and processing window for the cubic phase. In the case of the sol–gel synthesis, the processed powder exhibited a pure cubic phase with little secondary phases such as Li-deficient pyrochlore or LaAlO at calcination temperatures above 900 -C and a mixed phase of cubic and tetragonal structure at 800 -C. However, in the solid-state processed powder, the tetragonal phase was converted to a cubic one at a temperature of 1000 -C. When the amount of Li addition was varied, sol–gel synthesized LLZO powder also had a much wider range for cubic phases than that of the solid-state processed one. matches.text: In this study, we fabricated and characterized two kinds of Al-doped Li La Zr O (LLZO) powders with the modified sol–gel synthesis and solid-state processing, respectively. Moreover, the two kinds of LLZO powders were compared in detail examining the powder size and processing window for the cubic phase. In the case of the sol–gel synthesis, the processed powder exhibited a pure cubic phase with little secondary phases such as Li-deficient pyrochlore or LaAlO at calcination temperatures above 900 -C and a mixed phase of cubic and tetragonal structure at 800 -C. However, in the solid-state processed powder, the tetragonal phase was converted to a cubic one at a temperature of 1000 -C. When the amount of Li addition was varied, sol–gel synthesized LLZO powder also had a much wider range for cubic phases than that of the solid-state processed one. context.text: The XRD patterns of the Al-doped LLZO powders prepared by sol–gel and by solid-state at various calcination temperatures are compared in Figure 3. For the sol–gel LLZO powder, very small LLZO peaks were observed at the lowest temperature of 700 -C, implying that the driving energy for the transformation to the cubic phase is insufficient. The result is in good agreement with the TG/DSC results in Figure 2. At a temperature of 800 -C, the sol–gel LLZO powder has mixed cubic and tetragonal phases. And almost pure cubic phases are obtained above 900 -C. The determination was followed by a comparison with the ICSD collection codes 183686 (cubic LLZO, drawn in Fig. 3 for the comparison) and 183685 (tetragonal LLZO).22 At the high temperatures, some secondary phases such as Li deficient La Zr O and LaAlO phases are observed because significant Li loss could occur. In contrast, the LLZO powder processed by the solid-state reaction has tetragonal phases even at 900 -C. This is also evident from the peak splitting observed at various angles. A high temperature of 1000 -C is required to obtain a pure cubic phase in the solid-state LLZO powder. The XRD patterns of the solid-state LLZO powder contains more secondary phase peaks, compared to those of the sol–gel one.

context.text: In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

context.text: In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich,  98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z vs Z) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

context.text: Figure 1 shows the TG curve of the LLZO precursor solution fired in air in the temperature range from 30 to 1000 ◦C. The first weight change was observed for the disappearance of the residual solvent in the range 100 - 120 ◦C. The decomposition of PVP, which was used as a chelating agent, occurred at 330 ◦C, and the formation of the initial garnet phase through decomposition of the nitrate species and organic materials occurred at 350 - 600 ◦C. No significant weight change was observed at temperatures above 600 - 700 ◦C, indicating that the transformation of the mixture precursor to a crystalline oxide starts at temperatures above this range. Based on this observation, the cubic phase was confirmed to have been formed most stably at a temperature of 800 ◦C or higher.

context.text: Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = L(A R) , where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 × 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 × 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

context.text: Figure 4(c) shows the temperature dependence of the total ionic conductivity (Arrhenius plot) of the LLZO pellets at temperatures of 25 - 70 ◦C, where the Arrhenius equation is given by σ = AT exp - −EakBT  , where σ is the ionic conductivity, T is the absolute temperature, A is the pre-exponential constant, kB is the Boltzmann constant and Ea is the activation energy for the ionic conductivity. The activation energy for the LLZO material is lower (0.53 eV) than that for the reference LLZO material (0.67 eV) [26]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: # ABSTRACT

Lithium-ion (Li+) batteries suffer from problems caused by the chemical instability of their organic electrolyte. Solid-state electrolytes that exhibit high ionic conductivities and stable to lithium metal are potential replacements for flammable organic electrolytes. Garnet-type Li,LazZrO12 is a promising solid-state electrolyte for next-generation solidstate Li batteries. In this study, we prepared mono-, dual-, and ternary-doped lithium (Li) garnets by doping tantalum (Ta), tantalum-barium (Ta-Ba), and tantalum-bariumgallium (Ta-Ba-Ga) ions, along with undoped-Li,LazZrO (LLZO) cubic garnet electrolyte, using a conventional solid-state reaction method. The effect of multi-ion doping on the Li+ dynamics in the garnet-type LLZO was studied by combining analyses of joint Rietveld refinement against X-ray diffraction and high-resolution neutron powder diffraction with the results of Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and multinuclear magic angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance. Our results revealed that Li+ occupancy in the tetrahedrally coordinated site (24d) increased with increased multi-ion doping in LLZO, whereas Li+ occupancy in the octahedrally coordinated site (96h) remained constant. Among the investigated compounds, the ternary-doped garnet structure Li6.65Gao.05La2.95Ba0.05Zr1.75Tao.25O12 (LGLBZTO) exhibited the highest total ionic conductivity of 0.72 and 1.24 mS cm-1 at room temperature and 60 C, respectively. Overall, our findings revealed that the dense microstructure and increased Li+ occupancy in the tetrahedral-24du site played a key role in achieving the maximum roomtemperature Li-ion conductivity in ternary-doped LGLBZTO garnet, and that the prepared ternary-doped LGLBZTO was a potential solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries without polymer adhesion.

context.text: EDX mapping was carried out for the undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dualdoped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO samples to detect the respective dopants and their composition on grains and grain boundaries (Fig. 3). EDX analysis revealed that the Al was exclusively found in the undoped LLZO sample at the grain boundaries. The localization of O, La, Zr, and dopant ions (Ta, Ba, and Ga) was uniformly distributed among the crystal grains. Furthermore, a predominant distribution of Ga, Ba, and Ta was observed mainly inside the grains in the EDX maps, which confirmed the inclusion of dopant ions in the garnet lattice.

To study the effect of doping on Li+ transportation, the ionic conductivities of the undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dual-doped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO were measured using the AC impedance technique with Au as the blocking electrode. A typical Nyquist impedance plot for the ternary-doped LGLBZTO (Li6.65Gao.05La2.95Bao.0sZr1.75Tao.25O12)withAu|LGLBZTO|Au configuration was recorded at room temperature (Fig. 4a). The undoped LLZO, mono-doped LLZTO, dualdoped LLBZTO, and ternary-doped LGLBZTO all showed one partially depressed semicircle at the high-frequency region with a low-frequency diffusion spike. This semicircle can be assigned as the total impedance, including the contribution from bulk and grain boundary impedances, and the low-frequency spike can be attributed to Li+ blocking at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The impedance data were fitted using an equivalent circuit model consisting of (R;)(Rg,CPEg)(CPE). The right intercept of the semicircle on the real axis at the high-frequency region represents the bulk resistance of the sample, which was denoted as R, in the equivalent circuit. Rg was referred as grain boundary resistance; CPEg, and CPE were referred as the constant phase element contributions attributed to the grain boundary capacitance, and the diffusion capacitance at the electrode/electrolyte interface, respectively. The diameter of the semicircle at the middle frequency corresponded to the total resistance, which is the sum of the resistance of the grain and grain boundary response (R, + Rgt). The contributions of grain and grain boundary responses were difficult to distinguish from the impedance spectra. The total Li-ion conductivity of the specimen, ot (S cm-1), was achieved by the total resistance normalized with respect to the thickness and cross-sectional area of the specimen. The Li-ion conductivity of the LLZO cubic garnet depends on various key factors, such as (i) mobile Li+ concentration, (ii) Li+ vacancy (VLi) concentration, (ii) bottleneck size for Li+ migration, (iv) Coulombic repulsion between Li+-Li+ pair, and (v) specimen microstructure.40, 4549 It is well known that the nominal cubic garnet-type structure, Li7La3Zr2O12 is not stable at room temperature due the high Coulombic repulsion between Li+-Li+ pair.50 In the mono-doped LLZTO, the substitution of high valence of Ta5+ for Zr4+ led to Li+ vacancies and reduced Li+ concentration for charge compensation, which promoted the Li+ motion in the LLZTO framework. The substitution of Ta5+ for Zr4+ reduced the Coulombic repulsion between Li+-Li+ pair by creating Li+ vacancies. As a result, the mono-doped LLZTO showed conductivity higher than that of the undoped LLZO. Although VLi can promote ionic conductivity, there should be an optimal VLi. The excess increment of Vli may result in reduced mobile Li+ concentration in the garnet framework, which might reflect in low conductivities. Dual substation strategy can improve the Li+ dynamics in Sb-Ba co-doped LLZO.51 In the dual-doped LLBZTO, the substitution of Ta5+ for Zr4+ and Ba2+ for La3+ may lead to optimal Li+ concentration. Furthermore, the larger ionic radius r of Ba2+ than La3+ may cause lattice expansion, which enlarged the bottleneck size for Li+ migration and thereby resulted in a conductivity higher than that of the undoped LLZO and mono-doped LLZTO.

The Li rearrangement took place between the tetrahedral-24du1 and octahedral96hLi2 sites due to the electrostatic repulsion of either Li+-Li+ pair or Li+-dopant ion pair in the LLZO framework.48 The strong electrostatic repulsion of Li+-dopant ion pair may affect the neighboring Li+ site, which can lead to the high mobility of Li+. Therefore, the Coulombic interaction between Li+ and dopant cation was a determining factor for Li-ion conductivities. Strategic doping of ions at the Li site in the LLZO may create strong Coulombic repulsion between dopant ion and Lit, which can influence the mobility of Li+. In the ternary-doped LGLBZTO, the substitution of Ta5+ for Zr4+, Ba2+ for La3, and immobile Ga3+ for Li+ created a strong Coulombic repulsion at the Li site, added to the enlarged bottleneck size from Ba doping. Hence, we can expect a high conductivity for the ternary-doped LGLBZTO, attributed to the enhanced Li+ mobility arising from the Coulombic repulsion between Li+ ions and dopant Ga ion. With the increased amount of doped ions, the total conductivity linearly increased. The optimum total ionic conductivity (0i) achieved for the ternary-doped LGLBZTO (Li6.65Ga0.05La2.95Bao.05Zr1.75Tao.25O12) was 0.72 and 1.24 mS cm-1 at room temperature and 60 C, respectively.

As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = (ALR), where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(R CPE )(R CPE ), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A × Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 × 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li + LiOH, which is 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: # Introduction

Interest in Li-ion batteries (LIBs) is constantly growing from portable electronics; to electric vehicles; to flexible batteries in wearable electronics.1–3 Along with this increasing demand for LIBs, substitution of conventional flammable and volatile liquid electrolytes with inorganic solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) is essential to improve the safety and capabilities of the batteries.4 Thin film based all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) facilitate miniaturization of microelectronic devices and flexible batteries with higher safety and energy densities.2 In addition to the chemical and electrochemical stability, mechanical stability in particular at the interface of SSE/electrode of ASSBs is also essential for the batteries performances. On one hand, microcracks can form due to elevated internal and/or external stresses, leading to the crack propagation, delamination, and fragmentation of electrodes and SSEs/electrode interfaces. For example, electrode volume changes during charging/discharging increases internal stresses and introduces bending/ stretching to the SSE which eventually aggregate the formation of microcracks.5–9 On the other hand, Li dendrite formation and growth introduces stress at the SSE/Li electrode interface that results in mechanical deformation which is the very complex phenomena because all chemical, electrochemical, and mechanical factors are involved.6,10 Two main types of SSEs are polymer and inorganic electrolytes. Polymer SSEs are believed to facilitate the interfacial contact issues due to their soft and flexible nature, however the volume changes of electrodes especially Li anode, introduce partial delamination at the interface.11 Inorganic ceramic SSEs are also fabricated because of their higher strength and stability in air, while their poor interface stability remains as an issue.12 Among thin film fabrication techniques, atomic layer deposition (ALD) enables uniform, pinhole-free ultra-thin films which provides good interfacial contact between inorganic SSEs/ electrodes.13–15 Despite such contact establishment, the contact needs to be mechanically stable. Previous research has suggested that elastic deformation of SSEs materials accompanied by some degree of ductility is desirable to maintain good interfacial contact with an electrode during cycling in order to preserve the battery cycling performance.13,14,16 Low stiffness sulfide SSEs with a low range of Young’s modulus (E) (14–25 GPa for Li2S-P2S5) 8,17,18 were considered as favorable SSEs for the bulk battery design to accommodate volume changes of the electrodes.8 However, Bucci et al.19 developed a cohesive zone model to simulate damage evaluation and presented quantitative conditions that facture would occur. They indicated that electrolytes with E ∼ 15 GPa were more prone to micro-cracking in compare to SSEs with higher E. Based on this model for SSEs with E = 15 GPa, fracture was prevented when the electrode expansion was below 7.5%, and the fracture energy of SSEs was greater than Gc = 4 J m−2 . In addition, oxide electrolytes exhibiting high E (77, 150, and 192 GPa in amorphous LLZO, LIPON, and Li La TiO , respectively)16,20,21 have been reported; however, the impact of inorganic SSEs mechanical behavior on battery performance is unknown. Moreover, there are a few models that incorporated electro-chemo-mechanical behavior of solid electrolytes to address interface stability in contact with Li metal. Li nucleation in the grain boundary of ceramic electrolyte was modeled by Raj and Wolfenstine22 with coupling mechanical stresses and the electrical potential. They showed that critical current above Li nucleation depends on ionic conductivity and fracture strength of the SSE. Monroe and Newman23,24 modeled the lithium deposition in a polymer electrolyte and considered the contribution of bulk and surface stresses to Li deposition electrochemical reactions. They concluded that deposition stability increased by increasing electrolyte shear modulus because of more contribution of bulk pressure and surface stresses. Based on Monroe and Newman model,24 researchers constructed hybrid SSEs with high modulus (elastic of shear modulus) to suppress dendrite formation and growth, however it has been found that Li dendrite can grow and penetrate both polymer and rigid ceramics.25–27 It is still unclear which model can explain the mechanisms of Li dendrite growth. The SSE modulus is not the only mechanical factor that limits the Li dendrite growth and other mechanical properties such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, and flexure strength of brittle inorganic SSEs require more attention. Recently organic, inorganic and hybrid coating layers have shown potentials for suppressing Li dendrite at the interface of SSE/ Li metal.15 Fu et al.,28 designed and developed a hybrid system of polymer embedded with nano-sized ceramic domains called as “soft ceramic” structure as dendrite-suppressing SSE by applying a universal chemomechanical model that can assess fundamentally pressure- or density-driven dendrite suppressing. In addition to all the efforts on modelling and designing compatible interfaces, a study by LePage et al. 29 showed that “creep” is a dominant deformation mechanism for Li metal in batteries which further complicates the interfacial mechanical stability issues. These studies show that better understanding of mechanical behavior of nanoscale organic and inorganic SSEs are essential prior to investigate their theoretical and experimental electro-chemomechanical implications.

Previously studied amorphous LPO and LTO thin films with moderate ionic conductivity (∼10−8 S cm−1 at 25 °C) have been used as SSEs for ASSBs,30,31 and as coating layers on the electrodes of LIBs to significantly improve the battery performance.31–35 A summary of electrochemical studies of the impact of LTO and LPO coatings on electrode materials in LIBs cyclic performance is presented in Table 1. Both LPO and LTO exhibited electrochemical and chemical stability, and ionic conductivity for coating cathode materials as well as facilitating better contact between electrode materials and electrolytes as shown in Table 1.31–34 The mechanism behind preserving the structural degradation of electrode material is not well understood and a more detailed understanding of the mechanical stability of SSEs in ASSBs against internal and/or external stresses during charging/discharging is needed.14,15 In this study, the elastic and fracture behavior of ALD prepared LTO, and LPO SSEs thin films were studied and compared for the first time. The mechanical behavior of a range of ultra-thin ALD prepared suspended SSEs thin films (5 nm–30 nm thickness) were studied using an atomic force microscope (AFM) film deflection technique. The film under AFM deflection emulates stress levels present in the SSE at the nanoscale, and the results will help to identify the potential influence of SSEs mechanical performances for on their operation in flexible ASSBs.

Polymer SSEs are believed to facilitate the interfacial contact issues due to their soft and flexible nature, however the volume changes of electrodes especially Li anode, introduce partial delamination at the interface.11 Inorganic ceramic SSEs are also fabricated because of their higher strength and stability in air, while their poor interface stability remains as an issue.12 Among thin film fabrication techniques, atomic layer deposition (ALD) enables uniform, pinhole-free ultra-thin films which provides good interfacial contact between inorganic SSEs/ electrodes.13–15 Despite such contact establishment, the contact needs to be mechanically stable. Previous research has suggested that elastic deformation of SSEs materials accompanied by some degree of ductility is desirable to maintain good interfacial contact with an electrode during cycling in order to preserve the battery cycling performance.13,14,16 Low stiffness sulfide SSEs with a low range of Young’s modulus (E) (14–25 GPa for Li2S-P2S5) 8,17,18 were considered as favorable SSEs for the bulk battery design to accommodate volume changes of the electrodes.8 However, Bucci et al.19 developed a cohesive zone model to simulate damage evaluation and presented quantitative conditions that facture would occur. They indicated that electrolytes with E ∼ 15 GPa were more prone to micro-cracking in compare to SSEs with higher E. Based on this model for SSEs with E = 15 GPa, fracture was prevented when the electrode expansion was below 7.5%, and the fracture energy of SSEs was greater than Gc = 4 J m−2 . In addition, oxide electrolytes exhibiting high E (77, 150, and 192 GPa in amorphous LLZO, LIPON, and Li La TiO , respectively)16,20,21 have been reported; however, the impact of inorganic SSEs mechanical behavior on battery performance is unknown. Moreover, there are a few models that incorporated electro-chemo-mechanical behavior of solid electrolytes to address interface stability in contact with Li metal. Li nucleation in the grain boundary of ceramic electrolyte was modeled by Raj and Wolfenstine22 with coupling mechanical stresses and the electrical potential. They showed that critical current above Li nucleation depends on ionic conductivity and fracture strength of the SSE. Monroe and Newman23,24 modeled the lithium deposition in a polymer electrolyte and considered the contribution of bulk and surface stresses to Li deposition electrochemical reactions. They concluded that deposition stability increased by increasing electrolyte shear modulus because of more contribution of bulk pressure and surface stresses. Based on Monroe and Newman model,24 researchers constructed hybrid SSEs with high modulus (elastic of shear modulus) to suppress dendrite formation and growth, however it has been found that Li dendrite can grow and penetrate both polymer and rigid ceramics.25–27 It is still unclear which model can explain the mechanisms of Li dendrite growth. The SSE modulus is not the only mechanical factor that limits the Li dendrite growth and other mechanical properties such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, and flexure strength of brittle inorganic SSEs require more attention. Recently organic, inorganic and hybrid coating layers have shown potentials for suppressing Li dendrite at the interface of SSE/ Li metal.15 Fu et al.,28 designed and developed a hybrid system of polymer embedded with nano-sized ceramic domains called as “soft ceramic” structure as dendrite-suppressing SSE by applying a universal chemomechanical model that can assess fundamentally pressure- or density-driven dendrite suppressing. In addition to all the efforts on modelling and designing compatible interfaces, a study by LePage et al. 29 showed that “creep” is a dominant deformation mechanism for Li metal in batteries which further complicates the interfacial mechanical stability issues. These studies show that better understanding of mechanical behavior of nanoscale organic and inorganic SSEs are essential prior to investigate their theoretical and experimental electro-chemomechanical implications.

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

matches.text: Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li + LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. The activation energy for all samples is from 0.20 to 0.39 eV, but the conductivities of samples sintered with 15Li LiOH cover are significantly higher than those sintered with a 15Li cover powder. The activation energy of 0.2 eV for 30Li sintered with 15Li LiOH cover is lower than other reported values which are in the range of 0.3–0.4 eV.16,32,35,40,58,59 The EIS tests were performed in a narrow temperature range (20–40°C). Further EIS study is needed to figure out the reason for this low activation energy by obtaining more data points in the EIS tests on 30Li samples, which could be realized by performing the EIS test from a lower temperatures (below 20°C) to 40°C or in a shorter time interval between 20 and 40°C, like 5°C interval time instead of currently used 10°C.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

context.text: The microstructure of the Li7La3Zr2O12 powder and the cross-section of the pellet observed using SEM and AFM are shown in Fig. 3. As one can observe in the images, the particles are uneven, and the pellet has large particles and larger voids. The voids were revealed in the SEM image of the pellet (Fig. 3(c)), and the height deviation is large due to the voids seen in the AFM image (Fig. 3(d)). These voids inside the pellet reduce the density of the material and increase its resistance, thereby reducing its ionic conductivity [17,20].

Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = L(A R) , where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 × 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 × 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. [26] (3.12 10−7 S/cm), but is lower than the value for other cubic materials [15, 17]. This is a result of the impurity phase and the many voids observed from the XRD results and the SEM images.

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

The investigation of ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes at room temperature reported in the last two years is shown as the histogram in Figure 6 (The highest/lowest ionic conductivity of the various structural families counted here does not represent the limits they can achieve, but only based on the studies reported during this period). We have made a simple classification of the structural family, including Garnet type represented by Li7La3Zr2O12,[57] NASICON-like represented by Li1+xAlxTi2-x(PO4)3 (LATP),[58] Lithium-Sulfide represented by Li3PS4 (LISICON-like) and Li2S-P2S5 glass ceramics,[59] Perovskite represented by Li3xLa2/3−x□1/3−xTiO3 (LLTO),[60] and various composite polymer electrolytes (CPEs).[61] For the Na+ solid-state electrolytes, the ionic conductivity of sodium sulfide[59i,62] and various structures (NASICON type, borohydride, etc.)[61c,63] are mainly counted. The K+ solid-state electrolytes are no longer listed here due to the lack of reports. In the Garnet type structure, the ionic conductivity can be largely regulated by cation doping, the highly self-textured garnet-type lithium-ion conducting solid electrolyte of LLZO-Ga exhibits an extremely high ionic conductivity (2.06 × 10-3 S cm-1 at room temperature).[57c] Similarly, in NASICON-like structure, Li1+xTi2-xScx(PO4)3 doped with Sc exhibits an ion conductivity of up to 2.5 × 10-3 S cm-1 (X = 0.2),[58a] This is comparable to or even better than the LATP[58d,58e] reported in the literature. In Lithium

Sulfides, Li10GeP2S12 with LISICON-like structure has the highest ionic conductivity reported in this kind of materials (more than 10- 2 S cm-1 at room temperature[59e]). The ionic conductivity can be improved by adjusting the ratio of the two phases in the Li2S-P2S5 glass ceramic, the highest ionic conductivity reaches 4.8×10-3 S cm-1 after the doping of MoS2.[59i] The ionic conductivity of the Perovskite structure itself is only about 10-4 S cm-1,[60b,60d] but it could be greatly improved after compounding with other materials.[60a,60c] Studies on solid polymer electrolytes have focused on complexing with metal oxide nanoparticles, LLZO, and various polymers.[61] In the study of Na+ solid-state electrolytes, the equivalent substitution of Na3PS4 showed a significant increase in ionic conductivity,[59i,62a,62b] up to 3.7 × 10-3 S cm-1.[59i] However, the sodium sulfide Na10GeP2S12 with similar structure of Li10GeP2S12 does not show commensurately high ionic conductivity of Na+.[62e] The Na1+nZr2SinP3-nO12 possessing a NASICON type structure achieves ionic conductivity of up to 3.4 × 10-3 S cm-1, and even reaches 1.4 × 10-2 S cm-1 at 80 °C. The ionic conductivities of different structural families are strongly dependent on the internal crystal structure and conduction machanisim, which will be discussed in section 3.3.1. The latest computational studies will also be statistically discussed in the following section.

context.text: Diffusion of an alkali metal ion in the crystalline material is strongly dependent upon the interaction potential between the alkali metal ions and the host material structure. Figure 10 shows a lot of representative crystal structures.[98] According to the diffusion path of ions in the crystal, various structure types can be classified, such as materials with 1D channel (e.g. LiFePO4, Figure 10a), 2D layer structure(e.g. LiCoO2 and graphite, Figure 10b,e), and 3D diffusion channel (e.g. LiMn2O4, Figure 10c). However, such classification is not entirely applicable. The research on polymorphic LiFeSO4F (tavorite and triplite)[99] shows that, although the calculated migration energy proves that both isomorphs are Li+ conductors, the Li+ in triplite type LiFeSO4F move in a restricted migration path (one or two dimensions). while the tavorite type has continuous three-dimensional conductive network for Li+. Similarly, Li10GeP2S12 can be classified into a 3D conductor or a pseudo 1D conductor.

The conduction path and mechanism of ions in inorganic solid-state electrolytes (Figure 10f-j) is more complicated. The Garnet type (Figure 10f) is derived from the ideal garnet structure with the general formula A3B2(XO4)3, Li+ ions usually occupy the tetrahedral positions of X-site which is 4-fold coordinated. Meier et al.[79] identified the mechanisms (Figure 11a) responsible for the considerable difference in ionic conductivity between the tetragonal and the cubic phases of LLZO (Li7La3Zr2O12). In tetragonal LLZO, the motion of Li ions is of fully collective nature or synchronous, which requires a higher activation energy. However, in cubic LLZO, the asynchronous collective motion of Li ions caused by single ion hopping results in lower activation energy due to the presence of unoccupied Li sites. Substitution of Zr[100] with Ta, Sb, etc. can improve the distribution of Li ions in the crystal structure of LLZO and improve the ionic conductivity. Recent reports[101] indicate that when stabilizing the garnetstructured LLZO with Ga3+, it shows superior properties compared to LLZO stabilized with supervalent cations (such as Al3+). In the NASICON-like LiTi2(PO4)3 (Figure 10g) framework, Li ions occupy two sites of M1 and M2 (Figure 11b),[102] and lithium migration occurs through the jump between these two sites (Figure 11c). The partial occupancy of Li+ ions at these two sites is critical for fast Li+ ion conduction. The Li+ ion conduction activation energy decreases linearly with the bottleneck size between the M1 and M2 sites.[103] Li ions are introduced for charge compensation by substitution of a trivalent cation such as Al3+, but these additional Li ions are trapped near the trivalent ions, resulting in a limited increase in ion conductivity. The LISICON-like Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS) (Figure 10h) has the highest Li+ ion conductivity[104] reported so far because it forms a one-dimensional channel with very high Li mobility. The conduction path of Li+ ions in the b direction and the c direction is shown in Figure 11d,[105] and the recent theoretical calculation[106] shows that it is also possible for Li+ to diffuse in the ab plane. In the latest study, Paulus et al.[105] used spin-aligned echo (SAE) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques to directly detect the slow Li+ ion transitions with correlation times as low as about 10-5 s, which provides a new way to understand the mobility of Li+ in three dimensions. By introducing Li ions into the perovskite structure by heterovalent ion doping, a composition of Li3xLa2/3−x□1/3−xTiO3 (Figure 10i) can be obtained. The introduction of Li+ ions changes the concentration of lithium and vacancies, and its interaction[107] can significantly affect ionic conductivity. LLTO has a high volume ionic conductivity, but due to the high electrical resistance at the grain boundaries, its total conductivity tends to be two orders of magnitude lower than the volume ion conductivity.

Since different ions have different ionic radii, the introduction of other elements usually produces a change in lattice parameters[116] or phase transitions[101]. Figure 14a[117] shows the doping concentration dependence of the unit cell volume of Li3K3Ce2(BH4)12 and Li3K3La2(BH4)12 for different divalent cation (Ca2+, Sr2+, Eu2+) substitutions. For Sr2+, Eu2+ cations, the unit cell volume increases significantly as the doping concentration increases, and as a result, the Li+ ionic conductivities of the samples doped with divalent Sr2+ and Eu2+ are increased by an order of magnitude (Figure 14b/c) over the entire temperature range. So how does the change in lattice volume caused by doping of different elements affect the ionic conductivity? The key is that the increase in lattice volume can effectively reduce the activation energy within a certain range. Bachman et al.[25] made detailed statistics on change of activation energy and ionic conductivity changes caused by lattice volume. The study by Lang et al.[102] also proves that the substitution of Ti atoms in LTP by various trivalent, tetravalent and pentavalent cations X (LXTP) leads to structural changes, thus affecting Li mobility. The minimum energy path (MEP) of the Li jump between adjacent M1 sites is obtained by the nudged elastic band (NEB) method (as shown in Figure 14d), and the calculated activation energy of the migration vacancy is between 0.29 eV and 0.75 eV, which is related to the size of the LiO6 octahedron in the structure. Figure 14e/f further shows that the structures with a vacant Li position inside a larger polyhedron are more stable, this is because O atoms bind the Li+ ion more tightly in smaller polyhedral cages than in larger ones due to the 1/r dependence of the electrostatic Coulomb interaction. Shin et al.[118] demonstrated that the multidoping of additional Ta dopants in Al-doped LLZO shifts the most energetic favorable position of Al in the crystal structure from 24 d to 96 h Li sites, thereby it provides more open space for Li ion transportation. This synergistic effect makes the ion conductivity (6.14 × 10-4 S cm-1) of multi-doped LLZO approximately three times higher than that of single-doped LLZO. The substitution of elements can affect the lattice volume, while the direct doping of compounds can also significantly modify the ion conduction behavior. For example, Subbu et al.[119] observed the improvement of ionic conductivity in polymer electrolytes prepared by complexation of lithium salts with polyethylene oxide (PEO) and polyvinylidene chloride-co-acrylonitrile (PVdC-co-AN), and among the various lithium salts studied, the lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate [LiN(CF3SO2)2]-based electrolyte exhibits the highest ionic conductivity at room temperature of

0.265 × 10-5 S cm-1. Iranipour et al.[120] recently reported studies on the equilibrium phase behavior and the effect of lithium salt (lithium tetrafluoroborate) on the organic ionic plastic crystal (OIPC), N-ethyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium tetrafluoroborate [C2mpyr] [BF4]. In addition to the equilibrium phase transformations of the pure OIPC, new transitions are observed after the addition of the lithium salt (10 mol% and 20 mol% LiBF4), which significantly alters the ion conduction behavior of the material. The doping of these polymers usually has an important relationship with their concentration, but due to the lack of systematic theoretical research on the conduction in polymers, further exploration of its influencing factors is needed.

context.text: Recently, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been widely used as power sources for portable electronic devices, such as mobile phones, laptops and for electric vehicles owing to their high energy and power density [1–3]. However, common LIBs are based on flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which carry the inherent risks of leakage, fire, and explosion. For this reason, solid-state electrolytes with fast Li-ion diffusion were recognized as promising alternatives [4,5]. Thus, extensive efforts have been made to develop lithium-ion conductive inorganic materials, including NASICON, perovskite, and sulfide glasses, for use as solid electrolytes, an important component of all-solid lithium-ion batteries [6–10].

In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

In this research, cubic LLZO was synthesized through a solution-based synthesis method without any extrinsic dopants at temperatures lower than 1000 ◦C. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was used as the chelating agent, and the cubic phase was confirmed by using XRay diffraction. Finally, AC impedance measurements were conducted to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the synthesized material.

matches.text: In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

context.text: # III. CONCLUSION

An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

Garnet-type metal oxide such as Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is considered as one of the most promising solid electrolytes among the inorganic solid electrolytes4, for it shows high Li+ ionic conductivity, high stability with lithium metal and wide electrochemical window5. The sintering process6, doping strategy7-9, microstructure10 and composite design11 have been widely investigated to enhance its performance. The LLZO solid electrolyte can be synthesized by solid state reaction12, sol-gel method13, spark plasma sintering14 and hot-press sintering method15. Solid state reaction at high temperature is preferred because the cost is relatively low and the procedure is simple, which is suitable for large-scale industrial producing. The LLZO electrolyte sample prepared by solid state reaction has a moderate ionic conductivity in the order of 10-4 S/cm. Doping various elements into LLZO can increase the Li-ion conductivity and the Ta doped sample, Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12(x=0.6), has an ionic conductivity of about 1×10-3 S/cm 16, 17. However, because of the high volatility nature of Li element, Li is easy to lose during the high temperature sintering which leads to form the undesirable La2Zr2O7 as an impure phase. In order to prepare the stoichiometric LLZO, the lost Li should be compensated and the most common means is to cover the tablet samples up with the mother powder 18. The mother powder with the same chemistry composition as the samples acts as the sacrificial component to ensure the sample to form the right garnet phase. The amount of the sacrificed mother powder usually reaches the ratio 1:1 in weight to the samples and after sintering, the mother powder cannot be reused. That is the problem, as we know that the mother powder contains the rare earth element La and the element Ta that are expensive. Therefore, the conventional solid state reaction with mother powder protecting method is not economical. We noticed that the effect of the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

mother powder is merely providing another Li source to compensate the lost Li. We proposed an alternative method to compensate the lost Li where the mother powder is replaced by Li2CO3. In this method, Li2CO3 is separated from the sample and it will melt and decompound above 730ºC. The decomposed Li2CO3 provides a Li2O atmosphere and ensures the sample to form the pure garnet phase. The method is also suitable for other oxide solid electrolytes. Li2CO3 is much cheaper than the mother powder and this method will lower the synthesis cost of LLZO as well as other oxide solid electrolytes, which is important for the large-scale application of the solid state batteries in the future.

LLZO is usually prepared by solid-state reaction at high temperature above 1100 °C. In the experiment, Al2O3 was added to the preheated powders as a sintering aid that will form a liquid of LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4 eutectic 19. As Li2CO3 is much more excessive, the sintering temperature might be lowered. We prepared the LLZTO samples with 1g Li2CO3 providing the protective atmosphere (L1 sample) at different temperatures. Fig.3 (a) shows the XRD patterns of L1 samples prepared at 1060°C, 1100°C and 1140°C respectively. All these samples have LLZTO as the main phase and there exists LiAlO2 phase. As it can be seen in the patterns, the intensity of LiAlO2 increases as temperature increasing and the samples prepared at 1140°C contain considerable amount of LiAlO2. Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2, 5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 × 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g  1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g  0.94) and Li(2) site (g  0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22
