matches.text: Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2, 5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 × 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

context.text: Doping elements are usually used to stabilize the cubic phase from the tetragonal phase, which is performed by substituting cations for Li, La or Zr.18,23 Substitution of Al, Ga, Fe for Li,24–28 Rb, Nd, Ca, Ba for La,29–31 and/or Nb, Ta, Y for Zr30,32–35 have been reported. Aluminum contamination from the crucible has been found to be helpful in stabilizing the cubic phase.25 The reaction between Al2O3 from the crucible and LiOH or Li2CO3 has resulted in the production of an Al-containing phase, which plays two roles. A small amount of Al in the garnet phase could stabilize the cubic structure relative to the tetragonal phase.25 Secondly, a liquid phase introduced by the reaction between Li2O and Al2O3 could facilitate the sintering.27 According to the Li2O-Al2O3 phase diagram, a eutectic liquid forms at 23 mol% Al2O3, which has a melting point of 1055°C.36 This Al-containing phase has also been reported in other studies, and is typically located between grains.13,27,37

The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

A dense microstructure is also needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities (e.g. 8.9 × 10−6 S/cm at 25°C).43 Hot-pressing can be used to obtain an almost dense microstructure.41,44,45 Other methods like cold isostatic pressing,46–48 field assisted sintering technology,49 flowing oxygen sintering,50 sintering with microwave hybrid furnace,37 have also been reported to be effective methods to increase the density.

context.text: SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.

Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(R CPE )(R CPE ), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A × Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 × 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li + LiOH, which is 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. Arrhenius plots of total Li+ conductivities for 30Li and 65Li sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with different cover powders are shown in Figure 6 and the corresponding activation energies (Ea) are tabulated in Table II. context.text: Rechargeable lithium ion batteries have been widely used as energy sources for electronic mobile devices and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) because of their high energy densities. Recently, some researchers have tried to solve safety concerns by eliminating the liquid electrolyte and building an entirely solid-state battery that uses a ceramic electrolyte to separate the lithium anode from the cathode.1–3 The properties of the interface between the solid electrode and the solid electrolyte are one of the most important factors in fabricating an all-solid-state lithium ion battery.

Many types of solid-state electrolytes have been explored, including perovskite titanates, NASICON phosphates, LISICON sulfides, and cubic garnets. Among these materials, Li La Zr O (LLZO) with a cubic garnet structure has an ionic conductivity of above approximately 10−4 S/cm at room temperature and good thermal and chemical stability against prospective electrodes such as Li metal.4 5 Thus, the challenge has been to stabilize the cubic form because the conductivity of the tetragonal phase at room temperature is about 2 orders of magnitude lower than that of the cubic phase.5 6 Long sintering at a high temperature has been thought to be the key factor for controlling the transformation from tetragonal to cubic.7–10 However, improvement of its ionic conductivity is hindered by the high porosity related to the severe volatilization of the lithium components during high temperature sintering. Therefore, the most effective method for forming the cubic phase has been to dope some elements such as Al,11–13 Ta,14 15 Nb,10 16 and Sb17 during the preparation process.

The most famous method for fabricating a LLZO powder source has been the solid-state reaction because of its simplicity; however, the calcination temperature is so high that there exists unstable stoichiometry resulting from lithium volatilization and processing difficulty.7 8 10–12 18 Additionally, there has been much interest in the sol–gel synthesis of LLZO powder because of its many advantages in preparing a ceramic source, including a relatively low processing temperature, and the possibility of excellent control of the stoichiometry and homogeneous materials when using large amounts.19 20 To the best of the authors’ knowledge, few studies have been done directly comparing the two promising methods in a similar system and conditions.

context.text: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109-2125

The effect of relative density on the hardness and fracture toughness of Al-substituted cubic garnet Li6.19Al0.27La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) was investigated. Polycrystalline LLZO was made using solid-state synthesis and hot-pressing. The relative density was controlled by varying the densification time at fixed temperature (1050°C) and pressure (62 MPa). After hotpressing, the average grain size varied from approximately 2.7–3.7 lm for the 85% and 98% relative density samples, respectively. Examination of fracture surfaces revealed a transition from inter- to intragranular fracture as the relative density increased. The Vickers hardness increased with relative density up to 96%, above which the hardness was constant. At 98% relative density, the Vickers hardness was equal to the hardness measured by nanoindentation 9.1 GPa, which is estimated as the single-crystal hardness value. An inverse correlation between relative density and fracture toughness was observed. The fracture toughness increased linearly from 0.97 to 2.37 MPa√m for the 98% and 85% relative density samples, respectively. It is suggested that crack deflection along grain boundaries can explain the increase in fracture toughness with decreasing relative density. It was also observed that the total ionic conductivity increased from 0.0094 to 0.34 mS/cm for the 85%–98% relative density samples, respectively. The results of this study suggest that the microstructure of LLZO must be optimized to maximize mechanical integrity and ionic conductivity.

The logarithm of total ionic conductivity of hot-pressed LLZO as a function of relative density is shown in Fig. 9. From Fig. 9, it is observed that the total ionic conductivity increases with increasing relative density. This trend is typically observed in LLZO and is usually associated with a decrease in the grain-boundary resistance.15,16,19 The decrease in the grain-boundary resistance component could be a result of a change in the nature of the grain boundary as suggested by David et al.15 At 85% relative density, the total ionic conductivity is 0.0094 mS/cm and increases to 0.34 mS/cm for the 98% relative density sample. The value of 0.34 mS/ cm is in good agreement with the upper values of total conductivity for Al-substituted LLZO of similar composition (0.02–0.5 mS/cm).9,15,17,49 Extrapolation of the curve in Fig. 9 yields a total ionic conductivity of \~0.4 mS/cm, which is in excellent agreement with previously reported bulk conductivity values.9,15,21

context.text: The Li0.33La0.557TiO3 (LLTO) nanowires with high ionic conductivity were prepared through electrospinning and subsequent high temperature calcinations. It was filled in the blend of poly (ethylene oxide) (PEO) and poly (propylene carbonate) (PPC) as a filler and the novel solid PEO/PPC/LLTO nanowires polymer composite electrolytes were prepared via solution casting method with low cost. The addition of LLTO nanowires could effectively improve the ionic conductivity, electrochemical stability window, transference number, and compatibility with lithium metal of polymer composite electrolytes. The LiFePO /Li all solid state lithium ion battery assembled with the novel polymer composite electrolytes exhibited high electrochemical performance.

The study of Yu25 showed that the crystallinity of PEO could be effectively reduced by the addition of poly (propylene carbonate) (PPC) to the PEO matrix. So, the mechanical property and some electrochemical performances, such as ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability window, could be improved. However, the sole blending of amorphous PPC with PEO based SPEs still could not meet the requirements to enhance the electrochemical performances, such as ionic conductivity. So, the addition of fast ionic conductor fillers with high ionic conductivity, such as Li1.5Al0.5Ge1.5(PO4)3 (LAGP),26 Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS),27 Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO),28 and Li6.4La3Zr1.4Ta0.6O12 (LLZTO),29 or the ceramic fillers, such as Al O 30 SiO ,31 and Li N,32 was also needed. Due to the addition of fillers, the crystallization of polymer was reduced, and the ion transport channel was formed at the interface between fillers and polymers, which further improves the ionic conductivity of SPE. Additionally, to greatly enhance the ionic conductivity of PEO based SPEs, it required to fill as many fillers as possible. However, it would lead to the accumulation of the fillers, which reduced the mechanical properties of SPE.33 So, the filler with a larger specific surface area should be selected as a promising filler.

In this study, a novel solid polymer composite electrolyte (SPCE) was prepared by adding appropriate amount of PPC and fast ionic conductor Li0.33La0.557TiO3 nanowires (LLTO NWs) filler into the PEO matrix. The LLTO NWs, which were synthesized by electrospinning and subsequent calcination, had large specific surface area and wide electrochemical window. At the same time, the ionic conductivity, ITN, and electrochemical stability window of PEO PPC lithium bis (fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) LLTO SPCE, were also studied. LiFePO , as an active cathode material for lithium battery, which had stable structure, good thermal stability, good contact ability with electrolyte film, and could maintain capacity in a long charge discharge cycle, had already been prepared and applied successfully in laboratory.34,35 So, the button cell was assembled with LiFePO as a cathode active material, lithium metal as anode material, and the prepared SPCE film as electrolyte, and the cycle performance and rate capability were investigated.

context.text: Solid electrolytes for all solid state lithium batteries show unique advantages over organic based liquid electrolytes such as excellent battery lifetime, electrochemical and thermal stability, and enhanced safety.1-3 Accordingly, they received a lot of interest especially for the safety concerning applications such as electrical vehicles. Solid electrolytes can be divided into six different crystallographic orientations. These structures are NASICON (eg, LiTi2(PO4)3), LISICON (eg, Li10GeP2S12), perovskite (eg, Li0.34La0.56TiO3), sulfide (eg, Li7P3S11), antiperovskite (eg, Li3OCl), and garnet (eg, Li7La3Zr2O12) type solid electrolytes.4

Nowadays, garnet type solid electrolytes became popular because of their outstanding ionic conductivities among other types of solid electrolytes. Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) having a cubic crystal structure, as one of the garnet type solid electrolyte, was successfully adapted in the lab scale all solid state lithium battery assembly. However, the observed specific capacity was very limited for practical applications even if the slower charge/discharge rates were used.5 It is worth to emphasize that Al incorporation in LLZO lattice resulted in not only lowering the synthesis temperature but also increasing ionic conductivity by creating Li vacancies.6

context.text: Li4SiO4 was initially obtained via solid-state reaction by mixing lithium oxide (Li2O, Aldrich) and fumed silica (SiO2, Sigma-Aldrich) with a Li/Si molar ratio of 4.1:1. The powders were mechanically mixed during 15 min to obtain a homogenous precursor mixture, which was subsequently heated at 800 C for 6 h. On the other hand, pentalithium ferrite (LisFeO4) was synthesized by solid-state reaction using lithium oxide and iron oxide (Fe2O3, Aldrich) with a 20 mol % of lithium excess, according with the stoichiometric Li/Fe molar ratio of 5:1 due to its high tendency to sublimate. Initially, the powders were mechanically mixed and pressed into pellets (15 MPa). Subsequently, these pellets were heated at 850 C for 20 h.29 Both samples were analyzed by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm the presence of each phase. Then, Li4+xSi--Fe,O4 solid solution samples were obtained by dry ball milling process, using a Spex Sample-Prep 8000 M miller, during 15 min. The X-ray diffraction patterns of these samples were measured with the highest possible accuracy and signal/noise ratio. The smoothed XRD patterns (red lines) were fitted over the experimental profile line. In order to show the experimental diffraction profile, Figure 3-b presents the smoothed and free background XRD patterns. It must be pointed out that diffraction peaks corresponded to LisSiO4 structure, which means that the crystal structure of lithium silicate was preserved, and both, substitutional iron and interstitial lithium atoms must be into this crystal structure. The intensity of (2 0 -6) and (1 2 -3) diffraction peaks decrease as iron content increases, which is in a good agreement with the model presented before and which indicates that iron is located on silicon position. However, it can be noticed that additional peaks decreased their intensities as iron and lithium contents increased, for example, (1 1 4) and (1 1 -3) peaks. This behavior would be an effect of some changes in grain size. The average grain size on (1 1 -3) plane direction decreased as function of the iron content as it is shown in Table 1, from 18.86 to 8.48 nm, when iron content changed from 0 to 0.5, respectively. Between 0 and 0.2, grain size decreased from 18.86 to 9.49 nm. However, after that iron content, changes in the grain size were lower. It has been proved that milling processes induce a decrement in the average grain size.36 In this case all the samples were milled during the same time (15 min). Therefore, the difference between these grain size values should be an effect of the iron content, inhibiting the sintering process. Moreover, lithium excess could cause a delocalization of lithium atoms on those planes (Figure 4). In this figure, (1 2 -3) and (1 1 -3) planes are mostly composed by lithium atoms, thus this decrement on intensity would be explained with a delocalization of lithium atoms. It is worth noting that diffraction peak relative intensities vary considerably, in fact when the iron content increases the (2 0 -6) peak becomes the principal peak of this phase. Finally, the interplanar distances of (2 0 -6), (1 2 -3), (1 1 -3) and (1 1 4) planes were measured and they are presented on Table 2. In all these cases, it can be seen slightly increases of plane spacing as iron and lithium contents increase. This effect should be attributed to iron substitution in silicon positions and lithium incorporations.

context.text: BiFeO3 (BFO) ceramics were prepared by conventional solid-state reaction method without quenching. The effect of the sintering condition on the phase evolution and the ferroelectric properties of these BFO ceramics were investigated. A pinched polarization - electric field (P -E) hysteresis loop was observed in the sample sintered at high temperature for a short period (820 ◦C for 1 hour) because the domain wall motion is restricted by a large number of ionic defects such as oxygen vacancies. The BFO sample sintered at low temperature for a long period (760 ◦C for 6 hours) displayed a well-saturated P -E hysteresis loop due to its low ionic defect density.

context.text: Multiferroic materials, which have both ferromagnetic and ferroelectric properties, provide opportunities for potential applications such as memory devices, sensors, and spintronics [1–5]. Typical multiferroic oxides such as BiFeO3 (BFO) [1, 6, 7], BiMnO3 [2, 8], and BiCrO3 [9, 10] have attracted attention. BFO is one of the candidates for the end member of lead-free piezoelectric solid solutions with a morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) because it has a high phase transition temperature (TN 640 K and TC 1100 K) and a saturated polarization as high as  100 μC/cm2, which is very attractive not only for fundamental physics but also for applications [11–16]. However, a BFO ceramic with high resistivity and good ferroelectric properties can hardly be prepared by the conventional solid-state reaction due to impurity phases and ionic defects [17,18]. Leaching impurity phases with nitric acid [19], rapid liquid phase sintering [3,17,20], spark plasma sintering [21], and sintering with nano-sized homogeneous powders [21–24] have been adopted for producing a single-phase BFO ceramic.

Bi2O3 (99.9%, Sigma Aldrich Co., Ltd., USA) and Fe2O3 (99.9%, Sigma Aldrich Co., Ltd., USA) powders were carefully weighted according to the stoichiometric formula, mixed by using ball milling for 24 hours, and then pulverized again by using attrition milling with yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) balls at 350 rpm for 5 hours in high-purity ethanol. After drying, the powder mixture was formed into a disk shape by cold isostatic pressing (CIP) at a pressure of 120 MPa. The pressed samples were sintered at 760- 840 ◦C for 1 - 6 hours and cooled in a furnace. context.text: Drugs can exist in diverse polymorphic forms that have different physicochemical properties, including melting points, densities, morphologies, solubilities, and colors. This, in turn, may affect their chemical stability, bioavailability, and ability to be processed during manufacturing and/or in the final product. In extreme cases, an undesired polymorph can even be toxic. Therefore, characterization and control of the solid-state properties of a drug are important during early product development [17]. The aqueous solubility of a molecule is one of the key determinants of the success of new compounds as medicines [18].

context.text: In summary, a polymorphic form of valnemulin hydrogen tartrate (Form I) was prepared by crystallization. It was characterized by performing XRD, SEM, IR spectroscopy, DSC, and TGA. Compared to Form II, Form I has a different morphology and diffraction pattern and a lower melting point. The IR spectra of both forms were similar except for slight differences in their peak intensities, which were insufficient to clearly distinguish the two forms. Stability results showed that Form I and Form II were more stable than commercial valnemulin hydrochloride under irradiation and high humidity conditions. Form I was more soluble than Form II. In addition, pharmacokinetics studies in pigs showed that Form I has similar Cmax and Tmax values and a slightly higher AUClast value than valnemulin hydrochloride. In summary, the results showing that solubility of Form1 is higher than that of Form II and that its stability and bioavailability is similar to those of valnemulin hydrochloride indicate that Form I has the potential for application in novel veterinary drugs. Nevertheless, to study different polymorphs of the same drug and to develop favorable clinical medications, it is necessary to investigate the polymorphic pharmacokinetics of solid dry powder after oral administration. Further studies on the pharmacokinetics of different forms of solid-state valnemulin administered to Sprague Dawley rats are in progress and the results will be reported in the near future. Regardless, the present study provides data and technological information supporting the development of pharmaceutical polymorphs that can be used to improve drug quality and administration.

context.text: Synthesis procedure of LZTO.—Pristine LZTO and the LZTO@RGO samples were prepared with a solid-state method. RGO/LZTO composites with mass ratios of 0.1: 1, 0.25:1 and 0.5:1 were synthesized, which are designated as LZTO@RGO10, LZTO@RGO25 and LZTO@RGO50, respectively. Firstly, stoichiometric amount of Li2CO3 (Merck), Zn(CH3COO)2.2H2O (Merck), anatase TiO2 nanoparticles (20 nm, MTI) and GO were mixed in a 50 mL tungsten carbide jar. Five tungsten carbide balls and absolute ethanol were put in this jar. After being sealed, the jar was settled in planetary ball mill (Retsch, PM-200) and grinded at 400 rpm for 4 h. Ethanol was evaporated at 80°C in an oven for an overnight. After that, the grinded powders were settled in alumina crucible, and calcined at 800°C for 6 h under high-purity argon gas flow to obtain the LZTO@RGO composites. For comparison, bare LZTO was prepared in the same synthesis method without addition of GO. The formation mechanism of LZTO@RGO is shown in Scheme 1.

context.text: Many researchers have investigated this composite material using mainly metal nickel dispersed in Al2O3 [1-4]. However, the metallic particles tend often to oxidize after a period of exposure especially in high temperature environments; there is therefore a need to use, semi-metallic or non-metallic particles which have higher temperature stability [5]. In addition, NiO is more appropriate for this application due to its high electrophoretic mobility, rate of deposition ,smooth deposits and better control of the gradient profile [6]. NiO is a highly insoluble thermally stable nickel source suitable for optic and ceramic applications. Nickel oxide is very interesting for this application because it has been used in a variety of applications in electronic [7], thin films [8],electrochemical capacitors (EC) [9]. It is low cost, has an excellent durability and electrochemical stability with large span optical density. There are several methods to fabricate NiO and Al2O3 based composite including conventional powder mixing technique; Spray pyrolysis; chemical and physical vapour deposition (CVD or PVD), sputtering, sol-gel, like thermal and plasma spraying, precipitation approaches and the template synthesis, and electrophoretic deposition (EPD) [3, 10], [11, 12]. Among these methods, EPD is a fairly rapid and inexpensive way capable to producing a dense and uniform coating on substrates with complex geometries. Electrophoretic deposition is a process for ceramics [13] in which colloidal particles such as ceramics suspended in a liquid medium migrate toward the electrode of opposite sign to their charges under the influence of an electric field (electrophoresis) for deposition. EPD was first observed by a Russian scientist Reuss in his experiment with electric field to induce motion of clay particles suspended in water [14]. But the first practical use of this method is patented in the USA in 1933 with the deposition of thoria particles on a platinum cathode for electron tube [15].

context.text: LiMn2O4@Al2O3 cathode materials for lithium ion batteries are prepared through an sol-gel method with the assistance of tert-butanol. A uniform amorphous Al2O3 layer is formed on the surface of LiMn2O4 under the control of the hydrolysis mechanism of aluminum ion (Al3+) and hydroxyl group (OH). The products are investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), power X-ray diffraction (XRD), galvanostatic charge-discharge test system, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy(EIS) and inductively-coupled plasma emission spectrograph (ICP-AES). Structural and surface analysis reveal that the crystal structure and overall morphology of the LiMn2O4 electrode are found to be not significant unaffected by Al2O3 coating. Furthermore, EIS and ICP analyses show that the Al2O3 coating assisted by tert-butanol significantly improves the electro-conductivity and relieves the dissolution of Mn in electrolyte.

context.text: Nitrogen oxides (NO) and carbon monoxide (CO), are considered to be among some of the most dangerous gases produced as automotive industry emissions and can be extremely harmful to the human body. They are released into the atmosphere during manufacturing processes, mostly by combustion facilities, automobiles and other exhaust emission systems. NO, compounds pose a particular threat, as they convert themselves into nitric acid and toxic organic nitrates in common air conditions [1]. They are also a major component of smog. If undetected, the presence of NO, and CO in the atmosphere can cause the risk of health deterioration of all living organisms. Therefore it is very important to be able to precisely control the contents of those compounds in the air. One of the methods for controlling the amount of NO, and CO is the use of specialized gas sensors, known as resistive gas sensors. Under the influence of contamination, the sensors show a significant change in resistance. In the case of materials used as resistive gas sensors, catalytic layers or powders can be made out of simple metal oxides such as: WO3, CeO2, SnO2, or complex compounds such as perovskites of the general formula ABOs. Perovskites are very important and useful multi-functional materials that can be used in various applications, such as gas sensors [2, 3], automotive exhaust catalysts [4], methane reformers that produce syngas [5, 6], cathodes in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC's) [7, 8] or visible light photo-catalysts [9, 10]. They can be used as gas sensing materials due to their improved thermal stability at higher temperatures in various atmospheres. For these materials, catalytic activity is mostly influenced by the type of the B cation and its oxidation state cycling feasibility. LaCoO, has been proposed as an active perovskite for NO and CO oxidation reactions. Stoichiometric LaCoO usually presents some oxygen deficiency in the lattice structure, represented by LaCoO3-s, and the charge balance is accomplished by the presence of cobalt Co2+ ions. The modulation of the oxidation state of Co can be realized by the synthesis (calcination temperature) or substitution (Sr2+, Ca2+, Ba2+) of the lanthanum ion [1]. The substitution of La3+ by cations with lower oxidation states (e.g. Sr2+) generates a charge imbalance, which can be compensated by the alteration of the oxidation state of Co2+. Therefore, in this case, it is quite easy to influence the catalytic properties of the LaCoO3 perovskite. Say et al. [11] prepared LaCoO nanoparticles doped with Pd and reported that the adsorption of H2 increased in the presence of NOx - pre-treated LaCoO and Pd/LaCoO, surfaces could be associated with the changes in Co oxidation states, structural changes, reduction of the precious metal oxide (PdO) into metallic species (Pd) and the creation of oxygen defects in the perovskite structure. Perovskite oxides, i.e. LaCoO and LaMnO, doped by Sr were also produced by Onrubia et al. [1]. They demonstrated that LaSrCoO and LaSrMnO3 samples presented the highest NO conversion (83 % and 65 %, respectively), with a further improvement in comparison to non-substituted samples, (71 % and 63 %, respectively). LaCoO, based sensors in the form of thin films were tested by Ding et al. [12]. In this research, LaCoO, showed a high response to CO gas, excellent recovery and good stability at a low temperature T = 200 C. The sensor response to 1% CO was 49.23 at 600 C, and 7.83 at 200 C. LaCoO nanoparticles with a perovskite-type structure were successfully synthesized by Ortiz et al. [13]. The LaCoO3 pellets showed high sensitivity to both CO and C,Hg at different concentrations and operating temperatures. Perovskite LaCoO doped with different elements was used in the form of powders [14, 15] or layers. La1. xSr,CoO, compounds in the form of thin films were produced by the sol-gel, PLD or chemical methods and they are used as electrodes in fuel cells or gas sensors [16-18]. In this work, La1xSr,CoO3 (x = 0; 0.1; 0.2) perovskite thin films were prepared using the PLD method. The effect of Sr doping on the quality, structure and catalytic properties of the obtained thin films was investigated.

context.text: Deposition and characterization on chalcogenide semiconductors of II-VI group elements such as CdS and ZnS have been done for decades due to their impressive properties such as tunable optical, morphological and electrical properties.1–5 Among this group of semiconductor compounds CdS is the most investigated because of its potential applications, such as in photovoltaics (mainly as n-type window/buffer materials in CdTe,6 CuInSe,7 CuIn(Se,S)28 and Cu(In,Ga)Se2-based thin film solar cells9), photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting,10,11 biomedical labeling,12 electrically driven lasers,13 field effect transistors,14 gas sensors,15 photo-detectors,16 and light emitting diodes (LEDs).17 CdS has a wide energy bandgap of 2.42 eV in the bulk and exists in hexagonal, cubic and orthorhombic crystal structural phases.18–20 In the deposition of CdS thin films, deposition techniques and their associated parameters have significant influence on the physical and chemical properties of the thin films.21–23 CdS thin films can be deposited by different techniques including electrodeposition,24 chemical bath deposition,25 sputtering,26 metal organic chemical vapor deposition,27 pulsed laser deposition,28 close space sublimation,29 screen printing,30 Sol-gel,31 and physical vapor deposition.32 In photovoltaic solar cell research, researchers main focus is on two basic issues: (i) increasing the conversion efficiency of solar panels, and (ii) reducing the cost of solar panels. In this regard, to reduce cost of solar panels, deposition techniques have substantial role. Although each deposition technique has its own advantages and disadvantages,24,33,34 electrodeposition compared with other wet chemical based techniques such as, chemical bath deposition, has unique advantages such as self-purification of the deposition electrolyte, easily monitoring of the electrolyte reaction, minimum waste generation and long bath lifetime.24 However, electrodeposition has its own drawback. For example, the substrate must be an electrically conductive material for deposition to be effected.35 But, to explore the above unique advantages, electrodeposition technique is selected to grow CdS thin film for possible solar cell applications. In addition to avoid contamination of the electrolytic bath in the case of leaky or broken reference electrode and to reduce the cost of electrodeposition which arises due to the reference electrode, a simple low-cost, two-electrode set-up has been used. In electrodeposition, deposition of thin films is carried out by optimizing associated deposition parameters such as concentration of ions in the electrolytic bath, temperature of the electrolytic bath, stirring, pH, deposition time, electrodes used and applied voltage based on the application the films are intended for.36–39 In the literature, electrodeposited CdS (ED-CdS) thin films usually involve, the use of cadmium chloride (CdCl2), cadmium nitrate (Cd(NO3)2) and cadmium sulfate (CdSO4) as cadmium precursors and thiourea (NH2CSNH2) ammonium thiosulfate ((NH4)2S2O3) and sodium thiosulfate (Na2S2O3) as sulfur precursors.24,40,41 However, the use of cadmium acetate Cd(CH3COO)2, as Cd precursor, is not common in electrodeposition method although it is a familiar precursor in chemical bath deposition. Hence, this paper aimed to focus on two things: (i) The application of cadmium acetate as Cd precursor in the electrodeposition of CdS thin films for possible solar cell applications using two-electrode set-up. (ii) The study of the influence of deposition time on the optical and morphological properties of these same CdS thin films for solar cell application. These are not yet fully explored in the literature.

context.text: Powders Nb O were prepared by two different synthesis method, Sol-Gel and polymeric precursors (Pechini). In the Pechini method before adding the citric acid in the process, four different solutions were used to get the samples. For Sol-gel method, two different processes were also used in obtaining powders. The precursor was completely solubilized in ethanol and then hydrolyzed with ammonia and water. The calcination of the samples was between 500 and 750°C. The resulting powders were characterized by Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Brunauer, Emmett and Teller (BET) surface area measurements, UV-visible and Raman spectroscopy. The formation of T−Nb O orthorhombic took place upon calcination at 7500C. Crystallite sizes were determined using the Scherrer method which resulted in an uniformed size of about 25 − 65nm. Ultraviolet-Visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy indicated a variation in the optical band gap values (3.32-3.40 eV) in crystal growth process. The Raman vibrational modes indicate the presence of the orthorhombic phase of the material.

context.text: Tables of the synthesis procedure are shown in (1) and (2). The samples 1−Nb O and 2−Nb O were synthesized by the Sol-gel method according to literature procedures16. Niobium (V) ethoxide, (Nb(OC H ) 99.999% Alfa Aesar) was employed as the starting precursor and absolute ethanol for analysis (Merck) and Ammonia hidroxide 30% (Panreac) were also used. The samples 1−Nb O were prepared by adding 5g of Nb(OC H ) to 90ml of absolute ethanol which was stirred vigorously, then 5ml of Ammonia hydroxide was added to the precipitation system. The samples 2−Nb O were prepared by adding 5g of Nb(OC H ) to 94ml of absolute ethanol under vigorous stirring, then 1ml of distilled water was added to the precipitation system. context.text: Sol-gel and Pechini methods were chosen for their similarity and since these allow the preparation of homogeneous and highly pure powders and porous and high surface area oxides, with fine particles and adequate chemical composition. The Pechini route consists of the formation of chelates between metal ions and carboxylic acids. These are subsequently polymerized by a reaction with polyalcohols, which have a good distribution of metallic ions in the polymer structure, that when heated at moderate temperatures it favors the condensation reaction causing polyesterification to occur. The excess water is removed and a homogeneous gel is formed19,20. The sol-gel method enables homogenous samples to be obtained at low temperatures and the starting cationic composition to be maintained by the use of metal salts as raw materials and mixing them in a liquid solution. The principal advantage of the Sol-gel method is that reagents are mostly mixed in atomic levels, which may increase the reaction rate and decrease the heat treatment temperature21.

context.text: The stable Fe3O4 magnetorheological fuids were first prepared by coprecipitation method without using any surfactants and characterized by X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and vibrating sample magnetometer. The polyurethane elastomers were further polymerized in the presence of stable FeO4 magnetorheological fluids. Furthermore, the effect of FeO4 loading on mechanical, magnetic, thermal, electrical, and microwave-absorbing properties of the polyurethane elastomers were systematically investigated. The results indicated that the synthesis process and Fe304 loading had great effects on the properties of polyurethane elastomers. A synthesis-based in situ polymerization method using Fe3O4 magnetorheological fuids instead of dry powder could improve the dispersion of FeO4 nanoparticles in the polyurethane matrix. The FeO4/polyurethane nanocomposites showed high mechanical, magnetic, thermal, electrical, and microwave-absorbing properties at a low loading of 2 wt%, and could potentially be used for a wide range of applications. [doi:10.5254/rct.16.84817]

context.text: FegO4 magnetorheological fluids were prepared by using a chemical coprecipitation method. An iron salt solution was obtained by mixing 3.58 g of FeCl-4H2O and 6.08 g of FeCl36HO in 90 mL of distilled water. Then, 92.4 mL of NaOH aqueous solution (1.34 M) was added dropwise into the ferric salt solution under vigorous stirring. The reaction continued for 90 min at 50 C. Precipitated Fe3O4 nanoparticles were separated with a permanent magnet. The black precipitate was washed for several times with deionized water to remove excess materials. Finally, the Fe3O4 nanoparticles were dispersed in 90 mL of distilled water by ultrasonic treatment for 50 min to form the homogeneous, stable Fe3O4 magnetorheological fluids (33 mg/mL). Next, a small amount of THF organic solvent was added to the desired amount of stable Fe3O4 magnetorheological fluids, and the Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles were separated by centrifugation and an external magnetic field. The nanoparticles were washed with THF several times to ensure no water among nanoparticles. Finally, the Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles were dispersed in THF by ultrasonic treatment for 1 h to form homogeneous Fe3O4 THF dispersion fluids.

context.text: Hydroxyapatite, which has been widely used in the medical field in the last couple of years, is a superior biomaterial due to its biocompatibility and nontoxicity. Hydroxyapatite requires highly magnetic materials to perform maximally in specific medical fields. In this study, hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites mainly composed of limestone and natural iron sand were synthesized through a coprecipitation method, and composites having different hydroxyapatite-to-magnetite mass ratios were compared. The crystal structure, particle size, fractal dimension, morphology, functional group, and energy gap were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), synchrotron X-ray scattering (SAXS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and ultraviolent-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy. The research results showed that the hydroxyapatite and magnetite phases had a hexagonal structure and cubic structure, respectively. In general, from the FTIR data analysis, the hydroxyapatite and magnetite particles were identified from the functional groups of phosphate, iron-oxygen, carbonate, and hydroxyl. Moreover, depending on particle size, the samples consisting of 3.7-nm primary particles formed a cluster with a massive three-dimensional structure. Meanwhile, the energy gap showed various values ranging between 3.25 and 3.86 eV.

context.text: Magnetite (Fe3O4)-based iron oxide is known for its excellent magnetic property and high magnetization saturation. In addition, magnetite has other outstanding characteristics such as low toxicity and biocompatibility [19], its ability to be adjusted for specific applications, and its ability to prevent osteoblast mineralization [20]. Moreover, magnetite contributes to giving hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites a wide specific surface area (SSA) and a magnetic property [21]. In respect to this, previous research has shown that hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites can eliminate long-term toxic effect [22]. Moreover, if composite material performance is to be achieved for further applications in the medical field, particle size uniformity and morphology are crucial. Therefore, some attempts have been made to this end through fabrication methods such as coprecipitation [23], ultrasonic spray pyrolysis [24], and the sol-gel technique [25].

In addition, magnetite has other outstanding characteristics such as low toxicity and biocompatibility [19], its ability to be adjusted for specific applications, and its ability to prevent osteoblast mineralization [20]. Moreover, magnetite contributes to giving hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites a wide specific surface area (SSA) and a magnetic property [21]. In respect to this, previous research has shown that hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites can eliminate long-term toxic effect [22]. Moreover, if composite material performance is to be achieved for further applications in the medical field, particle size uniformity and morphology are crucial. context.text: Earlier studies have identified that hydroxyapatite/magnetite synthesized through the coprecipitation method contains a SSA of 109 m2/g [23]. Abramov et al. synthesized hydroxyapatite/magnetite/doxorubicin with a SSA of 110 m2/g by using a coprecipitation method [26]. Andronescu et al. synthesized a magnetite-enriched collagen/hydroxyapatite composite by using a coprecipitation method at a low temperature; however, the generated particles were still at a range of 100–300 nm. Moreover, some of them were still of a microscale size [27]. Trinkunaite-Felsen et al. synthesized magnetite-calcium hydroxyapatite in spherical form, but the composite still showed a relatively rough morphology with particles sizes ranging between 400 and 450 nm [25]. In another study, hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites with a core-shell morphology with a 30 to 450 nm particle distribution were synthesized; however, the particle size distribution was less homogeneous [24]. Unfortunately, several studies regarding hydroxyapatite/magnetite still used a relatively expensive commercial precursor, and thus far, detailed study on the nanostructural hierarchy in hydroxyapatite/magnetite composite has not been conducted. Therefore, in the present investigation, we utilized natural resources in the forms of iron sand and limestone, which are relatively affordable and abundant as they are found in all regions of Indonesia, as the main precursors in generating hydroxyapatite/magnetite composites. Natural limestone was used as the main material to produce hydroxyapatite while natural iron sand was used as the material to produce nano-magnetite particles.

context.text: ATP produced by ATP synthases is a key molecule for the metabolism of every living organism. ATP synthases belong to a family of enzymes known as rotary ATP synthases and are categorized as F- and V-type ATPases (Fig. 1A, B). They share many structural and mechanistic features, such as mechanochemical coupling of ion translocation and ATP hydrolysis/synthesis through rotation [1–6]. Reactions mediated by rotary ATPases are reversible, and consequently can function as molecular motors to synthesize or hydrolyze ATP depending on the physiological conditions [7–9].

context.text: According to statistics, the discarded cigarette butts was over 4.5 trillion annually,21 mainly including the filter tip and the adsorbed toxic substances (such as nicotine, heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic compounds and ethyl phenol).22 The cigarette butt filter tip is made of non-biodegradable cellulose acetate, needing about 18 months to break down.23 Thus, the recycling of cigarette butts is necessary to protect the environment. Due to its porosity, the cigarette butts and porous carbonized products derived from them have been applied in adsorption, energy storage and sound absorber.24–25 In addition, urea was an excellent nitrogen source for N-doped materials due to the high nitrogen content. Chen and co-workers prepared N-doped porous carbon materials with excellent cycling stability and rate capability by a facile one-step method.26 Furthermore, they reported that a high nitrogen doping level was benefit to improve the electrochemical performances. Liu and co-workers prepared N-doped graphene using urea as nitrogen source by a mechanochemical method,27 and the obtained samples are promising candidate for the anode materials of lithium ion battery. Wang and co-workers prepared N-doped porous carbon materials by KOH activation of urea-modified lignin,28 and the obtained products exhibited superior electrochemical properties as electrode materials. Tan and co-workers prepared N-doped porous carbon materials by using citric acid as carbon source and urea as nitrogen source, exhibiting an excellent capacitive performance.29 However, the study referring to N-doped porous carbon materials derived from waste cigarette butts using urea as nitrogen source is neglected.

context.text: We demonstrate that a SiO disproportionation reaction can be achieved simply by high energy mechanochemical milling. The planetary ball-milling of ZrO2 for a few minutes generated Si nano-crystals. Milling conditions including rotation speed, ball number, milling time, and type of ball material were able to control the oxidation states of Si. The ball-milled SiO powder was tested as an anode of a lithium battery. ZrO2 contamination from the vial and balls was eliminated by dipping the ball-milled SiO powder in (NH4)HSO4 molten salt and heating for 5 min. The disproportionated SiO powder showed characteristics comparable to those of a powder prepared by a conventional heating process taking several hours. © 2016 The Japan Society of Applied Physics

context.text: High energy mechanochemical milling (HEMM) is a simple and effective method to reduce particle size. It has also been applied to obtain chemical reactions in mechanical alloying.11) Moreover, several researchers have reported the synthesis of nano-sized chemical compounds using mechanochemical processes.12,13) Recently, Wang et al.14) obtained the SiO disproportionation just by ball-milling process to SiO powder. However, as far as we know, there is no study describing the relationship between ball-milling conditions and the reaction. In this study, we investigated the effects of ball-milling conditions such as rotation speed, ball number, milling time, and type of balls and vial material on the mechanochemical SiO disproportionation from the viewpoint of impact energy.

context.text: In the mechanochemical process, the locally aroused temperature by the impact of ball and vial can be the driving force of some chemical reactions, but it is usually less than ∼600 °C in the planetary ball-milling process.19,20) Since the SiO disproportionation is generally achieved by heating over ∼800 °C,2 5) the local temperature must not be the main driving force of SiO disproportionation by the ball-milling process. Considering this, the SiO disproportionation in the ball-milling process is possibly caused by a crystal structure change by the mechanical impact or an excessive energy supplied from the new surfaces created in the milling process. The -E of more than ∼27.3 mJ=hit was large enough to achieve the above effects, and hence, the SiO disproportionation was realized. The effect of ball number difference on the change of intensity for Si peak is smaller than that of rotation speed difference [Fig. 2(b)], which is in good agreement with the result of estimated -E . The largest Si(111) peak is obtained with 50 balls, as this is the best balance of the impact energy and frequency.

Along with the different solvent composition, the wt% of PVP in the needleless solution had to be increased to exceed the percentage of LLZO precursors, whereas the loading of precursor reagents was higher in the SNE solution. Using the solution optimized for the needleless reactor (viscosity of 0.17 Pa·s), 0.23 g/h of as-spun nanofibers could be obtained using a precursor feed rate of 10 mL/hr and applied voltage bias of 15 kV between the spinneret and collector. This production rate was increased by increasing the feed rate to 15 mL/hr and voltage to 20 kV, with an average rate of 1.023 ± 0.094 g/h over 14 reactions with good reproducibility (Table S1). Compared to a typical nanofiber production rate using SNE, the needleless electrospinning offers a higher production rate by approximately one order of magnitude. One disadvantage of the needleless reactor, as first observed by Holopainen et al.28, is the gelling or drying of the solution on the twisted wire, which requires cleaning in between use and limits prolonged synthesis. Typically, needleless electrospinning could be performed continuously for 45 min at a time to produce, on average, 767 mg of nanofibers, before needing to be stopped and cleaned. However, this gelling process, which occurs due to solvent evaporation, is analogous to clogging of the needle in conventional electrospinning33,34, which similarly limits SNE of LLZO to \~2 h of synthesis time before the needle needs to be cleaned.

Figure 2A shows a photograph of a nanofiber mat prepared after 45 min of reaction using needless electrospinning (approximate dimensions: 41 inch x 10 inch) . The deposition of nanofibers on the mat was very uniform, confirming the radial formation of liquid jets from the spinneret. The mat could be easily removed from the collector as a single piece (the lower left hand corner of the mat in Figure 2A is partially removed). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging showed that the as-spun nanofibers formed a nanoribbon morphology with more of a rectangular cross-section (Figure 2B), with average diameter/width of 650 nm (Figure 2C). The morphology of the as-spun nanofibers was consistent throughout the mat, except some curled fibers were observed close to the edges of the mat (Figure S2), likely due to non-uniform current distribution at either end of the collector. The nanoribbon morphology in materials produced with needleless electrospinning is different from what was observed in as-spun nanofibers prepared using SNE, which had cylindrical cross-sections. Similar morphologies have been observed previously and have been attributed to the formation of a thin polymer skin on the surface of the liquid jet, which subsequently collapses into a flat nanoribbon due to solvent evaporation35. In our case, this is a feasible explanation as well, since the needless electrospinning precursor required a large vol% of ethanol; the ribbon morphology may also be a feature of this type of reactor, as Holopainen et al. also reported similar morphologies for PVP and hydroxyapatite nanofibers produced in their setup28.

context.text: Mechanochemical synthesis

Novel nitride glass electrolyte Li3BN2 was prepared from Li3N and BN via a mechanochemical process using planetary ball milling. Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopies revealed that the glass was composed of Li+ and BN23− ions. The Li3BN2 glass exhibited good ductility, and the powder-compressed pellet showed a relative density of 84%. The hot-pressed pellet of the Li3BN2 glass showed a conductivity of 1.3 × 10−5 S cm−1 at 25 °C, which is much higher than that of oxide-based glass electrolytes such as Li3BO3 glass and LiPON thin films. Moreover, Young's modulus of the Li3BN2 glass was 51.1 GPa, which is an intermediate value between sulfides and oxides. The Li symmetric cell using the Li3BN2 glass electrolyte was cycled stably at 100 °C without short-circuiting. Nitride glassy materials are promising electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries because of their high conductivity, good mechanical properties, and electrochemical stability.

context.text: All-solid-state secondary batteries using nonflammable inorganic solid electrolytes have been expected to solve safety issues in commercially available lithium-ion batteries. For the fabrication of all-solidstate batteries, highly conducting solid electrolytes should be developed. Sulfide-based and oxide-based inorganic materials have been widely studied as promising electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries [1–8]. Some of the sulfide electrolytes were reported to show extremely high lithium ion conductivities of more than 10−2 S cm−1 at room temperature (Li7P3S11 [1], Li10GeP2S12 [2], Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S11.7Cl0.3 [3], and Li P Ge S I [4]). These conductivities are higher than those of typical organic liquid electrolytes. Moreover, sulfide electrolytes have good ductility, which enables their densification just by pressing at room temperature. Especially, glass electrolytes are more ductile than the corresponding crystalline ones, mainly due to the isotropic structure with free volume of the glasses [9]. This mechanical property is also the advantage to achieve favorable solid–solid contacts like electrode–electrolyte interfaces in all-solid-state batteries [10].

On the other hand, oxide-based materials have also attracted great attention because of their high chemical stability. Some of crystalline oxide electrolytes show high lithium ion conductivities of 10−4 –10−3 S cm−1 at room temperature (La0.51Li0.34TiO2.94 [5], Li7La3Zr2O12 [6], Li1.3Al0.3Ti1.7(PO4)3 [7], and LiTa2PO8 [8]). However, these crystalline oxide electrolytes have poor ductility at room temperature, which generates an extremely high grain-boundary resistance. Thus, to achieve high densification leading to high lithiumion conductivity, high temperature sintering at more than 1000 °C is needed in the case of Li La Zr O . In contrast to crystalline materials, glassy electrolytes tend to show better ductility. We prepared various oxide and sulfide glass electrolytes by melt-quenching and mechanochemical techniques [11–17]. Especially, by using a mechanochemical technique with a high-energy ball milling apparatus, glassy materials are prepared even in high alkaline content, and the conductivity of these glasses increases with the alkaline content [11,12]. For example, Li3BO3 (75Li2O25B2O3 in mol%) glass with a high lithium content was prepared via mechanochemistry [11]. The prepared glass powder can be densified simply by pressing under 360 MPa at room temperature like ductile sulfide materials; the powder-compressed pellet showed a relatively high relative density of 71%, leading to a conductivity of 3.4 × 10−7 S cm−1 at room temperature [11,13]. This good ductility for the glassy materials is favorable for constructing electrode–electrolyte interfaces in bulk-type all-solid-state batteries. However, the conductivity and ductility of oxide-based glassy electrolytes are not high enough, and thus various studies on the improvement of these properties of oxide glass materials were reported [14,15]. Nitrogen doping to Li3PO4 glass electrolytes is widely known to be effective in increasing their conductivity. By a partial substitute of nitrogen for oxygen in Li3PO4 glass thin films, the conductivity of glass electrolytes increased by one order of magnitude, and the lithium phosphorous oxynitride (LiPON) glass electrolyte exhibited a conductivity of about 10−6 S cm−1 at room temperature [18]. LiPON glass is practically used as an electrolyte in thin-film-type all-solid-state batteries. In oxynitride glasses, the glass transition temperature and the crystallization temperature increase with the nitrogen contents, which indicates that the thermal and chemical stabilities are improved by the substitution of nitrogen [19]; nitrogen is replaced with bridging oxygen to increase cross-linking of the glass network. Recently, we have reported that nitrogen doping is also effective in improving conductivity and chemical stability even of sulfide-based electrolytes [16]. Therefore, the incorporation of nitrogen to oxide or sulfide lithium-ion conductors is effective in enhancing performance of solid electrolytes.

In contrast to crystalline materials, glassy electrolytes tend to show better ductility. We prepared various oxide and sulfide glass electrolytes by melt-quenching and mechanochemical techniques [11–17]. Especially, by using a mechanochemical technique with a high-energy ball milling apparatus, glassy materials are prepared even in high alkaline content, and the conductivity of these glasses increases with the alkaline content [11,12]. For example, Li3BO3 (75Li2O25B2O3 in mol%) glass with a high lithium content was prepared via mechanochemistry [11]. The prepared glass powder can be densified simply by pressing under 360 MPa at room temperature like ductile sulfide materials; the powder-compressed pellet showed a relatively high relative density of 71%, leading to a conductivity of 3.4 × 10−7 S cm−1 at room temperature [11,13]. This good ductility for the glassy materials is favorable for constructing electrode–electrolyte interfaces in bulk-type all-solid-state batteries. However, the conductivity and ductility of oxide-based glassy electrolytes are not high enough, and thus various studies on the improvement of these properties of oxide glass materials were reported [14,15]. Nitrogen doping to Li3PO4 glass electrolytes is widely known to be effective in increasing their conductivity. By a partial substitute of nitrogen for oxygen in Li3PO4 glass thin films, the conductivity of glass electrolytes increased by one order of magnitude, and the lithium phosphorous oxynitride (LiPON) glass electrolyte exhibited a conductivity of about 10−6 S cm−1 at room temperature [18]. LiPON glass is practically used as an electrolyte in thin-film-type all-solid-state batteries. In oxynitride glasses, the glass transition temperature and the crystallization temperature increase with the nitrogen contents, which indicates that the thermal and chemical stabilities are improved by the substitution of nitrogen [19]; nitrogen is replaced with bridging oxygen to increase cross-linking of the glass network. Recently, we have reported that nitrogen doping is also effective in improving conductivity and chemical stability even of sulfide-based electrolytes [16]. Therefore, the incorporation of nitrogen to oxide or sulfide lithium-ion conductors is effective in enhancing performance of solid electrolytes.

However, there are few reports on nitride electrolytes. Crystalline nitride materials as lithium ion conductors were reported in systems Li–B–N, Li–Si–N, and Li–P–N [20], but they showed quite low conductivity; crystalline Li BN electrolytes exhibited a conductivity of 3 × 10−7 S cm−1 even at 400 K [21]. On the other hand, lithium-ion conducting amorphous nitride materials has never been reported so far. Therefore, it is important to synthesize novel amorphous electrolytes and evaluate their properties. Here, we report the mechanochemical synthesis of Li3BN2 glass electrolyte. Glassy Li3BN2 samples were prepared by using planetary ball milling, and their local structure and thermal properties were investigated. In addition, the mechanical and electrical properties were also examined, and these properties were compared with those of Li3BO3 and Li3PS4 in terms of electronegativity of X in Li3MXa.

context.text: The bonding characters of the Li3BN2 glass and crystal were investigated by XPS. Fig. 3 presents the XPS spectra for B1s and N1s of the

Li3BN2 glass and crystal before and after etching. In both B1s and N1s spectra, there was a slight difference between the peak positions of the glass and crystal. The B1s spectra of the Li3BN2 glass and crystal in Fig. 3a and b show two peaks around 190.5 eV and 187.5 eV. The peak at 190.5 eV is attributable to the BeO bond because Li3BO3 composed BO33− anions gave the peak at 191.0 eV in the B1s spectrum (Fig. 3a).

Since the peak assigned to the BN 3− ion was observed in the Raman spectra (Fig. 2), another peak at 187.5 eV can be attributed to the BeN bond. The peak intensity derived from the BeN bond increased relatively to that derived from the oxides after Ar+ etching, indicating that the main structure of the particle is nitrides.

context.text: In the N1s spectra of the Li3BN2 glass and crystal shown in Fig. 3c and d, two main peaks were observed at 394.7 eV and 396.2 eV. Considering that the peak attributable to BeN bond was observed in the B1s spectra shown in Fig. 3a, the peak assigned to the nitrogen anions bonding to boron should be observed. In the N1 s spectra of Li3N, the peak attributable to N3− was observed at 393 eV (Fig. 3c). In addition, the binding energies for the bridging nitrogen of Nd (–N=) and Nt (–N <) are reported to be at 397.0 eV and 398.6 eV, respectively [24,25]. On the other hand, Lacivita et al. mentioned the presence of apical nitrogen (non-bridging N) and proposed that N 1 s peaks at 397.8 eV and 399.2 eV for LiPON are attributable to N (apical N) and Nd, respectively [26]. Anyway, the two peaks at 394.7 eV and 396.2 eV for the Li3BN2 samples were located at the intermediate binding energy region between the N3− anion and the bridging nitrogen. It is thus suggested that the peak at 394.7 eV is attributable to the non-bridging nitrogen in the BN23− anion, and the other peak is possibly assigned to the nitrogen in the BN23− anion partially affected by oxygen as an impurity. Further structural analyses are needed to be done for clarifying the origin of the doublet peaks in N1s spectra observed in this study.

Fig. 4a shows the DTA curve of the Li3BN2 glass. Two exothermic peaks were observed at around 310 °C and 450 °C, which are higher than the crystallization temperature of Li3BO3 glass (240 °C) [11]. The crystallization behavior of the Li3BN2 glass was investigated by heating the glass at the temperatures beyond these exothermic peaks. In the following discussion, crystallized glass samples are referred to as “glassceramics”. Fig. 4b describes the XRD patterns of the Li3BN2 glass ceramics heat-treated at 400 °C and 500 °C. The pattern of the Li BN glass-ceramics heated at 400 °C was not assigned to any reported crystalline structures. A new thermodynamically metastable crystalline phase (unknown phase) is obtained. Metastable phases are often discovered when glass is heated above the crystallization temperature [14,27]. By heating the glass at 500 °C, the pattern attributable to bodycentered tetragonal Li3BN2 [28] and new unknown peaks, which would be indexed to monoclinic Li3BN2 (β-Li3BN2) [29], appeared. The exothermic peak at around 450 °C can be assigned to the phase transition from the unknown phase to these two crystalline phases.

To investigate the ductility of the Li3BN2 electrolyte, green compacts of the glass and crystal powders were prepared. Fig. 5 shows the cross-sectional SEM images of the Li3BN2 glass (cold-pressed and hotpressed) and the crystal (cold-pressed) pellets. The Li3BN2 glass was densified simply by pressing at 720 MPa at room temperature (Fig. 5a). The relative density of the powder-compressed pellet was 84%, which is higher than that of the Li3BO3 glass pressed at 720 MPa (79%). In the SEM image of the Li3BN2 crystal pellet (Fig. 5b), cracks and grain boundaries were clearly observed. Room temperature pressure sintering phenomena [10] occurred in the particle boundaries, and obvious grain boundaries observed in the crystalline Li3BN2 pellet were not noted for the glassy Li3BN2 pellets. The difference in the microstructure (amorphous or crystalline matrix) strongly affects the relative density for the compacts. Thus, the Li3BN2 glass has better formability (ductility) than the corresponding crystal. Better ductility of a glass electrolyte is favorable for preparing a dense electrolyte pellet and constructing favorable electrode–electrolyte interfaces in all-solid-state batteries. Glass becomes a supercooled liquid and shows a viscos flow under high pressure above the glass transition temperature. Thus, highly dense pellets can be obtained by hot pressing [30]. As shown in Fig. 5c, a further densified Li3BN2 glass pellet was successfully obtained by hot pressing at 300 °C. The relative density was 95%. The EDX mappings of the hot-pressed Li3BN2 pellet are also shown in Fig. 5c. In the EDX mappings, a signal of nitrogen was entirely detected, while that of oxygen as an impurity was observed especially in voids.

Furthermore, the elastic property of the powder-compressed pellet of the Li3BN2 glass was evaluated. The elastic property is important for solid electrolytes to keep solid-state interfaces even when active materials undergo volume changes during charge–discharge processes [10,31]. The elastic moduli of the Li3BN2 glass are summarized in Table 1. Those of the Li3BO3 glass and Li3PS4 glass are also listed for comparison. These values were evaluated using the hot-pressed glass electrolytes. Young's modulus (E) of the Li3BN2 glass was 51.1 GPa, which was an intermediate value between Li3PS4 sulfide and Li3BO3 oxide. For lithium silicate oxynitride glasses, the elastic modulus was increased with the nitrogen content in oxide glasses because of increasing the glass network connectivity by replacing bridging oxygen with nitrogen [19]. However, the Li3BN2 glass showed lower elastic modulus than the corresponding Li3BO3 oxide glass because nitrogen exists in non-bridging states based on the results from the Raman and XPS analyses.

Conductivity measurements were carried out using the AC impedance method. The Nyquist plots for the cold-pressed and hot-pressed Li3BN2 glasses at 30 °C are shown in Fig. 6. Only one semicircle was observed in both of the Nyquist plots. The capacitance for this semicircle was calculated to be about 10−10 F. The semicircle includes both bulk and grain boundary components, and their separation was difficult. Thus, the conductivity of the electrolytes was calculated from the total resistance calculated from the intersection at the X-axis of the semicircle in the lower frequency region.

Fig. 7 presents the temperature dependence of the conductivities of the Li BN glass electrolytes prepared by cold and hot pressing. Those of the Li3BN2 glass-ceramics heated at 400 °C, Li3BN2 crystal, and Li3BO3 glass are also shown for comparison. The temperature dependence of the conductivities obeyed the Arrhenius equation, and the activation energy for conduction was calculated. The results of the conductivity (at 25 °C and 100 °C) and activation energy are summarized in Table 2. The cold-pressed Li3BN2 glass showed a conductivity of 3.1 × 10−6 S cm−1 (25 °C) and 1.4 × 10−4 S cm−1 (100 °C) and an activation energy of 47 kJ mol−1 . This conductivity is about one order of magnitude higher and the activation energy is lower than those of the Li3BO3 glass electrolyte [11]. Moreover, by further densification by hot pressing, the conductivity increased to 1.3 × 10−5 S cm−1 at 25 °C and the activation energy decreased to 41 kJ mol−1 . It is considered that the conductivity increased and the activation energy decreased because the contribution of the grain boundary resistance decreased. As mentioned in the results of XPS (Fig. 3), the oxide species exist on the surface of the particle as an impurity phase, which would prevent the densification and ionic conduction. Thus, it is expected that removing surface oxygen will further improve the ductility and the conductivity of the cold-pressed pellet.

The Li3BN2 crystal (α-Li3BN2) exhibited a low conductivity of 2.9 × 10−11 S cm−1 at 25 °C. This is consistent with the previous report [21]. Therefore, the conductivity of Li3BN2 greatly increased after amorphization, and the Li3BN2 glass showed five orders of magnitude higher conductivity than the corresponding crystal. Moreover, we examined the crystallization of the Li3BN2 glass with the expectation of further improvement of the conductivity by the crystallization of highly conducting metastable phase [1,14,16,32,33]. Unfortunately, the conductivity of the Li BN glass-ceramics heated at 400 °C was 1.1 × 10−7 S cm−1 at 25 °C, which was lower than that of the Li3BN2 glass. However, it is noted that the Li BN glass-ceramics showed higher conductivity than the Li3BN2 crystal. Thus, the conductivity of the newly developed phase (unknown phase) should be higher than that of α-Li3BN2. The detailed structural analysis was not carried out for the glass-ceramic electrolytes. To understand the crystallization phenomena and the conduction property of the Li3BN2 glass-ceramic electrolytes, further structural analyses should be performed.

context.text: To study the composition and functional groups present in the product powder, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopic measurements were taken on Perkin-Elmer FTIR (model Midac 1000 series) spectrophotometer. Infrared spectra were recorded in the region of 500 cm-1 to 4500 cm-1 with a resolution of 16 cm-1.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were taken by using a Bruker D8 Discover powder diffractometer using Cu-K radiation with a wavelength of 1.54 Å. The instrument was operated at 40 kV with a current of 40 mA. The specimens were scanned between 2θ range of 15° to 70° at a scanning speed of 4°/min.

The nano powders were characterized including their particle size, shape and morphology by using a Jeol JSM 6340F field-emission scanning electron microscope. Thorough analysis of the crystallite size and shape within individual particles was carried out by using a JEOL 2100 transmission electron microscope also equipped with a field emission gun.

context.text: 2Department of Chemical Engineering, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama 36849, USA

Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I. 51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li SiO to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

In this work, Ta-doped LLZO (LLZTO) was synthesized through a co-precipitation method with a low sintering temperature of 1100°C. The effects of a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which is created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder, on the phase stabilization, densification and Li+ conductivity were examined. LiOH was chosen as the additive since it is one of the starting materials.

After drying at 80°C for 24 hours, the powders were cold pressed into pellets (10 mm in diameter and 1–3 mm in thickness) at a pressure of 200 MPa. The pellets were covered with cover powders, placed in a modified alumina crucible (shown in Figure 1b), with an alumina lid and sintered in air with a heating rate of 1°C/min to 1100°C for 1–32 hours. The detailed procedure for the preparation of LLZTO is shown in Figure 1a.

During sintering the pellets were covered with powders to reduce the loss of lithium. Four columns, with four pellets in each column, of samples were sintered at one time. Only the middle two pellets were used as the bottom pellet was in contact with the crucible and the top pellet exhibited different sintering behavior, presumably because the atmosphere was different as it was closer to the air above the cover powder. Two kinds of cover powders were used. One is referred to 15Li, which is the powder after the heat-treatment of 700°C and before the ball milling and with 15 wt% excess LiOH. The other one is referred to 15Li LiOH, which is a mixture of 15Li and 6 wt% LiOH. This mixture was jar milled for 12 hours before the use in sintering. The notches in the crucible were found to be necessary (Figure S1 in Supporting Information) to allow an optimal amount of gas exchange between inside of the crucible and surrounding atmosphere to establish the local gas atmosphere to promote the sintering behavior.

context.text: # Results and Discussion

Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li  LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li  LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li  LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.

A small amount of LiOH in the cover powder (3 wt% LiOH) led to nonuniform shrinkage, while with a cover powders containing 100 wt% LiOH all pellets melted and stuck to the crucible. The LiOH + 15Li mixture (6:94 by weight) cover promoted uniform sintering of pellets and resulted in desirable lithium ion conductivity from LLZTO.

SEM images of fracture cross sections of 30Li and 65Li are shown in Figure 3. After sintering with 15Li cover powder, large pores were observed in Figures 3a–3d. When the cover powder contained LiOH, fewer pores were observed as shown in Figures 3e–3h. The fracture surface of the pellets sintered with 15Li cover powder consisted of smooth rounded surfaces (Figures 3b–3d), but in the sample with 15Li LiOH cover powder, flat surface indicative of brittle or intergranular facture surface were observed (Figures 3f–3h) indicating that the grains are more connected when LiOH was added in the cover powder. These results indicate that LiOH in the cover powder helped with the sintering of LLZTO. An interparticle phase between grains was observed in Figures 3f–3h, which is circled in the figures and found from EDS analysis to contain aluminum as shown in Figure 4.
