Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(R CPE )(R CPE ), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A × Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 × 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li + LiOH, which is 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover.

context.text: LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: # Conclusions

The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: # Abstract:

Ta-doped Li7La3Zr2O12 (Ta-LLZO) is considered as a promising solid electrolyte due to high Li-ion conductivity and good chemical stability against electrode materials. In this work, Ta-LLZO was prepared by a conventional solid-state reaction. Ultrafine powders were obtained by ball-milling to improve the surface activity. Ta-LLZO is sintered in ZrO2 crucibles to avoid introducing Al into the samples. The particle size distribution, phase structure, morphology, ionic conductivity, electronic conductivity, density and electrochemical performance of semi-solid battery were characterized by laser diffraction particle size analyzer, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscope, AC-impedance, DC polarization, Archimedes method and a battery testing system, respectively. The results show that the ball milling to reduce the particle size is an effective way to solve the problem of relatively low density and Li-ion conductivity for Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12. For Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12, the increase of x (0.2  x  0.4) promotes the grain growth and sintering densification, but the increase of x (0.4 < x  0.6) has an adverse effect. Li6.7La3Zr1.7Ta0.3O12 sintered at 1180 °C for 12 h shows the relative density of 92 % and the highest Li-ion conductivity of 1.03×10-3 S/cm at 30 °C with the activation energy of about 0.37 eV, while Li6.6La3Zr1.6Ta0.4O12 sintered at 1180 °C for 12 h shows the highest relative density of 96 % and the Li-ion conductivity of 6.68×10-4 S/cm at 30 °C with the activation energy of about 0.46 eV. The electronic conductivity of Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 is 10-9 S/cm orders of magnitude. The semi-solid battery shows the first discharge capacity of 104.6 mAh/g and 92.5% capacity retention after 20 cycles.
Keywords: Al-free; Ta-LLZO; relative density; Li-ion conductivity; ultrafine powders semi-solid battery

Ga-doped Li7La3Zr2O12 that possesses the high Li-ion conductivity is not considered as a promising solid electrolyte material due to the low mechanical strength [7, 8]. Although Fe-doped LLZO shows Li-ion conductivity as high as 1.38 × 10-3 S/cm [9], the electronic conductivity increases which is harmful to all-solid-state batteries. Furthermore, Fe3+ is easily reduced to Fe when it contacts with lithium metal. Ta [10, 19-26], Nb [10, 11], Te [12], W [13, 14], Sb [15], and Mo [16-18] partial substituted Zr site was reported. Substitution on the Zr site with Ta has attracted great interest. Relative density, an important indicator of ceramic material, determines the level of conductivity. Many special sintering methods such as hot-pressing [19], spark plasma sintering (SPS) [28], oxygen atmosphere [7], and microwave assist [31] have been developed to enhance the relative density. Allen et al. reported that Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 sintered at 1050 °C for 1 h by hot-pressing showed the Li-ion conductivity of 8.7×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 96 % [19]. Thompson et al. reported that Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 sintered at 1050 °C for 1 h by hot-pressing showed the Li-ion conductivity of 8.16×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 97.8 % [27]. Yamada et al. reported that Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 sintered at 1000 °C for 10 min by SPS showed the Li-ion conductivity of 6.9×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 95.5 % [28]. Adding sintering aid is also an effective way to improve the density. Cao et al. reported that Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 with 1 wt% Li3PO4 sintered at 1175 °C for 6 h showed the Li-ion conductivity of 7.2×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 92.7 % [21]. Janani et al. reported that Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 with 1 wt% Li4SiO4 sintered at 1200 °C for 24 h showed the

Li-ion conductivity of 3.7×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 94 % [26]. Tang et al. reported that Li6.5La3Zr1.5Ta0.5O12 with 1.4 wt% B2O3 sintered at 1100 °C for 6 h showed the Li-ion conductivity of 1.86×10-4 S/cm at 25 °C with the relative density of 92.4 % [29]. Ta-LLZO is usually sintered in Al2O3 crucibles, so Al is easily introduced into the sample, which form amorphous phase LiAlO2 at grain boundaries to promote sintering densification process [37-38]. But the amount of amorphous phase LiAlO2 is hard to control.  Literatures have reported Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 with relatively low density and Li-ion conductivity [35]. The reason is that Al is not introduced into the sample. Using ultrafine powders can promote sintering densification process, which may be an effect way to solve the problem of relatively low density for Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 and now has not been reported.

The particle size distributions of Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 powders were characterized by laser diffraction particle size analyzer. To avoid introducing Al into the samples, we adopted ZrO2 crucibles. The influences of Ta contents (x = 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, and 0.6) on the relative density and Li-ion conductivity were investigated. In order to test applicability of Al-free Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 as solid electrolyte in Li-ion batteries, we test the electrochemical performance of semi-solid battery.

To prepare the sol–gel synthesized LLZO powder, Lithium nitrate hydrate (LiNO xH O, 99.999%, Alfa Aesar), Lanthanum nitrate hydrate (La(NO  6H O, 99.9%, Sigma Aldrich), and Zirconium(IV) Propoxide (Zr(OC H  , 70 wt% in 1-Propanol, Sigma Aldrich) were used as gel precursors. First, 1-propanol (anhydrous 99.7%, Sigma Aldrich) used as a diluting solvent was mixed and stirred with LiNO xH O and La(NO  6H O. Zr(OC H  was separately mixed and stirred with acetic acid (1.0 M CH COOH, Fluka) used as a chelating agent and 2-methoxyethanol (2-MOE, CH OCH CH OH, anhydrous 99.8%, Sigma Aldrich) solvent to prevent reactions with moisture. An aluminum element was added as cientific Publishersaluminum oxide (Al O , 20 wt% in isopropanol, Sigma Aldrich) particles with a diameter of 50 nm to the precursor solution before gelation occurs. The precursor solutions were then mixed along with the addition of the aluminum oxide powders. Gelation occurred in approximately 45 min., which was followed by 12 h of ageing to ensure that the reaction was completed. The gel was subsequently dried for 9 h followed by pre-calcination heat treatment at 450 -C in air to remove organics.21 Similar to the solid-state processing, the dried powder was cold pressed into pellets with a diameter of 20 mm using an oil-hydraulic pressing at 10 MPa, and they were sintered at various temperatures ranging from 700 to 1000 -C in a box furnace for 4 h. The detailed experimental procedures for the sol–gel synthesis are summarized in Figure 1. Alumina crucibles were used for the calcination. context.text: # 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The XRD patterns of Li6.4La3Zr1.4M0.6O12 (M=Sb, Ta, Nb) are exhibited in Fig. 2(a) to identify the phase composition. As presented, the positions and relative intensities of diffraction peaks of all samples are similar and consistent with the Li5La3Nb2O12 (PDF45-0109) 34 standard pattern which possesses garnet phase. Furthermore, no other diffraction peaks appear. This suggests that pure c-LLZO doped with Sb or Ta or Nb have obtained. The peaks of samples are narrow and sharp, indicating well sintering. Fig. 2(b) shows the high-angle magnified XRD patterns. It is obvious that the peak at approximate 52.9o gradually shifts to high-angle with the rise of the radius of doping ions. According to the formula of Bragg: 2dsinθ = λ, where d, 2θ and λ represent interplanar spacing, diffraction angle, and diffraction wave respectively, the larger diffraction angle suggest smaller cell parameter. On the other hand, the Al3+ of these samples cannot be detected by ICP-OES, suggesting these samples are not affected by Al3+ from Al2O3 crucible.

context.text: The use of solid electrolytes, rather than currently used organic carbonate liquid solutions, can improve battery safety, so solid electrolytes are considered as replacements for these liquid electrolytes. In last few years, garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows the most promising properties, such as high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity of 3×10-4 S∙cm-1 at 25℃ (1).

Garnet-type LLZO can form tetragonal and cubic phases, and the tetragonal phase has a much lower ionic conductivity (around 1.63×10-6 S∙cm-1) (1, 2). Elemental doping, such as Al, W and Ta (3-5) is an effective method to stabilize the cubic phase. Aluminum in LLZO can originate as contamination from alumina crucible used during the high temperature sintering period (7). Different Al molar concentrations will lead to different garnet-type structures. It is reported that the tetragonal LLZO formed at Al molar concentration between 0.074 and 0.1 (8), while cubic LLZO formed at an amount of 0.24-0.39 mole (9-11).

Garnet-type LLZO can be obtained by different synthesis methods, such as solid-state reaction (1, 12-14), and sol-gel techniques (10, 11, 15, 16). The former involves timeconsuming ball milling and sintering steps, while the latter contains only has one sintering step, which could greatly reduce the loss of lithium ions (1). Therefore this paper focuses on sol-gel method for fabrication of Al doped garnet-type LLZO.

context.text: # Experimental

Aluminum-doped and tantalum-doped LLZO was prepared by co-precipitation method. Powers of LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2∙8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), and Al2O3 (Johnson Matthey, 99.9+%, metals basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67-70%), ammonium hydroxide (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Due to evaporation losses of lithium during heat treatment, 15 wt.% excess of LiOH was added. The process flow is shown in Figure 1. LiOH and La(OH)3 were dissolved in HNO3 and ZrOCl2∙8H2O in deionized water, respectively. Both solutions were mixed and subsequently NH4OH was added. The resultant precipitates were filtered and then ambient dried for 48 hours followed by heat treatment at 700°C in air for 2 hours to remove the organic compounds. The dried powders were cold pressed into 12.5 mm diameter pellets. These pellets with additional unpressed powders under and above were sintered in alumina crucibles at temperatures in the range of 1000-1100°C for 4-16 hours in air, using a heating rate of 120°C/h.

The samples were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Bruker D8 diffractometer with Cu X-ray source. The working current and voltage were 40 mA and 40 kV, respectively. The densities of the sintered pellets were measured at room temperature with the Archimedes method using alcohol as the immersion medium. Morphology characterization was carried out using a JEOL JSM-7000F scanning electron microscope (SEM). Conductivity was analyzed by AC impedance spectroscopy using a frequency response analyzer (Solartron 1260, USA) in the frequency range 0.1 Hz-15 MHz with amplitude of 50 mV. The temperature was ramped from 20°C to 290°C in increments of 30°C and 30 minutes was allowed for temperature equilibration after each temperature change. Silver paste was painted on both sides of the pellets and they were cured at room temperature for 30 minutes to remove the organic binders. Impedance plots were fitted using ZView software.

context.text: In theory, different Li-diffusion pathways are possible,30 but calculations and Li nuclear magnetic resonance suggest a mechanism wherein the 24d Li ions are immobile, and Li migrates by hopping between the octahedral sites in garnets with lithium contents 5 and below.23,44–46 Based on ab initio calculations, Xu et al.47 have proposed two potential pathways of Li-ion migration in the cubic garnets (route A and route B) with lithium contents 45 per formula unit. In route A, the Li-ion migrates via the interstice between neighboring octahedral sites, bypassing their common tetrahedral neighbor as shown in Fig. 2b. In route B, the Li-ion moves through the shared triangular faces (‘‘neck’’) of the octahedral and tetrahedral sites. The Li-ion migration in route A is associated with an activation energy of 0.8 eV and is preferred when Li+ content is lower, such as Li5La3Nb2O12, while route B is associated with an activation energy of 0.26 eV and is preferred in highly Li-stuffed garnets such as Li7LaZr2O12. 19 Such a low-energy barrier explains why LLZO exhibits rather high ionic conductivity.

In 2009, it was reported by Awaka et al.29 that LLZO also adopts a tetragonal structure with space group I41/acd (no. 142) after sintering at a lower temperature of 980 1C. Percival et al.48 also reported a tetragonal structure for a garnet-type Li7La3Sn2O12 if sintered below 750 1C. Later on, it was shown that the tetragonal LLZO phase is the stable structure at room temperature.49 In general, it was suggested that partial substitution of LLZO by dopants such as Al3+ from the crucible or intentional doping stabilizes the cubic phase. Tetragonal t-LLZO is a slightly distorted cubic garnet-type structure.29 The lattice parameters reported in the literature are a = 13.07–13.12 and c = 12.67–12.72 Å.29,50–55 In the transition from the cubic to the tetragonal phase (tetragonal distortion), the 24d site in the cubic phase is transformed into fully occupied 8a sites and unoccupied 16e sites while the 96h site in the cubic phase is transformed into two 16f and 32g sites.29,37,56,57

The notable differences of t-LLZO from c-LLZO is the ordering of the Li atoms and occupation of lithium sites.58 The tetragonal distortion dramatically affects lithium distribution and lowers the ionic conductivity by two orders of magnitude at room temperature as shown in Fig. 3.28,29,35,39,40,50–55,57,59,60 The lower lithium-ion conductivity in t-LLZO (bulk conductivity B 1  10-6 S cm-1 )29 vs. c-LLZO (bulk conductivity B 1  10-4 S cm-1 ) 28 has been explained by Awaka et al.29 as suppressed hopping between Li sites by the complete tetrahedral 8a–vacancy ordering, and the decrease in equivalent Li positions in the tetragonal phase compared to the cubic garnet-related phase. Recently, Meier et al.61 have explained the difference in the mechanism of Li-ion conduction in tetragonal and cubic LLZO by first-principles calculations.

context.text: The study found that the motion of Li ions in t-LLZO is entirely collective or synchronous which can be interpreted as a consequence of the ordering within the Li-ion sublattice and the lack of available vacancies. In c-LLZO, the mechanism is an asynchronous type dominated by single-ion jumps and induced collective motion (Fig. 2b).61 The chance of single-ion jumps that can occur at much lower energetic cost than a fully synchronous collective motion of several ions at the same time (in t-LLZO) is increased due to a large number of vacancies and disorder in the Li-ion sublattice of c-LLZO. t-LLZO has a lower ionic conductivity than c-LLZO because the mechanism of synchronous collective motion requires a higher activation energy.61

The low Li-ion conducting tetragonal phase can undergo a phase transition to the high ionic conducting cubic phase at higher temperature. However, the specific temperature for the experimentally observed phase transition varies. Adams and Rao reported a tetragonal-to-cubic phase transition at 177 1C for LLZO based on in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) results32 while Geiger et al., using XRD, reported the transition to occur between 100 and 150 1C.59 Kokal et al.55 showed, using differential scanning calorimetry, that the phase transition temperature is much higher at approximately 700 1C. It is deemed necessary to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature to take advantage of its high ionic conductivity.

A significant amount of work has focused on the inclusion of dopants to stabilize the cubic phase and using various synthesis methods that usually require several calcination steps in the range 750–1230 1C and total synthesis times of over one day.28,36,40,41,59,62–64 A study on the effect of sintering temperature on the structure and ionic conductivity of LLZO found that the cubic structure forms in a temperature range of 1150–1230 1C,40 and that below the sintering temperature of 1150 1C, a tetragonal structure is formed. However, it was not mentioned whether care was taken to avoid aluminum contamination during the preparation. Some were able to retain the cubic phase LLZO at room temperature without the addition of dopants such as Al, but also found that cubic dopant-free LLZO does not exhibit a significant enhancement of ionic conductivity.46,65 Nowadays, doping with ions with ionic radii66 that is close to the host ions is the strategy of choice to promote the stabilization of the cubic LLZO phase at room temperature and to increase ionic conductivity.31,39,58,64,67–78

context.text: # Abstract

Ga-doped Li7La3Zr2O12 (Ga-LLZO) is a promising solid electrolyte because it shows higher Li-ion conductivity than LLZO doped with other cations. In this work, Ga-LLZO was prepared by a conventional solid-state reaction and sintered in ZrO2 crucibles to avoid introducing Al into the samples. The particle size distribution, phase structure, morphology, ionic conductivity, and bulk density of the samples were characterized by laser diffraction particle size analyzer, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM), AC impedance, and Archimedes method, respectively. The effects of sintering temperature and dopant content on Li-ion conductivity and density were investigated. As for Al-free Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12, the Li-ion conductivity and bulk density are improved with the sintering temperature rise. But when the sintering temperature is 1250 °C, the Li-ion conductivity and bulk density decline. As for Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12, the tetragonal phase disappears completely when x ≥ 0.15. The Li-ion conductivity and bulk density of Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 are improved with an increase of x (x ≤ 0.2). The ionic conductivity of Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 sintered in the air by liquid-phase sintering is close to Ga-LLZO sintered in dry O2 atmosphere. Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 sintered at 1200 °C shows the highest Li-ion conductivity of 1.5 × 10−3 S/cm at 30 °C, and the activation energy is about 0.28 eV.
Keywords Al-free . Liquid-phase sintering . Solid electrolyte . Li-ion conductivity . Bulk density

context.text: Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has two polymorphs: a tetragonal phase in the space of I41/acd (142) and a cubic phase in the space of Ia-3d (230) [5–7]. The framework structure of tetragonal phase and cubic phase is composed of LaO8 dodecahedron and ZrO6 octahedral. Li atoms are located in three types of crystallographic positions in tetragonal phase: the tetrahedral site (8 a) and distorted octahedral sites (16 f and 32 g) [8, 9]. The tetragonal phase exhibits an extremely poor Li-ion conductivity because the crystalline symmetry is low and the distribution of Li atoms is in order [4]. Li atoms are located in two types of crystallographic positions in cubic phase: the tetrahedral site (24 d) and distorted octahedral site (96 h) [10]. The Li-ion conductivity of tetragonal phase is lower than that of the cubic phase, but the cubic phase is not stabilized, so it needs to be stabilized by partial cationic substitution [11].

Much work has been done on Al-doped LLZO [12–20]. Appropriate Al3+ substitution increases Li+ vacancies, leading to the improvement of Li-ion conductivity and stability of the cubic phase [12–20]. The crystal-chemical behavior is similar between gallium and aluminum on the basis of the periodic table. Ga-doped LLZO has attracted considerable attention [21–24]. The structure of LLZO doped with Ga3+ or Fe3+ in the space group of I-43d was reported [7, 24]. Li atoms occupy three positions: two tetrahedrally coordinated sites (12 a and 12 b), and an octahedrally coordinated site (48 e) [7, 23, 24]. Wagner et al. reported that the bulk Li-ion conductivity of Fe-LLZO sintered at 1230 °C is 1.38 × 10−3 S/cm at room temperature [7]. Shinawi et al. reported that the Li-ion conductivity of Ga-doped LLZO is 5.4 × 10−4 S/cm [21]. Rettenwander et al. reported that the Li-ion conductivity of LLZO doped with Al3+ and Ga3+ is 1.2 × 10−3 S/cm at room temperature [23]. Ernuy-Lopez et al. reported that the Li-ion conductivity of Ga-LLZO sintered in dry O2 atmosphere is 1.3 × 10−3 S/cm at 24 °C [25]. Janani et al. reported that AlLLZO added with 1 wt% Li4SiO4 formed a Li-Al-Si-O liquid phase during the sintering process, and its Li-ion conductivity is 6.1 × 10−4 S/cm at room temperature [15]. Li Yiqiu et al. reported that Li-Al-O amorphous phase is formed at grain boundaries due to the introduction of Al from Al2O3 crucibles, which promotes the densification due to the formation of liquid phase [26–28]. As for Ga-LLZO, the liquid phase of the Li-Ga-O compounds is also formed during the sintering process [28]. Ga-LLZO sintered in Al2O3 crucibles leads to the introduction of Al into the sample, resulting in the formation of Li-Al-O liquid phase. So, the effects of Ga and Al on Li-ion conductivity and density cannot be clearly distinguished. Literature has reported that Ga-LLZO was sintered in Pt crucibles to avoid the introduction of Al into the samples to research the crystal chemical, but the Li-ion conductivity was not reported [22]. And the formation of Li-Ga-O liquid phase for Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 is closely related to the sintering temperature.

In this work, Ga-LLZO was prepared by a traditional solid-state method. Ultrafine powders were obtained by ball-milling. Ga-LLZO was sintered in ZrO2 crucibles to avoid the introduction of Al into the samples. The effects of sintering temperature and Ga-doping amount on Li-ion conductivity of Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 were investigated.

context.text: # Conclusions

Ga-doped Li7La3Zr2O12 is a promising solid electrolyte material due to the high conductivity. Ga-LLZO was prepared by a traditional solid-state method. Ultrafine powders were obtained by ball-milling. Ga-LLZO was sintered in ZrO2 crucibles to avoid the introduction of Al into the samples. The formation of Li-Ga-O liquid phase is beneficial for the improvement of Li-ion conductivity and bulk density. As for Al-free Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12, the Li-ion conductivity and bulk density are improved with the sintering temperature rise. But when the sintering temperature reaches 1250 °C, the Li-ion conductivity and bulk density decline. As for Al-free Li7- 3xGaxLa3Zr2O12, the tetragonal phase disappears completely when x ≥ 0.15. The Li-ion conductivity and bulk density of Al-free Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 are improved with an increase of x (x ≤ 0.2). The ionic conductivity of Al-free Li7- 3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 sintered in the air by liquid-phase sintering is close to Ga-LLZO sintered in dry O2 atmosphere. Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 sintered at 1200 °C exhibits the highest Li-ion conductivity of 1.5 × 10−3 S/cm at 30 °C, and the activation energy is about 0.28 eV.

context.text: # 2.1 Preparation of Ga-LLZO powders, green pellets and ceramics

Ga-LLZO with nominal composition of Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 was prepared through conventional solid-state reaction [15]. Starting materials (total 0.1mol) of LiOH·H2O (AR, 99%), Ga2O3 (4N), La2O3 (AR, 99%) and ZrO2 (AR, 99%) were weighted at the stoichiometric ratio. The La2O3 powders were heated at 900 °C for 6 h before use to remove volatiles. The mixture is then planetary ball milled with isopropanol at 250 rpm for 12 h, followed by drying at 75 °C and calcined in an Al2O3 crucible at 850 °C for 6 h. The powders were then wet ball milled again at 250 rpm for 12 h, dried and sieved over 200 mesh to obtain a finer powder. Afterward this powder was dry pressed at 90 MPa into green pellets with a diameter of 18 mm. Finally, the pellets were sintered using either single-step or two-step heating schedules in Pt crucibles at a heating and cooling rate of 5 °C/min. The Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 mother powder with 5% excess lithium was lined at the bottom of the Pt crucible to compensate the lithium loss during high temperature sintering.

context.text: # Results and discussion

Various LLZTO tablets were synthesized with 0, 0.5g, 1g and 1.5g Li2CO3 providing the protective atmosphere at 1060°C, 1100°C, and 1140°C in a corundum crucible, respectively. For the sake of convenience, we note the samples synthesized with 0, 0.5g, 1g and 1.5g Li2CO3 as L0, L0.5, L1 and L1.5. TG-DTA was taken to characterize the sintering process and heat treatment process of LLZTO and the result is shown in Fig.2. An endothermic peak at 732°C in the DTA curve of sintering indicates the Li2CO3 melting and decomposing process then a relative mass loss of about 10% happens in the process. As a comparison, the heat treatment of LLZTO has no endothermic peak at 732°C but has one at 1032°C, which is the melting of the eutectic of LiAlO2 and Li5AlO4 19. The TG curve of heat treatment of LLZTO shows that there is only 1% mass loss in the heat treatment of LLZTO pure phase even when it is heated to 1400°C. The result indicates that the garnet phase of LLZTO is stable at high temperature. Therefore, the Li2CO3 just need to
compensate the loss of lithium before the garnet phase is formed.

the same crystal structure of Li7La3Zr2O12 are shown below the patterns. From the Fig.3 (b), it can be seen that all the samples except the L0 have the main phase of LLZTO. However, the L0 sample, which has no Li2CO3 to compensate the Li loss, has the mixed phases of LLZTO and La2Zr2O7. The high intensity of the La2Zr2O7 phase indicates that massive La2Zr2O7 can form easily at a Li-deficient condition during the high temperature sintering process. The TG-DTA curve in Fig.2 shows that there is an exothermic peak at about 732°C, where Li2CO3 melts at this temperature and the process of Li2CO3 discomposing into Li2O will speed up. If Li2CO3 within the LLZTO sample decomposes into Li2O and CO2, and Li2O is easy to volatilize at high temperature. The protective Li2CO3 outside the samples will supply additive lithium source to compensate the loss of Li. In the experiment, the Li2CO3 on the bottle of crucible kept a high Li2O concentration in the atmosphere and thus suppressed the volatilization of Li2O. It is obvious that with the effect of Li2CO3 compensation, samples of L0.5, L1 and L1.5 eliminated the La2Zr2O7 phase and remained LLZTO as the dominant phase. For samples with a larger quantity of Li2CO3 compensation, such as L1 and L1.5 samples, also shows a certain amount of LiAlO2 phase in the patterns. The more the Li2CO3 is, the more LiAlO2 the samples have. Fig.5 (a) is for the L0 sample, and the sample is not dense with a large fraction of pores. Fig.5 (b) is for the L0.5 sample and the samples are much denser than the L0 samples. context.text: The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 2b. All spectra contained peaks for only the cubic garnet phase. The LiOH in the cover powder also helped with the phase stabilization, as 25Li showed the pure cubic garnet phase with the cover of 15Li LiOH but contained pyrochlore phase with the cover of 15Li.

Densification of LLZTO.—The densification results of different samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours are summarized in Table II. Shrinkage did not occur with the cover of 15Li, except for 75Li, which showed nonuniform shrinkage. When the cover was changed to 15Li LiOH, shrinkage was observed for all samples, except for 25Li which showed nonuniform shrinkage. 30Li and 65Li samples have relative densities of 58 and 55% with the cover of 15Li, which is different from Rosero-Navarro group’s work that when 12wt% excess LiOH was added into 10Li sample (22Li using the name convention used in this paper), relative density increased from 50% to 77% with the cover of 10Li.54 The relative densities were all increased to 92% and 90% when the cover powder contained LiOH. The densification of pellets sintered with mother powder of high Li amount was also noticed by another research group.48 As noted above, 75Li showed nonuniform shrinkage after the sintering with the 15Li cover, which indicates that sufficient excess LiOH could help with the densification. However, without LiOH in the cover, the shrinkage of 75Li was nonuniform. Subsequent studies focused on samples with 30 or 65 wt% LiOH as these samples all uniformly shrank after the sintering with the cover of 15Li LiOH.

context.text: # Methods

Synthesis.—NZTO was synthesized via conventional solid-state methods from Na2CO3 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.5%), ZnO (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%) and TeO2 (Sigma Aldrich, 99%). An excess of 10 wt% Na2CO3 was added to compensate for evaporation of Na at elevated temperature. All precursors were ball milled for 30 min and heated to 900°C at a heating rate of 5°C/min for 6 h in an alumina crucible. After calcination, the powder was ball milled for 1 h and cold pressed into 10 mm diameter pellets. The pellets were covered with the mother powder in a capped alumina crucible and re-heated to 900°C for 15 h (heating/cooling rate of 5°C/min). Additionally, quenched and longterm-annealed samples were synthesized for comparison: NZTO (ZQ) was quenched from 900°C to room temperature (RT) in air; long-term annealing of NZTO (ZA7d) was done at 600°C for 7 additional days and cooled to RT at a cooling rate of 5°C/min.
Data collection and analysis.—Initial sample characterization was done by powder X-ray diffraction measurements on a Bruker D8 diffractometer using Cu Kα1 radiation.

context.text: The recently discovered solid electrolyte with a garnet structure and the overall formula of Li7La3Zr2O12 attracted much attention since the first publication [3]. High lithium-ion conductivity combined with the stability in contact with metallic lithium, high decomposition voltage (6 V vs. Li+/Li), easy availability and low const of the initial materials make lithium–lanthanum zirconate Li7La3Zr2O12 promising as a solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries [3‒7]. In this connection, synthesis and study of ion conductivity Li7La3Zr2O12 are of current concern.

At present, different methods of Li7La3Zr2O12 synthesis are published: solid-phase, sol–gel, solid-phase with mechanical preactivation, combined solidphase-liquid, codeposition, sintering, synthesis from molten salts in the LiCl–KCl eutectics) [8–13]. The most widespread methods are high-temperature solidphase sintering of a multicomponent mix of the initial reagents in the form of lanthanum and zirconium oxides and lithium salts and also the sol–gel technique. A fault of the conventional method of solid-phase synthesis of lithium–lanthanum zirconate Li7La3Zr2O12 on the basis of refractory oxides of La2O3 (tmelt \~ 2320°C) and ZrO2 (tmelt \~ 2700°C) and lithium carbonate Li2CO3 is the high sintering temperature (1230°C) for a prolonged period of time and necessity of repeated burden changes to obtain a homogeneous final product. Thus, in [3] the initial powders of La2O3, ZrO2, and LiOH were ground using a ball mill for 12 h to obtain Li7La3Zr2O12; this process was repeated twice after thermal treatment at 900°C and after thermal treatment at 1125°C. The reaction product was compacted into tablets and sintered at 1230°C for 36 h under the mother powder. Ion conductivity (3 × 10–4 S/cm at 25°C) was measured at the example of tablets with the density of 92%. This value of specific ion conductivity of the new lithium–ion conductor of Li7La3Zr2O12 with a garnet structure is higher than the ion conductivity of all the earlier described lithium garnets [3]. However, synthesis of such a structure is related to prolonged conditioning of the lithium–containing material at the high temperature (36 h at 1230°C). The overall synthesis time was more than 90 h. One should point out that the authors obtained the cubic modification by sintering at the high temperature with a considerable conditioning time. Formation of the cubic modification of Li La Zr O was also favored by synthesis of the solid electrolyte in an alumina crucible, as the crucible material interacted with the reaction mixture, which resulted in the uncontrolled doping of Li7La3Zr2O12 by A13+ ions. In the further works, the doping of the solid electrolyte based on lithium and lanthanum zirconate by aluminum oxide was used for stabilization of the high-conductivity cubic modification.

The initial materials of Li2CO3, La2O3 and aqueous solution of ZrO(NO ) were used for synthesis of Li7La3Zr2O12 using the citrate–nitrate technique [9]. These components were dissolved in a mixture of dilute nitric and citric acids. The overall solution was evaporated at 80°C up to transparent gel. At the next stage, the gel was dried and subjected to pyrolysis at \~200°C. Then the powder was sintered at 900°C for 3 h, but the nonconducting impurity phase of La2Zr2O7 was present in the final product. The citrate–nitrate technique allows obtaining a product with a uniform grain size distribution. The faults of this method include a prolonged stage of gel formation and low ion conductivity value. Conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12 synthesized using the citrate–nitrate technique was 5.2 × 10−6 S/cm at 20°C. Conductivity of Li7La3Zr2O12 was measured for tablets with the density of \~70% of the theoretical value after their sintering at 1100°C for 1 h.

context.text: Fig. 5. Complex plane plot of LLZ samples synthesized with different excess amounts of Li2CO3 in the mix: (1) 20% excess of Li2CO3, (2) 30% excess of Li2CO3, (3) 40% excess of Li2CO3.

For measurement of ion conductivity of the synthesized solid electrolyte from a single-phase LLZ powder, cylindrical tables with the diameter of 12 mm and height of \~2 mm were compacted. Tablets were sintered under the mother powder in the following mode: heating to 1050°C at the rate of 10 deg/min, then heating from 1050 to 1150°C at the rate of 2 deg/min, and isothermal conditioning at 1150°C for 5–6 h. After the sintering, the tablet density was measured and graphite electrodes for impedance measurements, alongside with the Au or Ag paste, were applied on their faces. The tablet density was calculated as the result of dividing the sintered sample mass by its volume calculated on the basis of the geometric dimensions of the cylindrical tablet. The size of the prepolished sample was measured using a micrometer to the accuracy of ±0.01 mm and weighed at LV-210A electronic balance to the accuracy of ±0.0005 g. Due to the high porosity of samples, it was not practical to determine the density using the hydrostatic weighing technique. Conductivity measurements were carried out in a screened clamping cell.

To obtain a single-phase sample, the excess of the lithium-containing component (Li2CO3) in the initial mix were varied in order to compensate lithium losses in the course of the high-temperature treatment, as the data presented in the literature are contradictory [7]. It was found on the basis of the XRD data and conductivity measurements for the LLZ synthesized samples that the optimum excess of Li CO is 20%. The Li2CO3 phase in X-ray patterns and therefore high resistance in impedance complex plane plots were registered when Li CO excess above 20% was used (Fig. 5). Using the Li CO excess below <20% did not lead to synthesis of a single-phase product; the La2Zr2O7 impurity phase was present in the X-ray pattern.

context.text: # Experimental

The Li7-3xGaxLa3Zr2O12 samples (x = 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, and 0.3) were prepared by a conventional solid-state method. Stoichiometric amounts of Li2CO3, ZrO2, Ga2O3, and La2O3 were weighted with an excess of 10 wt% Li2CO3 to compensate for the loss of Li2O. The regents were ball-milled under absolute ethyl alcohol for 10 h at a milling speed of 500 rpm/ min, dried at 100 °C for 12 h, cold-pressed into pellets with a diameter of 20 mm at a pressure of 200 MPa for 5 min, and calcined at 850 °C for 6 h in ZrO2 crucibles at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The sintered pellets were ground, ball-milled under absolute ethyl alcohol for 10 h at a milling speed of 500 rpm/ min, dried at 100 °C for 12 h, pressed at 200 MPa into pellets with diameter of 10 mm for 5 min, and sintered at temperatures for 6 h covered with mother powder in ZrO2 crucibles.

context.text: # 2. Experimental

The Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12 (x =0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, and 0.6) samples were prepared by a conventional solid-state method. Stoichiometric amounts of Li2CO3, ZrO2, Ta2O5 and La2O3 were weighted with an excess of 10 wt% Li2CO3 to compensate for the loss of Li, ball-milled under absolute ethyl alcohol at a milling speed of 500 rpm, dried at 100 °C for 12 h, cold-pressed into pellets with diameter of 20 mm at a pressure of 200 MPa for 5 min, and calcined at 900 °C for 12 h in Al2O3 crucibles at a heating rate of 3 °C/min. The sintered pellets were ground, ball-milled under absolute ethyl alcohol at a milling speed of 500 rpm, and dried at 100 °C for 12 h. The particle size distributions of the resulting powders were characterized by a laser diffraction particle size analyzer. The resulting powders were pressed at 200 MPa into pellets with diameter of 10 mm for 5 min, and sintered at 1200 °C for 12 h covered with mother powder in ZrO2 crucibles.

The phase structures and the morphologies of the pellets were examined by a X-ray diffractometer (XRD) using Cu Ka (= 0.154056 nm) radiation in the range of 2 θ angles from 10-70 (°) and a scanning electron microscope (SEM), respectively. The density of the pellet was obtained by an Archimedes method using kerosene for measurement. Silver paste was screen-printed on both sides of the pellet, and calcinated at 850 °C for 10 min. The ionic conductivity of the pellets was measured by AC impedance spectroscopy (AUTOLAB PGSTAT 204) in the frequency range of 100 Hz – 0.2 MHz with an amplitude of 10 mV and in the temperature range from 30 to 70 °C. The electronic conductivity of Ta-LLZO was measured by DC polarization with a DC voltage of 0.1 V, and the current was recorded for 480 s. AC impedance spectroscopy of the semi-solid batteries was measured in a frequency range of 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz with an amplitude of 10 mV. And the performance of charge–discharge for semi-solid batteries was tested on a battery testing system between 2 and 4.2 V at 0.1 C.

context.text: # 2.1 Preparation of Ga-LLZO powders, green pellets and ceramics

Ga-LLZO with nominal composition of Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 was prepared through conventional solid-state reaction [15]. Starting materials (total 0.1mol) of LiOH·H2O (AR, 99%), Ga2O3 (4N), La2O3 (AR, 99%) and ZrO2 (AR, 99%) were weighted at the stoichiometric ratio. The La2O3 powders were heated at 900 °C for 6 h before use to remove volatiles. The mixture is then planetary ball milled with isopropanol at 250 rpm for 12 h, followed by drying at 75 °C and calcined in an Al2O3 crucible at 850 °C for 6 h. The powders were then wet ball milled again at 250 rpm for 12 h, dried and sieved over 200 mesh to obtain a finer powder. Afterward this powder was dry pressed at 90 MPa into green pellets with a diameter of 18 mm. Finally, the pellets were sintered using either single-step or two-step heating schedules in Pt crucibles at a heating and cooling rate of 5 °C/min. The Li6.4Ga0.2La3Zr2O12 mother powder with 5% excess lithium was lined at the bottom of the Pt crucible to compensate the lithium loss during high temperature sintering.

context.text: # Abstract

The garnet-type solid Li-ion conductor, Li6.4La3Zr1.4Ta0.6O12, is viewed as a promising solid state electrolyte for the next generation high performance Li-ion battery because of its high ionic conductivity and stability. The previous researches, in order to avoid Li volatilization loss during solid state reaction of sintering, mother powder with the same composition as green bodies was usually used to cover the samples, it would waste the expensive raw materials and increase the fabrication cost. In this paper, a new method was proposed to prepare the Li6.4La3Zr1.4Ta0.6O12 ceramic solid state electrolyte where the Li loss is compensated by the outside Li2CO3. Samples prepared by this method have pure garnet phase and compact micromorphology with few pores. These samples have a high Li-ion conductivity of 2.9×10-4 S/cm and a low activation energy of 0.37eV at room temperature. The electronic conductivity is 1.08×10-8 S/cm, which can be neglected for solid state electrolyte.

Garnet-type metal oxide such as Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is considered as one of the most promising solid electrolytes among the inorganic solid electrolytes4, for it shows high Li+ ionic conductivity, high stability with lithium metal and wide electrochemical window5. The sintering process6, doping strategy7-9, microstructure10 and composite design11 have been widely investigated to enhance its performance. The LLZO solid electrolyte can be synthesized by solid state reaction12, sol-gel method13, spark plasma sintering14 and hot-press sintering method15. Solid state reaction at high temperature is preferred because the cost is relatively low and the procedure is simple, which is suitable for large-scale industrial producing. The LLZO electrolyte sample prepared by solid state reaction has a moderate ionic conductivity in the order of 10-4 S/cm. Doping various elements into LLZO can increase the Li-ion conductivity and the Ta doped sample, Li7-xLa3Zr2-xTaxO12(x=0.6), has an ionic conductivity of about 1×10-3 S/cm 16, 17. However, because of the high volatility nature of Li element, Li is easy to lose during the high temperature sintering which leads to form the undesirable La2Zr2O7 as an impure phase. In order to prepare the stoichiometric LLZO, the lost Li should be compensated and the most common means is to cover the tablet samples up with the mother powder 18. The mother powder with the same chemistry composition as the samples acts as the sacrificial component to ensure the sample to form the right garnet phase. The amount of the sacrificed mother powder usually reaches the ratio 1:1 in weight to the samples and after sintering, the mother powder cannot be reused. That is the problem, as we know that the mother powder contains the rare earth element La and the element Ta that are expensive. Therefore, the conventional solid state reaction with mother powder protecting method is not economical. We noticed that the effect of the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

mother powder is merely providing another Li source to compensate the lost Li. We proposed an alternative method to compensate the lost Li where the mother powder is replaced by Li2CO3. In this method, Li2CO3 is separated from the sample and it will melt and decompound above 730ºC. The decomposed Li2CO3 provides a Li2O atmosphere and ensures the sample to form the pure garnet phase. The method is also suitable for other oxide solid electrolytes. Li2CO3 is much cheaper than the mother powder and this method will lower the synthesis cost of LLZO as well as other oxide solid electrolytes, which is important for the large-scale application of the solid state batteries in the future.

context.text: Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: Using a solid-state electrolyte instead of the commonly used organic liquid electrolyte to produce an all-solid-state lithium-ion battery is regarded as one promising way to overcome safety issues, such as flammability and leakage of electrolyte.1–4 A large number of solid-state electrolytes have been reported, such as solid polymer electrolytes using different Li salts of LiClO4, LiBF4, or LiN(CF3SO2)2,5,6 and ceramic electrolytes including perovskite-type titanates (LLTO),7,8 NASICON-type (sodium super ionic conductor) oxide electrolytes,9,10 sulfide-type and garnet-type materials.11 The cubic garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention due to its high chemical stability and high ionic conductivity (8.7 10−4 S/cm at 25°C).12–15

context.text: Besides the cubic structure, garnet-type LLZO can also exist with a tetragonal crystal structure with a Li+ conductivity of around 2 × 10−6 S/cm,16,17 which is two orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of the cubic phase structure. In the cubic crystal structure, Li ions occupy two types of crystallographic sites. A tetrahedral site, Li(1), and a distorted octahedral site, Li(2).16 In the tetragonal phase structure, Li atoms occupy three types of crystallographic sites: a tetrahedral site, Li(1), and two distorted octahedral sites, Li(2) and Li(3).17 The lower conductivity of the tetragonal crystal structure has been attributed to the ordering of Li atoms and Li vacancies in the tetrahedral and octahedral sites, as the tetrahedral or distorted octahedral sites are either full or empty.18 In the cubic phase, however, the Li sub-lattice is disordered, so both types of Li sites are partially occupied and the Li ion vacancies are also not ordered.18–20 In the tetragonal phase, all Li sites are fully occupied (g 1), while a reduced site occupancy of Li(1) site (g 0.94) and Li(2) site (g 0.35) were found in the cubic phase.17,21 Thus, compared to the tetragonal phase, in the cubic phase the larger number of vacancies and the disorder in the Li sub-lattice enable a lower activation energy for Li motion, which enhance the Li-ion conductivity in the cubic phase.22

context.text: The phase stability and the conductivity are affected by the Al incorporation, as the substitution mechanism of one Al atom for three Li atoms leads to a reduction of the Li content and an increase in the Li vacancies.25 Although the stabilization of cubic phase by Al doping could help to obtain high conductivity,12,16,17 an undesired Li5AlO4 phase forming at higher doping levels, has lower Li+ conductivity than LLZO.38,39 In addition, it has been reported that the substitutional Al ions sit in the conductive pathway of Li, lead to lower conductivity.25,40 The substitutional Ta ions occupy Li sites, which will not hinder the Li-ion motion.12 The addition of Al into Ta-doped LLZO has been shown to lead to a decrease in the ionic conductivity from 8.7 × 10−4 S/cm to 3.7 × 10−4 S/cm.12 The conductivity of Al-doped LLZO has been reported as 4 10−4 S/cm, while Ta-doped LLZO could reach 8.7 10−4 S/cm.12,41 In addition to the higher ionic conductivity, Ta-doped LLZO was also found to be stable with lithium metal electrode.34,40 While in Al-doped LLZO, intergranular Li metal was observed to propagate through the grain boundaries.42 Therefore, Ta was chosen as the doping element in this work.

context.text: When the simple method of cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air is used, additives are typically needed to obtain high density, details of which could be found in Table I.51–55 Additions of La2Zr2O7 and Li2O to Ta-doped LLZO and Li4SiO4 to Al-doped LLZO have led to improvements of 6–17% in density which increased conductivity 3–5 times.51–53 Even larger increases in densities have been reported with additions of LiOH, Li3BO3 and LiBO2 to Al- and Nb-doped LLZO, but the conductivities are all smaller than 1 × 10−4 S/cm.51,54,55 Samples with conductivities larger than 1 10−4 S/cm were sintered at temperature above 1100°C or prepared with cold uniaxial pressing.51–53

context.text: LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: Phase stabilization.—The XRD patterns of LLZTO samples sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours covered with the same cover powder of 15Li are shown in Figure 2a. For 25Li sample, with 25 wt% excess LiOH, La2Zr2O7 (pyrochlore) phase was observed in addition to the cubic garnet phase, presumably because of the loss of lithium during sintering. When the excess LiOH was increased to 30 wt% or larger, a pure cubic garnet phase was obtained. Even when the excess LiOH was increased to 65 and 75 wt%, no peaks related to LiOH were observed for any of the samples, indicating that there was no LiOH left or the remaining amount of LiOH was too small to be detected by XRD.

context.text: An LLZO electrolyte was synthesized by using a solution-based method. The sample formed a Li+ conducting cubic phase without any extrinsic dopants at 900 ◦C. Remarkably, cubic materials were synthesized at 900 ◦C, which is lower than the conventional synthesis temperatures of 1000 - 1200 ◦C range, by using a solution-based method. The synthesized LLZO pellet revealed relatively non-uniform particles as a result of impurities and reduced density. As a result, the total ionic conductivity of LLZO was found to be 1.09 10−6 S/cm.

context.text: The Li-ion compounds Li5La3M2O12 (M = Ta, Nb), with garnet structure, were reported in 1988, and the structure was examined by x-ray diffraction, without knowing the Li distribution, due to limited experimental resolution of Li atoms.[157] However, this system did not attract much attention as a solid electrolyte until 2003, when Thangadurai and Weppner found that it is a good Li-ion conductor with high conductivity and a wide electrochemical window.[158] In contrast to the common perovskite or NASICON solid state electrolyte, the garnet family excludes Li-reducible Ti4+, so it can directly contact Li metal without damage, which has been viewed as its distinguishing advantage.[159] In 2004, Thangadurai and Weppner, together with Adams, used the bond valence sum method to verify the structure, and they minimized the mismatch of the Li-bond valence state as the isosurface to map the conduction pathways visually. It was concluded that Li ions occupy the octahedral sites other than tetrahedral vacancies.[160] The Li-ion occupation pattern is of great importance for understanding the diffusion mechanism but was not located precisely until 2006, by Cussen. It was revealed from neutron powder diffraction data that Li ions occupy both tetrahedral (80%) and octahedral sites (43%), and the latter are responsible for the mobile carriers via a clustering mechanism.[161] NMR results indicate that the Liion distribution depends on the annealing temperature; that is, the high annealing temperature implies that more Li ions can be quenched at the octahedral sites as mobile carriers, which leads to higher ionic conductivity.[162] In 2012, Han and Yusheng Zhao utilized variable-temperature neutron diffraction (HTND), combined with the maximum-entropy method (MEM) for data refining, to estimate the Li nuclear-density distribution and visualize the conduction pathway experimentally for the first time. These results confirm that displacement is directly driven by temperature.[163] More efforts in calculation have gradually elucidated the Li-ion diffusion mechanism; for example, conductivity and distinct mechanisms for different M elements and various Li concentrations,[164] structural phase transition,[165] concerted[166,167] or asynchronous phenomena,[168] point defects,[169] local structure and dynamics performance,[170] often in combination with experimental data. Other efforts focused on enhancing conductivity. Substituting and doping with lower-valence elements, e.g., replacing La by Sr[171] or Ba,[172] replacing M (= Nb, Ta) partly[173] or totally[174] by Zr, can increase Li content and thus improve conductivity. The highest conductivity found was 4 × 10−4 S/cm in Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO),[174] the most attractive composition so far. LLZO has cubic and tetragonal phases. Cubic phase LLZO has higher conductivity and can be synthesized by doping Al or Ga, or by pulsed laser annealing.[175–179] Cubic phase thin film can be obtained from epitaxial growth[180] or aerosol deposition (AD).[181] The latter method prevents the electrolyte from reacting with the active electrode by avoiding the annealing process, although the obtained electrolyte exhibits extremely low conductivity (1.0 × 10−8 S/cm@140 ◦C) and worse cyclic performance if applied in all-solid-state batteries. Nebulized spray pyrolysis results in a thin-film hybrid of both phases.[182] The disadvantages of LLZO used in sandwich-structure all-solidstate batteries include high interface resistance and poor cyclic stability,[183] both of which can be ameliorated by introducing a thin Nb interlayer between the electrolyte and cathode (LiCoO2).[184]

context.text: Li6.4Gao.2La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) samples were prepared in this study via solid state reaction. The starting materials used were LiCO3 (>99.9%, Aldrich), Ga2O3 (>99.9%, Aldrich), La2O3 (>99.9%, Aldrich) and ZrO2 (>99.9%, Aldrich). The appropriate amount of starting materials were mixed thoroughly in a pestle mortar and then pre-dried at 150 C for 30 mins in an electric vacuum drying oven. The dried mixture was annealed in a tube furnace (GSL-1700X) at 850C for 4h under the flow of dry air to remove any volatile components. The resultant powders were ground thoroughly again in the pestle mortar. Then the annealed powders were loaded into an attrition mill (JM-1L) to achieve a thorough mix and reduce the particle size. The duration for the attrition milling was varied in the range of 8 h - 96 h. Ethanol was used as the solvent and the ratio of materials and balls was 1:3 in this study. And the rotation speed was maintained 600 rpm throughout the milling process. The attrition-milled powders were dried in an electric vacuum drying oven and then thermally treated again in the tube furnace at 850C for 4h under the flow of dry air. At this stage, the obtained powders were ready for the preparation of LLZO pellets. These obtained powders were pressed into a small coin in a 15mm diameter by applying a pressure of 10MPa for 10mins. Finally, the green pellets were sintered in the tube furnace at 1230C for 6h under the flow of dry air. All the sintered pellets were polished and painted with silver paste on both sides for electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) analysis.

context.text: In general, the solid electrolytes that have been studied extensively are mainly composed of sulfides and oxides; Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) is probably one of the most promising candidates to date for use in all-solid-state Liion batteries on account of its excellent chemical and electrochemical stabilities while exhibiting high Li-ion conductivity compared to those of other garnet structure conductors such as Li5La3M2O12 (M = Nb, Ta) [5,11– 13]. LLZO is a garnet-type material that has two stable phases: tetragonal and cubic. Although the tetragonal phase can be obtained at lower synthesis temperatures than the cubic phase, the cubic phase has a bulk conductivity of ∼ 10−3 S/cm compared to ∼ 10−6 S/cm for tetragonal LLZO [14]. For high ionic conductivity, the LLZO solid electrolytes should maintain a stable cubic structure, which usually require several calcination steps and long sintering times at temperatures greater than 1000 - 1200 ◦C [15–17]. However, during this hightemperature thermal process, significant Li loss unavoidably occurs, which often results in a structural collapse of LLZO accompanied by the formation of second phases, thereby reducing the ionic conductivity [18]. Doping with external elements is a well-known method to stabilize the cubic phase at lower temperatures compared to the conventional 1000 - 1200 ◦C range and increase Li+ conductivity by introducing additional Li-ion vacancies, which balance the ionic charge [19–24]. However, doping has the disadvantage of being difficult to control; therefore, finding other ways to stabilize the cubic phase at room temperature is of at most importance.

context.text: In order to obtain LLZO, we prepared the precursor by mixing a nitrate-based sol into a PVP solution. Lithium nitrate (LiNO3, Sigma-Aldrich, 98%), lanthanum(III) nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3 6H2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99%), and zirconium nitrate oxide dihydrate (ZrO(NO3)2·2H2O, KANTO, 99%) were prepared so that the Li:La:Zr ratio was 7:3:2, with 10% excess Li used to compensate for the loss occurring during calcination. The solution was pre-calcined at 350 ◦C for 10 h in air, followed calcination at 900 ◦C for 5 h in air. After calcination, the powders were pressed under 40MPa pressure and sintered at 1180 ◦C for 20 h in air. Thermogravimetry (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the as-prepared precursor were performed in the temperature range from 25 to 1000 ◦C in flowing air. The crystallinity of the sample was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D-5000) in the 2θ range from 10 - 70◦ with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 ˚A). The morphology of the obtained samples was observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Quanta 300) and atomic force microscopy (AFM; Multimode N3-AM). Impedance spectroscopy was carried out at room temperature. Frequencies were varied from 0.1 Hz to 7 MHz, and the alternating current signal had an amplitude of 10 mV. Nyquist plots (Z′ vs Z′′) were drawn and analyzed using the Z-plot and the Zview packages.

context.text: Garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has attracted much attention because it shows promising properties for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. A dense microstructure is needed to obtain a high Li+ conductivity, as porous microstructures result in much lower Li+ conductivities. In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: LLZTO synthesis.—Tantalum-doped Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) was prepared by the co-precipitation method. LiOH (Alfa, anhydrous, 98%), La(OH)3 (Alfa, 99.95% REO), ZrOCl2·8H2O (Alfa, 98%), Ta2O5 (Alfa, 99%, metal basis), nitric acid (Alfa, 67–70%) and NH4OH (Alfa, 5.0N) were used as starting materials. Different amounts of excess LiOH were added during different steps to compensate for the loss of lithium during sintering. All samples in this paper are named as xLi, where x refers to the total amount of excess LiOH. Transparent solutions of LiOH and La(OH)3 in nitric acid, and ZrOCl2·8H2O in deionized water were prepared first. Before mixing these two solutions, Ta2O5 powders were added into the nitric acid solution. After mixing, NH4OH was added to the mixture to obtain precipitates. The precipitates were dried at 80°C for 48 hours and then heated at 700°C under flowing air for 2 hours. The dried powders or the dried powders with additional LiOH were ball milled with zirconia balls in a planetary ball milling machine (Across International, PQN2 gear-drive planetary ball mill) at 500 rpm for 4 hours with 2-propanol as the dispersing reagent.

context.text: Figure 4(a) shows the Nyquist plots obtained from AC impedance spectroscopy analyses of the LLZO pellets. The ratios of the bulk and the grain boundary resistances to the total resistance were determined by fitting the experimental data to the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 4(b). The ionic conductivity of the sample was calculated as follows: σ = (ALR), where L is the length of the pellet, A is the surface area of the pellet, and R is the Ohmic resistance determined from the AC impedance. The bulk, grain boundary and total ionic conductivities determined in this fashion are 2.91 10−5 S/cm, 1.13 10−6 S/cm and 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, respectively. The equivalent circuit was of the form RB/CB+RGB/CGB+Wo, where RB is the bulk resistance, RGB is the grain boundary resistance, and Wo is the Warburg element [5,25]. The calculated total Li+ conductivity of LLZO is 1.09 × 10−6 S/cm, which is higher than that reported by Kokal et al. context.text: Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(R CPE )(R CPE ), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A × Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 × 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li + LiOH, which is 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li  LiOH cover.

context.text: The addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder used to minimize vaporization from the LLZTO pellet during the sintering has been shown to improve densification and increase Li+ conductivity, such that a relative density of 92% and a total Li+ conductivity of 6.9 10−4 S/cm was achieved through a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in air. The 15Li LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary. The increased aluminum content promoted phase stabilization and densification, but the Al-containing phase also limits LLZTO phase continuity. The Li+ conductivity value reached 3.5 10−4 S/cm at a sintering time of 8 hours and did not change significantly between 8 and 32 hours. Further study is needed to determine the role of aluminum and chlorine on the densification and conductivity of LLZTO by using a zirconium salt that does not contain chlorine, using different levels of aluminum by adding Al salt in the co-precipitation process, and sintering with aluminum-free crucibles.

context.text: Presently, the electrolyte of the vast majority of commercial Li-ion batteries utilizes a carbonate-based organic liquid electrolyte. Safety concerns have inspired researchers to investigate alternative solid electrolytes, which may consist of ceramics, polymers, or lithiated oxides, with higher safety margins with respect to shock sensitivity, puncture resistance, or temperature compared to traditional liquid organic electrolytes.[13–16] These electrolytes must transport lithium ions through the medium with high ionic conductivity; however, further development is needed to improve the mobility to reach levels comparable with liquid electrolytes.[17, 18] Currently, garnet LiLaZrO2 (LLZO) and sulfide electrolyte materials are popular candidates.[19, 20] Properties including morphology, crystallinity, grain size, grain boundaries, and porosity play a significant role in dictating the performance of ionic systems.[21] To this end, we selected a series of first-row transition metal oxides (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) synthesized through an evaporative-induced self-assembly method, which gives rise to nanostructured particles with regular porosity and crystallinity,[22] and chemically lithiated them using a simple method. These materials were then pelletized and incorporated into two-electrode cells for electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements.

In this work, tantalum-doped cubic garnet-type Li6.75La3Zr1.75Ta0.25O12 (LLZTO) with a relative density of 92% was prepared by a simple co-precipitation method with cold uniaxial pressing and sintering in a lithium-rich air atmosphere, which was created by the addition of LiOH to the LLZTO cover powder. This LiOH-containing cover powder (15Li + LiOH) has been shown to improve densification and increase the room temperature total conductivity to 6.9 × 10−4 S/cm with an activation energy of 0.2 eV. This 15Li + LiOH cover powder results in the formation of an Al-containing interparticle phase, which facilitates the densification of LLZTO. The aluminum concentration increases during sintering and is located in the grain boundary.

context.text: Room temperature impedance spectra for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with cover powders of 15Li or 15Li LiOH are shown in Figure 5. As shown in the typical Nyquist plot for LLZTO pellets in Figure 5, the spectra were fit to an equivalent circuit of L(RtCPEt)(ReCPEe), where L, R and CPE are the inductor, resistor and the constant phase element, and the subscript t and e refer to the total and electrode contribution, respectively. The inductive contribution is attributed to the wires connected to the sample and is not used for the sample properties. The first semicircle is attributed to the total resistance (Rt). The total conductivity is calculated as σtotal t / (A Rt), where t is the sample thickness and A is the cross-sectional area of the sample. The grain and grain boundary contributions overlapped with each other and cannot be separated, which is consistent with other works.53,56,57 The RT total Li+ conductivity for 30Li and 65Li pellets sintered at 1100°C for 16 hours with 15Li or 15Li LiOH cover powder are tabulated in Table II. The RT total conductivity of 30Li with 15Li cover powders is 2.0 10−5 S/cm. It is significantly lower than that sintered with 15Li LiOH, which is 6.9 10−4 S/cm. Compared to the 30 wt% LiOH samples, samples with higher lithium content (65Li) showed a lower RT σtotal when the cover was 15Li, but similar RT σtotal when the cover contained LiOH. 75Li also showed a similar RT σtotal with 30wt% and 65 wt% LiOH samples when the cover contained LiOH, which indicates that the amount of Li content in the pellets does not affect RT σtotal once it is over 30 wt%. The higher conductivity is consistent with the higher relative density in the samples sintered with 15Li + LiOH cover.

The conventional solid-state method was used to prepare the Li-based garnet-type ceramic materials. As-received, high purity precursor powders including LiNO, (99%, Alfa Aesar), La2O3 (99%, Alfa Aesar), Gd2O3 (99%, Alfa Aesar) and Nb2O5 (99%, Alfa Aesar) were used. LaO3 and GdO3 were dried in a furnace at 900 C for 8h prior to the mixing of the materials. Stoichiometric amounts of the required precursors were used to prepare Gd-doped Lis+2xLa3Nb2-xGdO12 (0  x  0.45). A 10 wt. % excess of Li salt was added to compensate for Li volatilization during the high temperature sintering stages. All syntheses were carried out in alumina crucibles, in air. The powders were mixed with isopropanol in zirconia bowls with zirconia balls, using a ball mill (Pullverisette, Frtisch, Germany) for 6h at 200 min'. The direction of rotation was changed every hour to ensure even mixing. Powders were dried in air, placed in crucibles and heated at 700 C for 6 h. Sintered powders were ball-milled once more under the previously mentioned conditions. After ball-milling, dried powders were pressed into pellets (\~1cm diameter, \~2 cm length) using an iso-static pressure of 200 kN for 5 minutes (isostatic press, P.O Weber). The pellets were covered with some of the powder to help reduce LiO volatilization, then sintered at 900 C for 24 h. Powder was also placed on the bottom of the alumina crucible to minimize Al contamination. A second sintering step (1100 C for 6 h) was used to improve the density of the samples.

The mixture was dried at 105 °C for 3 h. The precursor powders were calcined at 800 °C for 5 h in Ar to obtain the LTO/graphene composite (denoted GLTO-1). The molar ratio of Li:Ti was 4:5 and excess Li (5%)

was added to compensate for Li volatilization during calcination. To explore the effect of graphene on the structure and electrochemical properties of the Li4Ti5O12/graphene composites, LTO/graphene composites with the other two increasing mass percentages of graphene (the content of graphene solution is 16.36 mL and 36.72 mL respectively) were prepared, and the obtained materials were denoted GLTO-2 and GLTO-3, respectively. For comparison, pure LTO was prepared under the same conditions without graphene addition.

Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD, Ultima IV, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu K radiation was used to identify the phase composition of all samples. The diffraction patterns were collected at room temperature by scanning stepwise between 2θ values of 10 to 90° at 0.02° per 10 s. The mass percentage of graphene in the GLTO composites was determined by thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA, STA 449 F3 Jupiter, NETZSCH, Germany) with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 in air from 30 to 750 °C. The material morphology was studied by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU 8020, Hitachi, Japan) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100 plus, JEOL, Japan). The surface composition of the GLTO-2 composite was examined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI5600, Physical Electronics, USA). Raman measurements were conducted on a Raman microscope (RM2000, Renishaw, England) with a 633 nm Ar-ion laser and charge-coupled device detector.

On the other hand, the 900 °C-fired powder contained coarse particles of about 10 μm in addition to several aggregates of primary particles with a size of few micrometer before ball-milling (Fig. S1(d)). The powders were pressed into pellets with a diameter of 10.0 mm, and then isostatically cold pressed under a pressure of 120 MPa. They were sintered in Al2O3 crucibles for 20 h at 1230 °C in air. The LMZxTO ceramics were prepared by solid state reaction technic. The raw materials of Mg(OH)2·4MgCO3·5H2O (>99.5%), Li2CO3(99.9%), Ta2O5(99.9%), and ZnO(99.9%) were weighed according to the stoichiometry of Li3Mg2-xZnxTaO6 (x=0\~0.5). These raw powders were ball milled in alcohol for 7h in nylon jars with zirconia balls. After drying, the mixtures were calcined at 1000ºC for 4h, then reground for 3h, dried and mixed with an 6wt% PVA as a binder. context.text: Fig. 5 The bulk densities and the mass loss of (1 − x)LMTxCT-4 wt% LiF (0.05 ≤x≤ 0.2) ceramics as functions of sintering temperatures and composition x

Figure 6 illustrates the ε values and Q × f values of (1 − x) LMT-xCT-4 wt% LiF (0.05 ≤ x ≤ 0.2) ceramics as function of sintering temperatures and composition x. As shown in Fig. 6a, εr values increased frst and then kept relatively stable with increasing temperature. Obviously, the ε values with sintering temperatures are not consistent with that of bulk densities especially when sintered at 850–1150 °C. The main reason that the ε values have not changed so much like bulk densities was because Li volatilization at elevated sintering temperature, resulted in an increase proportion of CT content. Since ε value of CT (ε \~ 162) is much higher than that of LMT (ε \~ 17.5), so, the ε values of composite ceramics did not decline in the range of 850–1150 °C. The ε values of 4 wt% LiF-doped (1 − x)LMT-xCT composite ceramics increased from 17.9 to 20.1 with increasing x from 0.05 to 0.2 at 850 °C. Furthermore, the interpolation table of Fig. 6a exhibits the measured ε values and calculated ε values of composite ceramics. It is obvious that the variation tendency of the calculated dielectric constant is in accordance with the measured ones. It can be seen in Fig. 6b that the Q × f values changed dramatically with the increase of sintering temperature and the maximum Q × f values were obtained at about 1100 °C for each composition. It should be noted that the Q × f values of the samples sintered around 1100 °C were approximate 4 times higher than those sintered at 850 °C. The increase of Q × f values with the sintering temperature was mainly attributed to grain growth, indicating that the grain size is the dominating factor to control Q × f values in LiF-doped LMT-CaTiO systems [28]. At 850 °C, Q × f values decreased from 32,840 to 21,736 GHz with x increased from 0.05 to 0.2, due to the lower Q × f values of CT than that of LMT.
